In Tobit 12:15, the angel Raphael identifies himself: "I am Raphael, one of the seven holy angels who present the prayers of the saints and enter into the presence of the glory of the Holy One" (LXX: ego eimi Raphael, heis ek ton hepta hagion angelon, hoi prospherousin tas proseuchas ton hagion kai eisporeuontai enopion tes doxes tou hagiou). The parallel is striking: Tobit's seven angels present the prayers of the saints, and the incense angel of Revelation 8:3-4 offers incense with the prayers of the saints. In 1 Enoch 20:1-7, seven archangels are named and their roles described. In the Testament of Levi 8:1-2, seven "men in white clothing" give Levi the priesthood. The tradition of seven principal angels who attend the divine throne and execute divine purposes was widely known in Second Temple Judaism. The author draws on this tradition without explaining it, assuming his audience recognizes the reference.

"Seven trumpets were given to them" (edothesan autois hepta salpigges). The divine passive edothesan ("were given") continues the pattern established throughout the seal sequence (6:2, 4, 8, 11): the instruments of judgment are given by God. The trumpets are not self-appointed but divinely distributed. The seven angels receive their instruments from the authority they serve.
The trumpet (salpigx) carries a dense complex of associations in Israel's tradition:

First, the trumpet of theophany. At Sinai, "the sound of the trumpet grew louder and louder" (Exodus 19:19, LXX: hai phonai tes salpiggos proebainon ischyroterai sphodra). The trumpet accompanied God's descent onto the mountain to establish the covenant. The trumpet is the auditory signature of God's self-revelation.

Second, the trumpet of alarm and warfare. Numbers 10:9: "When you go to war in your land against the adversary who attacks you, then you shall sound an alarm with the trumpets (salpieite tais salpigxin), that you may be remembered before the LORD your God, and be saved from your enemies." Joel 2:1: "Blow a trumpet in Zion, and sound an alarm on my holy mountain! Let all the inhabitants of the land tremble, for the day of the LORD is coming" (LXX: salpisate salpiggi en Sion, keryxate en orei hagio mou). The trumpet sounds the alarm that the Day of the LORD has arrived. The seven trumpets of Revelation 8 are precisely this: the announcement that the Day declared in 6:17 is now being executed.

Third, the trumpets of Jericho. In Joshua 6:4-20, seven priests carried seven trumpets (LXX: hepta salpiggas) before the ark of the covenant. They marched around Jericho for seven days, and on the seventh day marched seven times; when the seven priests blew the seven trumpets, the walls of the city collapsed. The sevenfold trumpet pattern — seven trumpets blown in sequence, bringing the destruction of the enemy's stronghold — provides the closest structural parallel to Revelation's seven trumpet judgments. The fall of Jericho was the paradigmatic event of divine warfare: not human military strategy but the power of God, signaled by trumpets, brought down the walls. The seven trumpets of Revelation replicate this pattern on a cosmic scale.

Fourth, the trumpet of the new year and the Day of Atonement. Leviticus 25:9: "Then you shall sound a trumpet everywhere on the tenth day of the seventh month; on the Day of Atonement you shall sound a trumpet throughout all your land" (LXX: diangeleite salpiggi en pase te ge hymon). The trumpet of the Jubilee announced release, restoration, and the resetting of all debts and claims. The trumpet tradition encompasses both judgment (Jericho, Joel) and restoration (Jubilee). The seven trumpets of Revelation may carry both dimensions: judgment on the unrepentant and the announcement of God's restored order.
div.title: Verses 3-4: The Incense Offering
div.p: "Another angel came and stood at the altar, holding a golden censer; and much incense was given to him, so that he might add it to the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar which was before the throne. And the smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, went up before God out of the angel's hand."

"Another angel" (allos angelos). This angel is distinct from the seven trumpet-bearing angels. The word allos ("another") differentiates this figure: he has a different role. The seven angels hold trumpets; this angel holds a censer. His function is priestly, not military.

"Came and stood at the altar" (elthen kai estathe epi tou thysiasteriou). The altar (thysiastеrion) in the heavenly throne room has already appeared in this document. In 6:9, the souls of the slain were located "underneath the altar" — the altar of burnt offering, where sacrificial blood was poured at the base (Leviticus 4:7). Now the text mentions "the golden altar which was before the throne" (to thysiastеrion to chrysoun to enopion tou thronou, 8:3). In the earthly tabernacle, two altars existed: the bronze altar of burnt offering in the courtyard (Exodus 27:1-8) and the golden altar of incense inside the holy place, positioned before the veil of the Most Holy Place (Exodus 30:1-6). The altar of incense was overlaid with gold (Exodus 30:3, "you shall overlay it with pure gold"), hence "the golden altar." Its position was "before the veil that is near the ark of the testimony, before the mercy seat" (Exodus 30:6) — that is, directly before the place of God's enthroned presence. The golden altar "before the throne" in Revelation 8:3 corresponds to the golden incense altar "before the mercy seat" in the earthly tabernacle. The heavenly temple is the reality of which the earthly tabernacle was the copy.

"Holding a golden censer" (echon libanоton chrysoun). The word libanоtos refers to the vessel used for carrying and burning incense. The adjective chrysoun ("golden") matches the golden altar. In Leviticus 16:12-13, on the Day of Atonement, the high priest was to "take a censer (pyrion, LXX) full of coals of fire from off the altar before the LORD, and two handfuls of sweet incense beaten small, and bring it within the veil and put the incense on the fire before the LORD, that the cloud of the incense may cover the mercy seat." The angel performs the function of the high priest on the Day of Atonement: taking fire from the altar, adding incense, and producing the cloud of fragrant smoke that ascends into God's presence. The heavenly scene replicates the most solemn ritual in Israel's liturgical calendar.

"Much incense was given to him, so that he might add it to the prayers of all the saints" (edothe auto thymiamata polla hina dose tais proseuchais ton hagion panton). The divine passive edothe ("was given") again marks God as the source: God provides the incense. The purpose clause hina dose ("so that he might add/give") specifies the function: the incense is to be added to, or offered alongside, the prayers of all the saints.

The identification of incense with the prayers of the saints was already established in 5:8, where the golden bowls held by the twenty-four elders were "full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints" (gemousas thymiamaton, hai eisin hai proseuchai ton hagion). The connection is drawn from Psalm 141:2 (LXX 140:2): "Let my prayer be set before you as incense (hos thymiama enopion sou), the lifting up of my hands as the evening sacrifice." In the temple, the rising smoke of the incense visually represented the ascent of prayer to God. The angel's action makes this visual: he adds the incense to the prayers so that they rise together before the throne.

The phrase "the prayers of all the saints" (tais proseuchais ton hagion panton) is comprehensive: not some of the saints' prayers but the prayers of all of them. This includes the cry of the martyrs under the altar in 6:9-10 ("How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood?"), the prayers of the persecuted assemblies in chapters 2-3, and the intercessions of every faithful person who has called upon God for justice and deliverance. The incense gathers and amplifies all of these prayers into a single offering presented at the golden altar before the throne.

"The smoke of the incense, with the prayers of the saints, went up before God out of the angel's hand" (anebe ho kapnos ton thymiamaton tais proseuchais ton hagion ek cheiros tou angelou enopion tou theou). The verb anebe ("went up, ascended") describes the upward movement of the smoke. The phrase enopion tou theou ("before God") indicates that the prayers reach their destination: they arrive in the divine presence. The prayers are not lost, not ignored, not dissipated in the cosmos. They ascend as incense-smoke directly before God. The angel's hand (ek cheiros tou angelou) is the instrument of conveyance — the prayers pass through angelic mediation to reach the divine throne.

The image is one of the most important in the entire document for understanding its theology of prayer. The suffering assemblies on earth pray. Their prayers are gathered in golden bowls (5:8). Their martyred members cry "How long?" from under the altar (6:9-10). Now, at the opening of the seventh seal, an angel takes all of these prayers, adds incense to them, and presents them before God. The prayers have been accumulating throughout the seal sequence. The moment of their presentation is the moment that triggers the trumpet judgments.
div.title: Verse 5: The Censer Hurled to Earth
div.p: "Then the angel took the censer and filled it with the fire of the altar, and threw it to the earth; and there followed peals of thunder and sounds and flashes of lightning and an earthquake."

"The angel took the censer and filled it with the fire of the altar" (eilephen ho angelos ton libanоton kai egemisen auton ek tou pyros tou thysiasteriou). The same censer that carried incense upward now carries fire downward. The transition is immediate: the incense ascends (v. 4), and then the censer is filled with fire and hurled to earth (v. 5). The same instrument serves both prayer and judgment. The connection is not accidental but causal: the prayers go up; the fire comes down. The judgment that falls on the earth is the divine response to the prayers that have risen from the saints.

The fire of the altar (to pyr tou thysiasteriou) is the fire that burns on the altar of God's presence — the same fire from which the incense was offered. In the earthly tabernacle, the fire on the altar was to be perpetual: "Fire shall be kept burning continually on the altar; it is not to go out" (Leviticus 6:13, LXX: pyr dia pantos kauthesetai epi to thysiastеrion, ou sbesthesetai). This perpetual fire was the fire of God's own presence, originally kindled by God himself: "Then fire came out from before the LORD and consumed the burnt offering and the portions of fat on the altar" (Leviticus 9:24). The fire the angel hurls to earth is not ordinary fire but the fire of God's altar — divine fire, the fire of his presence and judgment.

The precedent in Ezekiel 10:2 is direct and unmistakable. In Ezekiel's vision, God commanded the man clothed in linen: "Enter between the whirling wheels under the cherubim and fill your hands with coals of fire from between the cherubim and scatter them over the city" (Ezekiel 10:2, LXX: eiselthe eis meson ton trochon ton hypokatо ton Cheroubim kai pleson tas drakas sou anthrakon pyros ek mesou ton Cheroubim kai diaskorpison epi ten polin). The city in Ezekiel was Jerusalem, and the coals of fire scattered over it represented divine judgment on the unfaithful city. The angel of Revelation 8:5 performs Ezekiel's action on a cosmic scale: coals of fire from the heavenly altar are hurled not upon a single city but upon "the earth" (ten gen). What Ezekiel saw done to Jerusalem, the author of Revelation sees done to the world.

"And threw it to the earth" (kai ebalen eis ten gen). The verb ballo ("to throw, to cast, to hurl") is forceful and violent. The casting is not gentle; it is a decisive act of projection from heaven to earth. The direction is downward: from the altar before God's throne to the earth below. The vertical axis of the document — prayers ascending (v. 4), fire descending (v. 5) — makes the exchange explicit. Heaven receives prayer; earth receives judgment.

"There followed peals of thunder and sounds and flashes of lightning and an earthquake" (egenonto brontai kai phonai kai astrapai kai seismos). This fourfold sequence — thunder, sounds/voices, lightning, earthquake — is the signature of theophany in this document. It appeared first in 4:5, where "from the throne come flashes of lightning and sounds and peals of thunder" (ek tou thronou ekporeuontai astrapai kai phonai kai brontai). It will recur with increasing intensity at the seventh trumpet (11:19, with the addition of "great hail") and at the seventh bowl (16:18, with the earthquake described as "such as there had not been since man came to be upon the earth, so great an earthquake"). The sequence escalates through the three judgment cycles: at 4:5, it proceeds from the throne as ambient manifestation; at 8:5, it results from the hurling of the censer; at 11:19 and 16:18, it accompanies the climactic moments of the trumpet and bowl sequences.

The theophanic sequence is drawn from the Sinai event. Exodus 19:16 (LXX): "On the third day when morning came, there were thunders and lightnings (egenonto phonai kai astrapai) and a thick cloud upon the mountain, and the sound of the trumpet exceedingly loud" (phone tes salpinggos echei mega). Exodus 19:18: "Now Mount Sinai was all in smoke because the LORD descended upon it in fire... and the whole mountain quaked violently" (eseisthe de pan to oros sphodra). Thunder, lightning, and earthquake at Sinai accompanied God's descent to establish the covenant. The same phenomena at the seventh seal accompany the transition from the sealed scroll's opening to the trumpet judgments — from revelation to execution. The Sinai theophany is the template: God's self-manifestation in power, accompanied by phenomena that overwhelm human capacity to stand.

The earthquake (seismos) connects to the earthquake at the sixth seal (6:12) and anticipates the earthquakes at the seventh trumpet (11:13) and seventh bowl (16:18). Each occurrence marks a moment of intensified divine intervention, and each successive earthquake is greater than the last.
div.title: Verse 6: Preparation to Sound
div.p: "And the seven angels who had the seven trumpets prepared themselves to sound them."

"Prepared themselves to sound them" (hetoimasan hautous hina salpisosin). The verb hetoimasan ("prepared") from hetoimazo ("to make ready, to prepare") indicates a deliberate, purposeful readiness. The preparation follows the incense offering and the hurling of the censer — the theological groundwork has been laid. The prayers have been presented. The fire has been cast. Now the seven angels make ready to execute the judgments. The sequence is liturgical: preparation precedes action, as in the temple ritual where the priest prepared the incense, offered it, and then the congregation received the result. The trumpet blasts are the result of the heavenly ritual just completed.

The verb salpisosin ("might sound, might trumpet") is from salpizo, the verb specifically used for sounding the trumpet. The seven will sound their trumpets one at a time (8:7, 8, 10, 12; 9:1, 13; 11:15), in sequence, each producing its own distinct judgment. The progression from first to seventh is not simultaneous but serial, each building on the previous.

div.title: Verse 7: The First Trumpet — Hail, Fire, and Blood Strike the Earth
div.p: "The first sounded, and there came hail and fire, mixed with blood, and they were thrown to the earth; and a third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all the green grass was burned up."

"There came hail and fire, mixed with blood" (egeneto chalaza kai pyr memigmena en haimati). The first trumpet produces a combination of hail, fire, and blood that is thrown to the earth (eblethe eis ten gen — divine passive again: "they were thrown," by implication from heaven). The imagery draws directly on the seventh plague of Egypt. Exodus 9:23-24: "The LORD sent thunder and hail, and fire ran down to the earth. And the LORD rained hail on the land of Egypt. So there was hail, and fire flashing continually in the midst of the hail" (LXX: edoken kyrios phonas kai chalazan, kai dietrechen to pyr epi tes ges, kai ebrexen kyrios chalazan epi pasan gen Aigyptou. en de he chalaza kai to pyr phlogidzon en te chalaze). The correspondence is close: hail and fire together, sent from heaven, striking the earth. The Exodus plague struck "all that was in the field through all the land of Egypt, both man and beast; the hail also struck every plant of the field and shattered every tree of the field" (Exodus 9:25).

The addition of blood (haima) intensifies the Exodus allusion. Blood is the defining element of the first Egyptian plague, where the waters of the Nile were turned to blood (Exodus 7:20). The first trumpet combines elements of two Egyptian plagues — the blood of the first and the hail-and-fire of the seventh — into a single judgment. This compression of multiple plagues into a single event signals that the author is not simply retelling the Exodus story but using the Exodus plagues as a typological vocabulary. The plagues of Egypt are the pattern; the trumpet judgments are the cosmic-scale fulfillment.

In Joel 2:30 (LXX 3:3), the Day of the LORD is accompanied by "blood and fire and columns of smoke" (haima kai pyr kai atmida kapnou). The prophet Joel's description of the Day of the LORD uses the same elements — blood and fire — that the first trumpet produces. The first-century hearer, steeped in the prophetic tradition, would recognize both the Exodus plague pattern and the Day of the LORD imagery.

"A third of the earth was burned up, and a third of the trees were burned up, and all the green grass was burned up" (katekaе to triton tes ges, kai to triton ton dendron katekaе, kai pas chortos chloros katekaе). The verb katekaе ("was burned up") from katakaio ("to burn down, to consume with fire") describes total combustion. The fraction "a third" (to triton) governs the earth and the trees: one-third of the land surface and one-third of the trees are consumed. But "all the green grass" (pas chortos chloros) is burned — no fraction limits this element. The distinction may reflect the relative vulnerability of grass versus trees: grass burns completely and quickly in a fire, while trees, being larger and more resistant, survive in greater proportion.

The escalation from the seals is evident. The fourth seal gave Death authority over "a fourth of the earth" (6:8). Now a third is struck. The fraction has increased. The progression is deliberate: each cycle of judgment intensifies from the previous.

The mention of trees (dendra) and green grass (chortos chloros) connects to 7:1-3, where the four angels were told: "Do not harm the earth or the sea or the trees" (me adikesete ten gen mete ten thalassan mete ta dendra). The protection was temporary — "until we have sealed the bond-servants of our God on their foreheads" (7:3). Now that the sealing is complete (7:4-8), the restraint is partially lifted. The earth and trees are harmed, but only by one-third. The judgment is real but still restrained. The word chloros ("green") is the same word used for the pale/green horse of the fourth seal (6:8, hippos chloros). There, chloros described the color of death; here, it describes living vegetation. The same word bridges death and life across the two judgment sequences.

div.title: Verses 8-9: The Second Trumpet — The Burning Mountain and the Sea
div.p: "The second angel sounded, and something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea; and a third of the sea became blood, and a third of the creatures which were in the sea and had life, died; and a third of the ships were destroyed."

"Something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea" (hos oros mega pyri kaiomenon eblethe eis ten thalassan). The phrase hos oros mega ("something like a great mountain") uses the comparative hos ("like, as, something resembling") to indicate that John is describing what he saw in approximate terms. He did not see an actual mountain; he saw something that resembled a great mountain, burning with fire, hurled into the sea. The divine passive eblethe ("was thrown") again indicates that the agent is God or a heavenly power.

The image of a burning mountain has prophetic precedent. Jeremiah 51:25 (LXX 28:25): "Behold, I am against you, O destroying mountain, declares the LORD, which destroys all the earth; and I will stretch out my hand against you, and roll you down from the crags, and I will make you a burnt mountain" (LXX: eis oros empepremenon). In Jeremiah, the "destroying mountain" is Babylon — the world empire that has devastated the nations. God declares that he will turn it into "a burnt mountain," a volcanic ruin incapable of further destruction. If the first-century audience knew this Jeremiah text, the burning mountain hurled into the sea would evoke the judgment of a great oppressive power, cast down from its exalted position and destroyed.

In 1 Enoch 18:13, Enoch sees "seven stars like great burning mountains" in a place of punishment, and in 1 Enoch 21:3, "a great fire there which burnt and blazed." The image of a burning mountain in apocalyptic literature carries connotations of divine judgment upon powers that have exalted themselves beyond their proper station.

"A third of the sea became blood" (egeneto to triton tes thalasses haima). The turning of water to blood directly echoes the first Egyptian plague. Exodus 7:20-21: "All the water that was in the Nile was turned to blood. The fish that were in the Nile died, and the Nile became foul, so that the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile." The first plague struck the Nile; the second trumpet strikes "the sea" (ten thalassan). The scope expands: from river to ocean. But the judgment remains partial: only a third becomes blood.

"A third of the creatures which were in the sea and had life, died" (apethane to triton ton ktismaton ton en te thalasse ta echonta psychas). The phrase ta echonta psychas ("those having life/souls") distinguishes living creatures from inanimate features of the sea. The word psyche ("life, soul") is the same word used for the "souls" under the altar in 6:9. The sea creatures that possess life die by the third. The death of sea life echoes the Egyptian plague: "The fish that were in the Nile died" (Exodus 7:21). The connection is maintained: what God did to Egypt's waters, he now does to the world's seas, in measured proportion.

"A third of the ships were destroyed" (to triton ton ploion diephthare). The destruction of ships adds a dimension absent from the Exodus plague narrative. Ships represent commerce, trade, and economic life — the maritime infrastructure on which the Mediterranean world depended. The destruction of a third of the ships suggests economic devastation accompanying the ecological catastrophe. In 18:17-19, at the fall of "Babylon the great," the shipmasters and sailors will mourn: "for in one hour such great wealth has been laid waste!" and they will cast dust on their heads, weeping, because "all who had ships at sea grew rich by her wealth." The destruction of ships in the second trumpet foreshadows the total economic collapse that will accompany Babylon's fall. The author is connecting ecological judgment to economic consequence: the disruption of the sea disrupts the commerce that depends on it.

div.title: Verses 10-11: The Third Trumpet — The Star Called Wormwood
div.p: "The third angel sounded, and a great star fell from heaven, burning like a torch, and it fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of waters. The name of the star is called Wormwood; and a third of the waters became wormwood, and many men died from the waters, because they were made bitter."

"A great star fell from heaven, burning like a torch" (epesen ek tou ouranou aster megas kaiomenos hos lampas). The star (aster) is described as "great" (megas) and "burning like a torch" (kaiomenos hos lampas). The word lampas ("torch, lamp") connects to 4:5, where the "seven lamps of fire burning before the throne" (hepta lampades pyros kaiomenai enopion tou thronou) were identified as the seven spirits of God. A burning torch is an image of intense, focused light. The star falls from heaven (ek tou ouranou) — its origin is the heavenly realm, and its descent to earth is part of the judgment sequence initiated from the throne.

Stars in prophetic and apocalyptic literature frequently represent spiritual or angelic beings. In Isaiah 14:12, the king of Babylon is addressed: "How you have fallen from heaven, O star of the morning, son of the dawn!" (LXX: pos exepesen ek tou ouranou ho heosphoros ho proi anatellon). In Daniel 8:10, the horn "grew up to the host of heaven and caused some of the host and some of the stars to fall to the earth" (LXX: kai epesen epi ten gen apo ton asteron). In this document, 1:20 identified the "seven stars" in the right hand of the son-of-man figure as "the angels of the seven churches." In 9:1, "a star from heaven which had fallen to the earth" receives the key to the bottomless pit — clearly an angelic or spiritual being, not a literal astronomical object. The "great star" of the third trumpet may represent a spiritual agent of judgment, though the text does not explicitly identify it as such. What is explicit is its function: it poisons the fresh waters.

"It fell on a third of the rivers and on the springs of waters" (epesen epi to triton ton potamon kai epi tas pegas ton hydaton). The first trumpet struck the earth/land; the second struck the sea; the third strikes the fresh waters — rivers (potamoi) and springs (pegai). The progression moves through the domains of the created order: land, salt water, fresh water, and (in the fourth trumpet) the heavens. The fourfold structure echoes the creation narrative of Genesis 1, where God ordered the land, seas, waters, and heavenly bodies. The trumpet judgments systematically strike each domain of creation, as if reversing or undoing the creative work of Genesis 1.

The springs of waters (pegai ton hydaton) are the sources — the headwaters from which rivers flow. Striking the springs contaminates the water at its source, ensuring that the pollution extends downstream through the entire water system. In the promises to the great multitude in 7:17, the Lamb was said to "guide them to springs of the water of life" (pegas hydaton zoes). The springs of life that the Lamb provides for his people stand in contrast to the poisoned springs of the third trumpet. The same word (pegai) describes both: the faithful receive springs of life; the earth receives springs of death.

"The name of the star is called Wormwood" (to onoma tou asteros legetai ho Apsinthos). The word apsinthos ("wormwood") refers to Artemisia absinthium, a plant with an extremely bitter taste, native to the Mediterranean region and the Near East. Wormwood was proverbially associated with bitterness and suffering in Israel's tradition. In Proverbs 5:4, the seductive woman's "end is bitter as wormwood" (LXX: pikroteron cholеs). In Lamentations 3:15, 19: "He has filled me with bitterness (pikria), he has sated me with wormwood (apsinthou)... Remember my affliction and my wandering, the wormwood and the gall (apsinthon kai cholen)."

The primary prophetic background is Jeremiah. In Jeremiah 9:15 (LXX 9:14), the LORD declares judgment on Israel for forsaking his law: "Behold, I will feed them, this people, with wormwood (apsinthon) and give them poisoned water to drink." In Jeremiah 23:15, the same judgment is pronounced against the false prophets: "Behold, I am going to feed them wormwood (apsinthon) and make them drink poisonous water, for from the prophets of Jerusalem pollution has gone forth into all the land." In both texts, wormwood and poisoned water are instruments of divine judgment directed against unfaithfulness and false prophecy. The star called Wormwood in Revelation 8:11 enacts at a cosmic level what Jeremiah declared against Jerusalem and its false prophets: the poisoning of the waters as divine judgment.

"A third of the waters became wormwood, and many men died from the waters, because they were made bitter" (egeneto to triton ton hydaton eis apsinthon, kai polloi ton anthropon apethanon ek ton hydaton, hoti epikranthesan). The verb epikranthesan ("were made bitter") from pikraino ("to make bitter") describes the transformation of drinkable water into water that kills. The fraction "a third" (to triton) governs the waters, but the death toll is described differently: "many men" (polloi ton anthropon), not "a third of mankind." The word polloi ("many") indicates a large but indefinite number. The distinction between the fractional scope (a third of the waters affected) and the human consequence (many deaths) suggests that the devastation, while proportional in its cosmic scope, produces widespread human suffering.

The theological connection to Jeremiah is precise. In Jeremiah, God fed wormwood to his people because they forsook his law and followed Baals (Jeremiah 9:13-14). The wormwood was a consequence of covenant violation — specifically, of idolatry and disobedience. If the author of Revelation is drawing on this tradition (and the verbal correspondence strongly suggests he is), then the poisoning of the waters is not arbitrary suffering but covenantal judgment: the world's waters are embittered because the world has departed from God. The same logic will be explicit in 9:20-21, where the failure to repent from idolatry and wickedness is named as the context for the ongoing judgments.

div.title: Verse 12: The Fourth Trumpet — The Heavenly Bodies Darkened
div.p: "The fourth angel sounded, and a third of the sun and a third of the moon and a third of the stars were struck, so that a third of them would be darkened and the day would not shine for a third of it, and the night in the same way."

"A third of the sun and a third of the moon and a third of the stars were struck" (epleges to triton tou heliou kai to triton tes selenes kai to triton ton asteron). The verb epleges ("was struck") from plesso ("to strike, to smite") describes a blow delivered against the heavenly bodies themselves. The passive voice (divine passive) indicates that the striking agent is God. The fraction "a third" applies to all three categories of heavenly luminaries: sun, moon, and stars. The entire celestial order is affected.

The fourth trumpet completes the progression through the domains of creation: the first trumpet struck the earth (8:7), the second the sea (8:8-9), the third the fresh waters (8:10-11), and the fourth the heavens (8:12). The sequence follows the created order of Genesis 1: land and vegetation (Day 3, Genesis 1:9-13), seas and sea creatures (Day 5, Genesis 1:20-23 — though Revelation reverses the order of seas and waters), water sources, and heavenly luminaries (Day 4, Genesis 1:14-19). The trumpet judgments move through creation domain by domain, as if systematically reversing or undoing the creative ordering of Genesis 1. Creation itself is being struck, its structures partially dismantled. The judgment is not directed only at human beings but at the created order that sustains them.

"So that a third of them would be darkened" (hina skotisthe to triton auton). The verb skotisthe ("might be darkened") from skotizo ("to darken") echoes the ninth plague of Egypt. Exodus 10:21-22: "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be darkness over the land of Egypt, even a darkness which may be felt.' So Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was thick darkness in all the land of Egypt for three days." The ninth plague brought total darkness over Egypt. The fourth trumpet brings partial darkness — one-third of the light is removed. The pattern is consistent: what struck Egypt totally now strikes the world partially. The trumpet judgments are exodus plagues on a cosmic scale but with a fraction that signals restraint.

The prophetic tradition of darkened heavenly bodies as a sign of the Day of the LORD is extensive. Joel 2:10: "The earth quakes, the heavens tremble. The sun and the moon grow dark, and the stars lose their brightness" (LXX: ho helios kai he selene syskotasousin, kai ta astra dysousin to phengos auton). Joel 2:31 (LXX 3:4): "The sun will be turned to darkness and the moon to blood, before the great and terrible day of the LORD comes." Isaiah 13:10: "For the stars of heaven and their constellations will not flash forth their light; the sun will be dark when it rises, and the moon will not shed its light." Amos 8:9: "It will come about in that day, declares the Lord GOD, that I will make the sun go down at noon and make the earth dark in broad daylight." Ezekiel 32:7-8, concerning the fall of Pharaoh: "When I blot you out, I will cover the heavens and make their stars dark; I will cover the sun with a cloud, and the moon shall not give its light. All the bright lights of heaven will I make dark over you and set darkness on your land."

At the sixth seal (6:12-13), the sun became "black as sackcloth" and the moon "like blood" and the stars fell — a total transformation of the heavenly bodies, described in the language of Joel 2:31 and Isaiah 34:4. The fourth trumpet does not repeat the sixth seal's total cosmic collapse but presents a partial diminishing: one-third darkened. The relationship between the sixth seal and the fourth trumpet is not simple chronological sequence but thematic recapitulation at a different register. The seals presented the Day of the LORD as announced; the trumpets present it as executed in stages.

"The day would not shine for a third of it, and the night in the same way" (he hemera me phane to triton autes, kai he nyx homoios). The consequence of the heavenly bodies being struck is a reduction in the duration and intensity of light. A third of the day lacks its normal illumination, and the night similarly loses a third of its light (from moon and stars). The created function of the sun, moon, and stars as established in Genesis 1:14-18 — "to give light upon the earth" and "to govern the day and the night, and to separate the light from the darkness" — is partially impaired. The luminaries still function, but at reduced capacity. The governance of light and darkness established at creation is disrupted but not destroyed.

The restraint of the fraction is again significant. Full darkness was the ninth Egyptian plague — the penultimate plague before the death of the firstborn. In the Exodus sequence, the escalation moved from partial to total judgments, culminating in the Passover itself. The fourth trumpet's partial darkness positions the trumpet sequence at a mid-point of escalation: worse than the seal judgments but not yet the final, unmitigated judgments of the bowls. The trumpets are warnings, escalated from the seals but still leaving room for the response that 9:20-21 will look for and fail to find: repentance.

div.title: Verse 13: The Eagle and the Three Woes
div.p: "Then I looked, and I heard an eagle flying in midheaven, saying with a loud voice, 'Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the remaining blasts of the trumpet of the three angels who are about to sound!'"

"An eagle flying in midheaven" (henos aetou petomenou en mesouranеmati). The word aetos ("eagle") denotes the largest and most powerful bird of prey in the Mediterranean world. Some manuscripts read angelos ("angel") rather than aetos ("eagle"), but the reading "eagle" is better attested and more consistent with the document's visionary style, which uses animals as agents of communication (the four living creatures of 4:6-8 include one "like a flying eagle," homoion aeto petomeno, 4:7). The eagle is not an angel disguised as a bird but a visionary creature performing a herald's function.

The eagle flies "in midheaven" (en mesouranеmati) — the zenith, the highest point of the sky, directly overhead, where it would be visible and audible to everyone on earth below. The word mesouranеma ("midheaven, zenith") appears in this document in 14:6, where "another angel flying in midheaven" proclaims "an eternal gospel," and in 19:17, where an angel standing "in the sun" calls the birds to the great supper of God. The position of midheaven indicates universal visibility: the eagle's message is for all the earth to hear.

The eagle in Israel's prophetic tradition carries associations of both divine protection and divine judgment. In Exodus 19:4, God told Israel: "You yourselves have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and how I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to myself." Deuteronomy 32:11: "Like an eagle that stirs up its nest, that hovers over its young, he spread his wings and caught them, he carried them on his pinions." These are images of protection. But the eagle also functions as an agent of judgment. In Deuteronomy 28:49: "The LORD will bring a nation against you from afar, from the end of the earth, as the eagle swoops down" (LXX: hos horma aetos). In Hosea 8:1: "Put the trumpet to your lips! Like an eagle over the house of the LORD, because they have transgressed my covenant and rebelled against my law" (LXX: eis kolpon auton hos ge, hos aetos ep' oikon kyriou). In Habakkuk 1:8, the Chaldean horses are "swifter than eagles" (LXX: hyperarousi hyper aetous). The eagle's appearance in Revelation 8:13, announcing woe, operates in this judgment tradition: the eagle is the herald of coming devastation.

"Woe, woe, woe" (ouai, ouai, ouai). The threefold ouai ("woe") is an intensified form of the prophetic woe-oracle. The single ouai appears frequently in the prophetic tradition as a cry of distress and judgment. Isaiah 5:8-23 contains six woe-oracles (ouai hoi...) against specific forms of wickedness. Amos 5:18: "Woe to you who desire the day of the LORD!" (ouai hoi epithymountes ten hemeran kyriou). Habakkuk 2:6-19 contains five woe-oracles. The threefold repetition in Revelation 8:13 corresponds to the three remaining trumpets: each "woe" announces one of the three trumpet judgments yet to come. The fifth trumpet is identified as "the first woe" in 9:12; the sixth trumpet is the second woe (11:14); the seventh trumpet brings the third woe (11:14-15). The three woes mark a further intensification within the trumpet sequence itself: the first four trumpets struck the natural order; the final three strike humanity directly and with greater severity.

"To those who dwell on the earth" (tois katoikousin epi tes ges). The phrase "those who dwell on the earth" (hoi katoikountes epi tes ges) has functioned as a near-technical term throughout this document. It appeared in 6:10, where the martyrs under the altar cried for God to avenge their blood "on those who dwell on the earth." It will recur in 11:10 (twice, where the earth-dwellers rejoice over the death of the two witnesses), 13:8 (the earth-dwellers worship the beast), 13:12, 14 (the earth-dwellers are deceived), 14:6, and 17:2, 8. In every occurrence, "those who dwell on the earth" refers not to all humanity indiscriminately but to humanity in its posture of opposition to God — those who have aligned themselves with the world-system that opposes the Lamb and persecutes his witnesses. The eagle's woe is directed at this specific group: those whose earthbound allegiance sets them against the purposes of the throne.

The differentiation is significant. The trumpet judgments do not fall on "all people" without distinction. The sealing of God's servants in 7:1-8 preceded the trumpets precisely to establish a protected group. The earth-dwellers — those without the seal, those whose identity is defined by their attachment to the earth and its powers — are the targets of the three woes. The assemblies of chapters 2-3, insofar as they remain faithful, belong to a different category. But the assemblies that have compromised — Pergamum tolerating Balaam's teaching, Thyatira tolerating Jezebel, Sardis dead though reputed alive, Laodicea lukewarm — are in danger of becoming what the document means by "earth-dwellers." The line between the sealed community and the earth-dwellers is drawn by faithfulness, not by membership or label.

"Because of the remaining blasts of the trumpet of the three angels who are about to sound" (ek ton loipon phonon tes salpiggos ton trion angelon ton mellonton salpizein). The phrase ton mellonton salpizein ("who are about to sound") uses the participle of mello ("to be about to") to indicate imminence: the three remaining trumpets are on the verge of sounding. The eagle's cry is a warning — one final announcement before the most severe judgments arrive. The warning structure is consistent with the document's theology of judgment: judgment is never unannounced. The seals were opened by the Lamb in full view of the heavenly court. The trumpets are preceded by the incense offering and the hurling of the censer. And now, before the final three trumpets, an eagle flies across the sky proclaiming what is coming. God's judgment is not arbitrary, not secret, and not without warning. Even in the midst of devastating plagues, the structure of announcement-then-execution is maintained.

div.title: Summary of the Chapter's Argument

list.item: The seventh seal is both a conclusion and a transition. The seal sequence that began in 6:1 reaches its climax in 8:1, but the climax does not produce a dramatic event. It produces silence. The structure of the document nests the trumpet judgments within the seventh seal: the opening of the final seal does not reveal the scroll's content directly but initiates a new and more intense cycle of judgment through seven trumpets. The nesting structure (seventh seal contains seven trumpets; seventh trumpet will contain seven bowls) creates a literary architecture of escalating depth. Each series reaches its climax by opening into the next series. The effect is one of progressive intensification: the judgments do not proceed in a simple linear sequence but in waves, each more severe than the last.

The silence in heaven is the prophetic silence of anticipation. Drawing on Habakkuk 2:20, Zephaniah 1:7, and Zechariah 2:13, the silence that follows the seventh seal is the hush that falls before God acts. The heavenly realm, defined throughout chapters 4-5 by continuous worship, falls still. The silence is not emptiness but expectation — the entire created order holding its breath. The half-hour duration gives the silence weight without making it permanent. It is a measured pause, long enough to be felt, brief enough to indicate that what follows is imminent. If the heavenly scene corresponds to the temple's incense ritual, the silence is the congregation's silent prayer during the offering of incense — the liturgical stillness that precedes divine action.

The incense scene (8:3-5) is the theological hinge of the chapter and the key to understanding the trumpet judgments. The angel takes the prayers of the saints — prayers that have been accumulating since 5:8 and crying out since 6:9-10 — combines them with incense, and presents them before God at the golden altar. The smoke and prayers ascend. Then the same angel fills the censer with altar-fire and hurls it to the earth, producing the theophanic phenomena of Sinai (thunder, lightning, earthquake). The sequence is causal: prayers go up, fire comes down. The trumpet judgments are the divine answer to the prayers of the saints. The martyrs who asked "How long, O Lord?" are answered by the judgments that follow. The suffering assemblies are not passive victims of a history that ignores them; their prayers are the very mechanism by which divine justice is set in motion. The golden bowls of incense in 5:8, the cry from under the altar in 6:9-10, and the incense offering of 8:3-5 form a single theological arc: the prayers of the suffering faithful ascend to God, and God's response descends as judgment on the earth-dwellers who persecuted them.

The connection to Ezekiel 10 is structural and deliberate. In Ezekiel's vision, a figure clothed in linen was commanded to take coals of fire from between the cherubim and scatter them over Jerusalem (Ezekiel 10:2). The city of Jerusalem, because of its "abominations" (Ezekiel 8-9), received the fire of divine judgment from the heavenly temple. The angel of Revelation 8:5 performs the same action on a universal scale: fire from the heavenly altar is hurled upon "the earth." The pattern of judgment that Ezekiel saw applied to the unfaithful city, the author of Revelation sees applied to the world that has aligned itself against God. The fire is the same fire — altar-fire, divine fire, the fire of God's presence turned from acceptance to judgment.

The four trumpet judgments systematically recapitulate the Exodus plagues on a cosmic scale. The first trumpet (hail and fire mixed with blood) combines the seventh plague (hail and fire, Exodus 9:23-25) with the first plague (blood, Exodus 7:20). The second trumpet (sea turned to blood, sea creatures dying) echoes the first plague applied to the sea rather than the Nile. The third trumpet (waters made bitter) echoes the wormwood and poisoned water of Jeremiah 9:15 and 23:15 — God's declared punishment for forsaking his law — and also inverts the Exodus miracle at Marah, where bitter water was made sweet (Exodus 15:23-25). The fourth trumpet (darkness over a third of the heavenly bodies) echoes the ninth plague (Exodus 10:21-23). The author of Revelation presents the trumpet judgments in the vocabulary of the Exodus: God is doing to the world what he once did to Egypt. The Exodus was the foundational act of divine judgment and liberation in Israel's memory. By casting the trumpet judgments in Exodus plague language, the author declares that a new exodus is underway — a new act of divine judgment against the oppressor and liberation of God's people. The plagues that freed Israel from Pharaoh now fall upon the world-system that oppresses the Lamb's people.

The fraction "one-third" governs the entire chapter and signals that the trumpet judgments are severe but restrained. A third of the earth is burned (8:7), a third of the sea becomes blood (8:8), a third of the sea creatures die (8:9), a third of the ships are destroyed (8:9), a third of the rivers are poisoned (8:10-11), a third of the sun, moon, and stars are darkened (8:12). The insistent repetition of "a third" — the word appears twelve times in the chapter — establishes the trumpet judgments as partial, not total. They are devastating but not final. The escalation from the seals' "one-fourth" (6:8) to the trumpets' "one-third" indicates progressive intensification, but two-thirds remain untouched. The partiality serves a theological purpose that 9:20-21 will make explicit: the judgments are intended to provoke repentance. They are warnings, not the final sentence. The fact that the world does not repent (9:20-21) makes the subsequent total judgments of the bowls (chapters 15-16) the consequence of refused warning.

The four trumpet judgments follow the created order of Genesis 1 in a pattern of de-creation. The first trumpet strikes the earth and vegetation (corresponding to Day 3 of creation, Genesis 1:9-13), the second strikes the sea and its creatures (Day 5, Genesis 1:20-23), the third strikes the fresh waters (the rivers and springs that sustain terrestrial life), and the fourth strikes the heavenly luminaries (Day 4, Genesis 1:14-19). The systematic progression through creation's domains suggests that the trumpet judgments undo or reverse what creation established. The world that God ordered and pronounced "good" is being disordered by judgment. The de-creation theme is consistent with the prophetic tradition: Isaiah 24:1-6 describes the earth "polluted by its inhabitants" and subjected to the LORD's curse, with the result that the earth "mourns and withers" and "the inhabitants of the earth are burned, and few men are left." The de-creation of the trumpet judgments is the consequence of the earth's pollution by those who dwell on it — the same earth-dwellers whom the eagle addresses in verse 13.

The eagle's threefold "woe" (8:13) divides the seven trumpets into two groups: four and three. The first four trumpets strike the natural order — earth, sea, waters, sky — and do not directly target human beings (though human death results from the poisoned waters, 8:11). The final three trumpets, announced as "woes" (ouai), will directly and deliberately target humanity. The division echoes the seal sequence, where the first four seals (the four horsemen) formed a visually unified group, and the fifth, sixth, and seventh seals each introduced a qualitatively different kind of revelation. The structural pattern of 4+3 is characteristic of this document's use of the number seven: seven divides into four and three, each group possessing its own character while both belonging to the single sequence. The eagle's cry at the boundary between the groups serves as a warning and a narrative marker: what has been severe will now become terrible.

The chapter's treatment of "those who dwell on the earth" maintains the document's consistent distinction between God's people and the world-system. The sealing of the 144,000 in chapter 7 preceded the trumpet judgments, establishing a protected community before the blows fell. The eagle's woe is directed specifically at "those who dwell on the earth" — the document's term for humanity aligned against God. The trumpet judgments are not indiscriminate; they are directed. This will become explicit in 9:4, where the locust-plague of the fifth trumpet is told to harm "only the men who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads." The sealed community is not immune to the general effects of ecological devastation (burned vegetation, poisoned water, diminished light affect everyone on earth), but the woes — the targeted judgments of the fifth, sixth, and seventh trumpets — are aimed at the earth-dwellers specifically. The assemblies addressed in chapters 2-3 are warned that their standing depends on faithfulness: those who conquer are sealed; those who compromise risk becoming indistinguishable from the earth-dwellers against whom the woes are directed.

The chapter as a whole presents prayer as the driving force of divine justice. This is not a peripheral observation but the central structural claim of Revelation 8. The silence of verse 1 prepares for the incense offering of verses 3-4. The incense offering presents the saints' accumulated prayers before God. The hurling of the censer in verse 5 transforms the altar of prayer into the source of judgment. The trumpet sequence of verses 7-12 is the content of that judgment. The eagle's cry of verse 13 announces that more is coming. The chapter's architecture — silence, prayer, fire, trumpets, warning — makes the prayers of God's people the mechanism by which the sealed scroll's judgments are executed. The suffering assemblies are not spectators of divine justice; they are participants in it. Their prayers, gathered in golden bowls, presented with incense at the golden altar, and answered with fire from that same altar, are the agency through which God responds to the injustice of the earth-dwellers. The "How long?" of 6:10 is answered not with a shrug but with trumpets. The delay that troubled the martyrs ("rest a little while longer," 6:11) has ended. The prayers have ascended. The fire has fallen. The trumpets are sounding.

div.title: Revelation 9 — First-Century Reading
Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (Revelation 8): Chapter 8 opens with the Lamb breaking the seventh seal, producing "silence in heaven for about half an hour" (8:1). After six seals of escalating intensity — horsemen, martyrs' cries, cosmic upheaval — the seventh seal does not bring a climax but a pause. The silence is the hush of the heavenly court before the next phase of judgment begins. Into this silence, seven angels receive seven trumpets (8:2), and a separate angel stands at the golden altar with a golden censer, offering "much incense" with "the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar which was before the throne" (8:3). The smoke of the incense, mingled with the prayers, rises before God (8:4). Then the angel takes the censer, fills it with fire from the altar, and hurls it to the earth, producing "peals of thunder and sounds and flashes of lightning and an earthquake" (8:5) — the Sinai-theophany formula that recurs at each climactic moment in the document (4:5; 8:5; 11:19; 16:18).

The connection between the prayers and the judgments is structural, not incidental. The prayers of the saints — the same prayers held in golden bowls in 5:8, the same cry of "How long?" from the martyrs under the altar in 6:9-10 — are offered on the golden altar, and then fire from that same altar is cast to the earth, initiating the trumpet sequence. The prayers of the suffering faithful are not unanswered; they are ingredient in the judgments that follow.

The first four trumpets (8:7-12) affect the natural world in an escalating pattern that recapitulates the Egyptian plagues at cosmic scale. The first trumpet brings hail and fire mixed with blood, burning a third of the earth, a third of the trees, and all the green grass (8:7) — echoing the seventh Egyptian plague of hail (Exodus 9:23-25). The second trumpet turns a third of the sea to blood and kills a third of sea creatures (8:8-9) — echoing the first Egyptian plague of the Nile turning to blood (Exodus 7:20-21). The third trumpet poisons a third of the rivers and springs with wormwood (8:10-11) — extending the water-corruption plague to freshwater sources. The fourth trumpet darkens a third of the sun, moon, and stars (8:12) — echoing the ninth Egyptian plague of darkness (Exodus 10:21-23). The fraction "a third" governs every trumpet judgment, an escalation from the "fourth" of the seal judgments (6:8) but still a bounded, partial destruction.

Chapter 8 concludes with a pivotal announcement. An eagle flying in midheaven cries out: "Woe, woe, woe to those who dwell on the earth, because of the remaining blasts of the trumpet of the three angels who are about to sound!" (8:13). The phrase "those who dwell on the earth" (tois katoikousin epi tes ges) is the document's recurring designation for humanity in its God-opposing posture (6:10; 11:10; 13:8, 14; 17:2, 8). The eagle's announcement divides the seven trumpets into two groups: the first four, which strike the natural world (earth, sea, rivers, heavenly bodies), and the final three, which are designated as "woes" — direct afflictions on the earth-dwellers themselves. Chapter 9 contains the first two of these three woes.

What the author argues immediately after (Revelation 10-11:14): Between the sixth and seventh trumpets, just as between the sixth and seventh seals (chapter 7), the author inserts an interlude. In 10:1-11, a "strong angel" (angelon ischyron) descends from heaven wrapped in a cloud, with a rainbow over his head, his face like the sun and his feet like pillars of fire — imagery drawn from the chapter 1 vision and from the theophany traditions. He holds an open small scroll (biblaridion) and plants one foot on the sea and one on land, signifying authority over the entire created order. He cries out with a loud voice, and seven thunders speak, but John is told to seal up what the thunders said and not write it (10:4). The angel then swears by the Creator of heaven, earth, and sea that "there will be no more delay, but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he is about to sound, then the mystery of God is finished, as he announced to his servants the prophets" (10:6-7). John is told to take the scroll and eat it — an action drawn from Ezekiel 2:8-3:3, where the prophet ate the scroll of lamentations, mourning, and woe. The scroll is sweet in John's mouth but bitter in his stomach (10:9-10), and he is commissioned to "prophesy again concerning many peoples and nations and tongues and kings" (10:11).

The interlude continues in 11:1-13 with the measuring of the temple and the account of the two witnesses who prophesy for 1,260 days, are killed by the beast from the abyss (to therion to anabainon ek tes abyssou, 11:7 — the same abyss opened in 9:1-2), lie dead in the street for three and a half days, are raised to life, and ascend to heaven. An earthquake kills a tenth of the city (11:13), and "the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven" (11:13) — a response of acknowledgment, contrasting sharply with the refusal to repent in 9:20-21. Then comes the announcement: "The second woe is past; behold, the third woe is coming quickly" (11:14).

How chapter 9 connects the surrounding argument: Chapter 9 is the direct fulfillment of the eagle's announcement in 8:13. The eagle warned of three woes corresponding to the final three trumpets; chapter 9 delivers the first two. The shift from the first four trumpets to the fifth and sixth is marked by a change in target: the first four trumpets struck the natural world (earth, sea, rivers, heavenly bodies); the fifth and sixth trumpets strike humanity directly. The escalation is deliberate. God's preliminary judgments on the created order (trumpets 1-4) did not produce repentance; now the judgments fall on the earth-dwellers themselves.

The chapter also maintains the unbroken chain of divine authority that has governed the entire sequence from chapter 4 onward. The divine passive edothe ("was given") appears repeatedly: the key was given to the star (9:1), power was given to the locusts (9:3), they were told what they could and could not do (9:4-5), the four angels were released by a command from the golden altar (9:13-14). Every destructive force in this chapter operates under the same authorization that governed the seal judgments: God permits, bounds, and directs the destruction. The chain of authority runs unbroken from the throne through the Lamb through the scroll through the trumpets to the agents of judgment.

The chapter's theological climax comes not in the spectacular visions of locust-scorpions or fire-breathing cavalry but in the two concluding verses (9:20-21), where the survivors of these plagues refuse to repent. The purpose of the intensifying judgments — to provoke recognition of God and abandonment of idolatry — is stated by its failure. The survivors continue worshipping demons and idols "which can neither see nor hear nor walk" (9:20) and do not repent of their murders, sorceries, immorality, or thefts (9:21). This refusal mirrors the pattern of Pharaoh during the Egyptian plagues: despite escalating devastation, the heart remains hardened (Exodus 7:22; 8:15, 19, 32; 9:7, 12, 34-35; 10:20, 27). The recapitulation of the Egyptian plagues in the trumpet judgments is not merely formal but structural: the same pattern of divine judgment met by human obstinacy that characterized the exodus is now operating at cosmic scale.

The connection backward to the prayers of the saints is critical. In 8:3-5, the prayers of the saints were offered on the golden altar, and fire from that altar was hurled to earth. In 9:13, the command to release the four angels comes from the four horns of the golden altar. The same altar that received the prayers now issues the command for judgment. The martyrs' cry of 6:10 — "How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" — is being answered progressively through the trumpet sequence. The judgments of chapter 9 are, in part, the divine response to the prayers of the suffering faithful.

div.title: Verses 1-2: The Fifth Trumpet — The Star and the Abyss
div.p: "Then the fifth angel sounded, and I saw a star from heaven which had fallen to the earth; and the key of the bottomless pit was given to him. He opened the bottomless pit, and smoke went up out of the pit, like the smoke of a great furnace; and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit."

"The fifth angel sounded" (ho pemptos angelos esalpisen). The fifth trumpet continues the sequence begun in 8:7. The first four trumpets were announced in quick succession, each affecting a different domain of the natural world. The fifth trumpet marks the transition to the woe-trumpets announced by the eagle in 8:13. From this point, the targets are no longer trees, seas, rivers, and stars but human beings — specifically, "those who dwell on the earth."

"I saw a star from heaven which had fallen to the earth" (eidon astera ek tou ouranou peptokota eis ten gen). The word peptokota is a perfect active participle of pipto ("to fall"): the star "had fallen" — the fall is already complete when John sees it. This is not a star falling as John watches (as in 8:10, where "a great star fell from heaven," epesen ek tou ouranou) but one that has already descended and now stands on the earth. The masculine pronoun auto ("to him") in the next clause confirms that this "star" is a personal being, not a celestial object. Stars in Israel's scriptures frequently represent angelic beings. In Job 38:7, "the morning stars sang together, and all the sons of God shouted for joy" — the parallelism identifies stars with the heavenly court. In Daniel 8:10, the little horn "grew up to the host of heaven and caused some of the host and some of the stars to fall to the earth." In Isaiah 14:12, the taunt against the king of Babylon employs the image of a fallen celestial figure: "How you have fallen from heaven, O star of the morning, son of the dawn!" (LXX: pos exepesen ek tou ouranou ho heosphoros ho proi anatellon).

Whether this fallen star represents a demonic being, a fallen angel assigned a specific task, or an angelic agent of judgment who has "fallen" only in the sense of descending to earth cannot be determined from the text alone with certainty. What the text does make clear is that this figure acts under divine authority: the key is given to him (edothe auto — the divine passive that governs the entire chapter). The fallen star does not seize the key by force; it is entrusted to him by the same sovereign authority that has governed every action since the Lamb opened the first seal.

"The key of the bottomless pit was given to him" (edothe auto he kleis tou phreatos tes abyssou). The word kleis ("key") appeared in 1:18, where the risen Christ declared: "I have the keys of death and of Hades" (echo tas kleis tou thanatou kai tou hadou). In 3:7, the Philadelphia message identifies the speaker as the one who holds "the key of David; who opens and no one will shut, and who shuts and no one opens" — language drawn from Isaiah 22:22. Keys in this document represent authority over access. The risen Christ holds the ultimate keys; this star receives a specific key for a specific purpose. The authority is derivative, granted, bounded.

The "bottomless pit" (to phrear tes abyssou, literally "the shaft/well of the abyss") introduces a location that will recur at critical points in the document. In 11:7, "the beast that comes up out of the abyss" kills the two witnesses. In 17:8, the beast "is about to come up out of the abyss." In 20:1-3, an angel descends from heaven "holding the key of the abyss" and binds the dragon for a thousand years, throwing him into the abyss, shutting it, and sealing it over him. The abyss functions as a prison for hostile spiritual powers — a place of confinement from which they can emerge only when permitted and to which they will ultimately be returned.

In the LXX, abyssos translates the Hebrew tehom — the primordial deep of Genesis 1:2 ("darkness was over the surface of the deep," epi tes abyssou). In later Jewish literature, the abyss became associated with the place of imprisonment for rebellious spiritual beings. In 1 Enoch 18:11-16 and 21:1-10, fallen angels are confined in a fiery abyss. In Jubilees 5:6-10, the watchers are bound "in the depths of the earth." In Luke 8:31, the demons possessing the Gerasene man "were imploring him not to command them to go away into the abyss" (eis ten abysson). A first-century audience familiar with this tradition would understand the abyss as the holding place for hostile spiritual forces — forces that are confined, not autonomous, and released only by divine decision.

"Smoke went up out of the pit, like the smoke of a great furnace; and the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit" (anebe kapnos ek tou phreatos hos kapnos kaminou megales, kai eskotisthe ho helios kai ho aer ek tou kapnou tou phreatos). The opening of the abyss produces smoke that darkens the sun and the air. The image has multiple scriptural roots.

First, Genesis 19:28: when Abraham looked toward Sodom and Gomorrah after their destruction, "he saw, and behold, the smoke of the land ascended like the smoke of a furnace" (LXX: anebaine he phlox tes ges hosei atmis kaminou). The phrase "like the smoke of a great furnace" (hos kapnos kaminou megales) echoes this image directly. The opening of the abyss produces smoke reminiscent of Sodom's destruction — the smoke of divine judgment on a civilization given over to wickedness.

Second, Exodus 19:18: at Sinai, "the LORD descended upon it in fire; and its smoke ascended like the smoke of a furnace" (anebaine ho kapnos hosei kapnos kaminou). The furnace-smoke image is associated with both judgment (Sodom) and theophany (Sinai). The smoke from the abyss participates in both associations: it is the manifestation of divine judgment and the terrifying effect of God's action in the world.

Third, the darkening of the sun connects to the fourth trumpet (8:12), where a third of the sun was struck, and to the prophetic Day of the LORD language drawn from Joel 2:10: "The sun and the moon grow dark, and the stars lose their brightness." The progressive darkening through the trumpet sequence represents the intensifying withdrawal of created light — the un-making of the first act of creation (Genesis 1:3, "Let there be light").

div.title: Verses 3-6: The Locusts from the Abyss
div.p: "Then out of the smoke came locusts upon the earth, and power was given them, as the scorpions of the earth have power. They were told not to hurt the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree, but only the men who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads. And they were not permitted to kill anyone, but to torment for five months; and their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings a man. And in those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, and death flees from them."

"Out of the smoke came locusts upon the earth" (ek tou kapnou exelthon akrides eis ten gen). The locusts (akrides) emerge from the smoke of the abyss. Locusts are one of the most devastating natural phenomena known in the ancient Near East. A locust swarm could strip a region of all vegetation in hours, leaving famine in its wake. Locusts constituted the eighth plague on Egypt (Exodus 10:1-20), where they "covered the surface of the whole land, so that the land was darkened; and they ate every plant of the land" (Exodus 10:15). The connection to the Egyptian plagues, which has governed the trumpet sequence from the beginning, continues here.

But the most important scriptural background for this locust vision is Joel 1-2. Joel describes a devastating locust invasion as the vehicle of the Day of the LORD. In Joel 1:6, the locusts are described as "a nation" that "has invaded my land, mighty and without number; its teeth are the teeth of a lion, and it has the fangs of a lioness." Joel 2:2-11 describes the locust horde in military terms: "Their appearance is like the appearance of horses; and like war horses, so they run. With a noise as of chariots they leap on the tops of the mountains" (Joel 2:4-5). Joel 2:10: "Before them the earth quakes, the heavens tremble, the sun and the moon grow dark." Most significantly, Joel 2:11 identifies the locusts as God's own army: "The LORD utters his voice before his army; surely his camp is very great, for strong is he who carries out his word." And Joel 2:25 confirms the identification: "My great army which I sent among you." The locust army in Joel is not a random natural disaster but a divine instrument — God's own military force deployed in judgment.

The author of Revelation draws extensively on Joel's locust-army imagery but transforms it. Joel's locusts devour vegetation; these locusts are forbidden from harming vegetation and instead torment humans. Joel's locusts look like horses and chariots; these locusts will be described with an elaborate composite appearance (9:7-10). The transformation signals that the author is working with Joel's imagery at a heightened, symbolic level: these are not natural locusts but spiritual agents of torment that operate within the prophetic framework Joel established.

"Power was given them, as the scorpions of the earth have power" (edothe autais exousia hos echousin exousian hoi skorpioi tes ges). The divine passive edothe ("was given") again marks the source of authority. The locusts' power is not inherent but granted. The comparison to scorpions introduces a new element not present in Joel or Exodus. A scorpion's sting is not immediately lethal to an adult human but produces intense, burning pain — an agony that is debilitating but temporary. The comparison signals the nature of the locusts' weapon: they inflict torment, not death. In Deuteronomy 8:15, the wilderness through which God led Israel is described as containing "fiery serpents and scorpions" — creatures of the desolate, hostile wasteland. In Ezekiel 2:6, God tells the prophet: "Do not be afraid of them or their words, though briers and thorns are with you, and you sit among scorpions." In Luke 10:19, Jesus tells the seventy: "Behold, I have given you authority to tread on serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy." Scorpions represent hostile, painful forces that operate in the domain of darkness and wilderness — appropriate to creatures emerging from the abyss.

"They were told not to hurt the grass of the earth, nor any green thing, nor any tree" (errethe autais hina me adikesousin ton chorton tes ges oude pan chloron oude pan dendron). The verb errethe ("it was said to them, they were told") is a divine passive — the command comes from God, though the speaker is not named. The instruction is remarkable: natural locusts devour vegetation. That is their defining behavior. Joel's locusts stripped the land bare (Joel 1:4, 7). The Egyptian locusts "ate every plant of the land" (Exodus 10:15). But these locusts are specifically prohibited from doing what locusts do. The prohibition separates them decisively from their natural counterparts and confirms that they are symbolic-spiritual agents operating under a commission that inverts the natural locust pattern.

The prohibition also creates a notable tension with 8:7, where the first trumpet burned "a third of the trees" and "all the green grass." The same grass that was burned in the first trumpet is now protected in the fifth. This tension may indicate that the trumpet sequences are not strictly chronological but represent overlapping or recapitulated perspectives on divine judgment — the same reality viewed from different angles. Alternatively, the detail functions within the literary logic of the chapter: the locusts' prohibition against harming vegetation underscores that their sole target is humanity.

The verb adikeo ("to hurt, to harm, to act unjustly toward") appeared in 7:2-3, where the angel with the seal cried out to the four angels: "Do not harm (me adikesete) the earth or the sea or the trees until we have sealed the bond-servants of our God on their foreheads." The same verb now governs the locusts' restrictions. The protection of vegetation and the protection of the sealed are governed by the same divine command structure.

"But only the men who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads" (ei me tous anthropous hoitines ouk echousin ten sphragida tou theou epi ton metopon). The seal (sphragis) of God on the foreheads connects directly to 7:2-8, where 144,000 servants of God were sealed before the trumpet judgments began. The sealing in chapter 7 was not a decorative interlude; it was the necessary precondition for the judgments that follow. The sealed are protected; the unsealed are exposed. The distinction between the sealed and the unsealed mirrors the distinction in the Egyptian plagues between Israel and Egypt. In Exodus 8:22-23 (LXX 8:18-19), God declared: "I will set apart the land of Goshen, where my people are living... I will put a division between my people and your people." In Exodus 9:4: "The LORD will make a distinction between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt." In Exodus 12:13, the blood on the doorposts was the sign that protected Israel's firstborn from the destroyer. The seal of God in Revelation 7 and 9 functions as the new exodus sign: those marked by God are protected through the judgment, not removed from it.

The precedent in Ezekiel is equally precise. In Ezekiel 9:4-6, God commands the man clothed in linen: "Go through the midst of the city, through the midst of Jerusalem, and put a mark (tav, LXX: semeion) on the foreheads of the men who sigh and groan over all the abominations which are being committed in its midst." The destroying angels that follow are told: "Do not touch any man on whom is the mark" (Ezekiel 9:6). The mark on the forehead in Ezekiel protected the righteous from the divine judgment falling on Jerusalem. The seal of God on the foreheads in Revelation serves the identical function: it identifies those who belong to God and protects them from the judgment falling on the earth-dwellers.

"They were not permitted to kill anyone, but to torment for five months" (edothe autois hina me apokteinousin autous, all' hina basanisthesontai menas pente). The divine passive edothe ("it was given to them," here rendered "they were not permitted") again marks divine limitation. The locusts are given a dual restriction: they may not kill, and they may operate only for five months. The judgment is bounded in both intensity and duration.

The five months (menas pente) corresponds to the natural life cycle of locusts in the Mediterranean region. The locust season runs roughly from late spring to early autumn — approximately five months. The author uses the natural time frame of a locust plague to set the duration of this supernatural torment. The specificity reinforces both the locust imagery and the deliberate limitation of the judgment. This is not endless torment but a defined, temporary affliction with a divinely imposed expiration.

The word basanisthesontai ("they will be tormented") is from basanizo ("to torture, to torment, to test by the touchstone"). The basanos was originally a touchstone used to test the purity of metals — the word carries the connotation of testing, examining, proving. In the LXX and first-century usage, it refers to intense suffering and distress. In Matthew 8:29, the demons cry to Jesus: "Have you come here to torment (basanisai) us before the time?" The torment inflicted by the locusts is severe but explicitly non-lethal — it tests and afflicts but does not destroy.

"Their torment was like the torment of a scorpion when it stings a man" (ho basanismos auton hos basanismos skorpiou, hotan paise anthropon). The scorpion sting is intensely painful. In the Mediterranean and Near Eastern world, scorpion stings were a well-known hazard. The pain is sharp, burning, and debilitating, sometimes producing convulsions, but rarely fatal for a healthy adult. The comparison specifies the quality of the torment: acute, agonizing, but not lethal.

"And in those days men will seek death and will not find it; they will long to die, and death flees from them" (zetesousin hoi anthropoi ton thanaton kai ou me heuresousin auton, kai epithymesousin apothanein kai pheugei ho thanatos ap' auton). The torment is so severe that its victims desire death as escape, but death is denied to them. The image inverts the normal human relationship to death: ordinarily, death is feared and fled from; here, death is sought and it is death that flees. The inversion is deliberate and devastating.

The language echoes Job 3:21, where the afflicted man speaks of those "who long for death, but it does not come, and dig for it more than for hidden treasures." It also recalls Jeremiah 8:3: "And death shall be preferred to life by all the remnant that remains of this evil family." In both Job and Jeremiah, the preference for death over life represents the extremity of suffering. But in both, death is merely preferred; here, death is actively sought and actively withheld. The risen Christ holds "the keys of death and of Hades" (1:18). If death flees from these sufferers, it is because the one who controls death's access has decreed that this torment will not be resolved by death. The purpose of the torment is not destruction but affliction — a chastisement that, by its very refusal to allow escape through death, presses the sufferers toward another response. The response the author intends to highlight — repentance — will be addressed explicitly in verses 20-21.

div.title: Verses 7-10: The Appearance of the Locusts
div.p: "The appearance of the locusts was like horses prepared for battle; and on their heads appeared to be crowns like gold, and their faces were like the faces of men. They had hair like the hair of women, and their teeth were like the teeth of lions. They had breastplates like breastplates of iron; and the sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots, of many horses rushing to battle. They have tails like scorpions, and stings; and in their tails is their power to hurt men for five months."

"The appearance of the locusts was like horses prepared for battle" (ta homoiomata ton akridon homoia hippois hetoimasmenois eis polemon). The description opens with the comparison that governs the entire portrait: the locusts look like war horses. This image comes directly from Joel 2:4: "Their appearance is like the appearance of horses; and like war horses, so they run." The connection between locusts and horses was a commonplace in the ancient world. An old Arabic proverb observed that the locust's head resembles a horse's head. But the author goes beyond natural observation to construct a composite creature that combines elements of multiple fearsome realities into a single symbolic figure.

The word hetoimasmenois ("prepared, made ready") is the same word used in 9:15 for the four angels "prepared for the hour and day and month and year." The locusts are not a random swarm but an army equipped and deployed for a specific mission.

"On their heads appeared to be crowns like gold" (epi tas kephalas auton hos stephanoi homoioi chryso). The crowns (stephanoi) are described with double approximation: "appeared to be" (hos, "like, as if") crowns "like gold" (homoioi chryso, "resembling gold"). They are not true gold crowns but the appearance of crowns. The stephanos throughout this document signifies victory and authority: the crowns of the twenty-four elders (4:4, 10), the crown of the first horseman (6:2), the crown of life promised to Smyrna (2:10).
