But these crowns are only "like" gold — they are imitations, parodies of genuine authority. The locusts carry a semblance of royal authority, but it is derivative and counterfeit. This distinguishes them from the genuine crown-bearers in the heavenly court.

"Their faces were like the faces of men" (ta prosopa auton hos prosopa anthropon). The human faces on insect bodies create a disturbing hybrid. The effect is uncanny — these are not mere animals but intelligent agents with human-like awareness. The human face suggests purposefulness, intention, and comprehension. These creatures know what they are doing.

"They had hair like the hair of women" (eichon trichas hos trichas gynaikon). The detail is visually striking and has been interpreted in various ways. Some ancient commentators connected it to the antennae of actual locusts, which can appear hair-like. Others see a connection to the hairstyles of Parthian warriors, who wore their hair long. Within the composite image, the detail adds to the unsettling, boundary-crossing nature of the creatures: they combine the features of horses, men, women, lions, scorpions, and insects into a single being that defies every natural category. The transgression of natural boundaries is itself a mark of their origin — they come from the abyss, not from the created order.

"Their teeth were like the teeth of lions" (hoi odontes auton hos leonton esan). Lion teeth signify tearing, devouring power. Joel 1:6 provides the direct background: "a nation has invaded my land, mighty and without number; its teeth are the teeth of a lion, and it has the fangs of a lioness." Joel described natural locusts in terms of a lion's destructive capacity. The author of Revelation picks up Joel's exact language and incorporates it into the composite portrait.

"They had breastplates like breastplates of iron" (eichon thorakas hos thorakas siderous). The breastplates (thorakas) make the military imagery explicit. Joel 2:7-8 describes the locust army: "They run like mighty men, they climb the wall like soldiers; and they each march in line, nor do they deviate from their paths. They do not crowd each other, they march everyone in his path." Joel portrayed the locusts as disciplined soldiers; the author of Revelation equips them with armor. Iron breastplates signify invulnerability — these creatures cannot be struck down or stopped. In the ancient world, iron was the metal of military might. Daniel 2:40 describes the fourth kingdom as "strong as iron" that "crushes and shatters all things." The iron breastplates make the locusts an unstoppable force.

"The sound of their wings was like the sound of chariots, of many horses rushing to battle" (he phone ton pterygon auton hos phone harmaton hippon pollon trechonton eis polemon). Joel 2:5: "With a noise as of chariots they leap on the tops of the mountains." The connection to Joel continues. The sound of a locust swarm is genuinely terrifying — ancient writers compared it to the roar of an approaching army or a prairie fire. The author draws on this natural observation but amplifies it through Joel's prophetic lens: the sound is of an army charging into battle. The auditory image complements the visual: these creatures look like armored war horses and sound like a cavalry charge.

"They have tails like scorpions, and stings; and in their tails is their power to hurt men for five months" (echousin ouras homoias skorpiois kai kentra, kai en tais ourais auton he exousia auton adikesai tous anthropous menas pente). The scorpion element, introduced in verse 3, is now specified as the tail and sting. The word exousia ("power, authority") is the same word used throughout the document for granted authority (6:8; 9:3; 13:5, 7). Their authority to inflict harm is located specifically in their tails — an unusual detail that will be echoed in the sixth trumpet's cavalry, whose horses also have destructive power in their tails (9:19). The five-month duration is repeated, emphasizing the bounded nature of the judgment.

The composite creature defies literal interpretation and demands symbolic reading. The author is constructing a vision of terrifying spiritual forces through the accumulation of fearsome attributes drawn from the natural and prophetic worlds. No single natural creature is being described. The effect is cumulative: the locust-army of Joel, the destructive teeth of a lion, the intelligence of a human face, the invulnerability of iron armor, the agonizing sting of a scorpion — all combined into a single vision of divinely authorized torment descending on those who lack God's seal.

div.title: Verse 11: The King of the Abyss
div.p: "They have as king over them, the angel of the abyss; his name in Hebrew is Abaddon, and in the Greek he has the name Apollyon."

"They have as king over them, the angel of the abyss" (echousin ep' auton basilea ton angelon tes abyssou). Natural locusts have no king. Proverbs 30:27 makes this explicit: "The locusts have no king, yet all of them go out in ranks." The detail that these locusts have a king confirms once more that they are not natural creatures but a supernatural army under organized command. Their king is "the angel of the abyss" (ton angelon tes abyssou) — an angelic figure whose domain is the same abyss from which the locusts emerged. Whether this angel is the same as the "star" who received the key in verse 1, or a different figure, the text does not specify. The angel's identity is given through his name.

"His name in Hebrew is Abaddon" (onoma auto Hebraisti Abaddon). The Hebrew word Abaddon derives from the root 'abad ("to perish, to destroy, to be lost"). In the Hebrew scriptures, Abaddon functions as a synonym for Sheol — the realm of the dead, the place of destruction. Job 26:6: "Sheol is naked before him, and Abaddon has no covering." Job 28:22: "Abaddon and Death say, 'With our ears we have heard a report of it.'" Job 31:12: "For it would be a fire that consumes to Abaddon." Psalm 88:11 (LXX 87:12): "Will your steadfast love be declared in the grave, your faithfulness in Abaddon?" Proverbs 15:11: "Sheol and Abaddon lie open before the LORD; how much more the hearts of the children of man." Proverbs 27:20: "Sheol and Abaddon are never satisfied." In every occurrence, Abaddon is the place of death, destruction, and the grave — the realm where things perish. By naming the locust king "Abaddon," the author personifies the destroying power of the abyss. The place of destruction has a ruler, and his name is Destruction itself.

"And in the Greek he has the name Apollyon" (kai en te Hellenike onoma echei Apollyon). The Greek name Apollyon means "Destroyer" (from apollymi, "to destroy, to ruin, to kill"). The author provides both the Hebrew and Greek names, a practice that serves two functions. First, it ensures comprehension by both Jewish and Gentile hearers in the assemblies. Second, the Greek name Apollyon carries a phonetic resonance that a first-century audience in the Roman province of Asia would not have missed: Apollyon echoes Apollon — Apollo, the Greek god. Apollo was the patron deity of the emperor Augustus, who claimed Apollo's special protection. The temple of Apollo at Didyma, near Miletus, was one of the most important oracles in Asia Minor — within the immediate geographical sphere of the seven assemblies. Apollo was also associated with plagues (in Homer's Iliad 1.43-53, Apollo sends a plague upon the Greek camp by shooting arrows from his bow) and, paradoxically, with their cure. In some Greek traditions, Apollo bore the epithet Parnopios ("the locust god"), worshipped as a protector against locust plagues.

The author does not make the connection to Apollo explicit. The text does not say "Apollyon is Apollo." But the phonetic echo, combined with the locust imagery and the plague associations, would have been audible to a Greek-speaking audience in Asia Minor. If the hearers registered the resonance, the effect would be devastating: the divine patron of the imperial order is not a heavenly protector but the angel of the abyss, the king of demonic locusts, the Destroyer. The name that the empire reveres belongs, in this vision, to the ruler of the pit.

div.title: Verse 12: The Transition Between Woes
div.p: "The first woe is past; behold, two woes are still coming after these things."

"The first woe is past" (he ouai he mia apelthen). This editorial note connects back to the eagle's announcement of three woes in 8:13. The fifth trumpet constitutes the first woe; the sixth trumpet (9:13-21) will constitute the second. The third woe corresponds to the seventh trumpet (11:14-15), though it is not announced until 11:14, after the interlude of 10:1-11:13. The announcement serves as a structural marker, orienting the audience within the sequence and emphasizing that the worst is yet to come. The word apelthen ("has passed, has gone") uses the same verb used in 21:4 for the former things that "have passed away." The first woe is complete; it has run its course.

"Behold, two woes are still coming after these things" (idou erchontai eti duo ouai meta tauta). The word idou ("behold, look") calls attention to what follows, signaling that the pace of judgment is not slowing but accelerating. The two remaining woes will be more severe than the first, just as the first four trumpets were more severe than the seals and the sixth trumpet will be more severe than the fifth. The trajectory of the document's judgment sequences is one of intensification: from a fourth (seals) to a third (trumpets), from torment without death (fifth trumpet) to the killing of a third of humanity (sixth trumpet).

div.title: Verses 13-15: The Sixth Trumpet — The Four Angels at the Euphrates
div.p: "Then the sixth angel sounded, and I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar which is before God, one saying to the sixth angel who had the trumpet, 'Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates.' And the four angels, who had been prepared for the hour and day and month and year, were released, so that they would kill a third of mankind."

"I heard a voice from the four horns of the golden altar which is before God" (ekousa phonen mian ek ton tessaron keraton tou thysiasteriou tou chrysou tou enopion tou theou). The voice that initiates the sixth trumpet comes from a specific location: the four horns of the golden altar before God. The golden altar (thysiastеrion chrysoun) is the altar of incense, which in the tabernacle and temple stood before the veil of the holy of holies (Exodus 30:1-6). This is the same altar introduced in 8:3, where the angel offered incense "with the prayers of all the saints on the golden altar which was before the throne." The horns of the altar (kerata) were the four projections at the corners of the altar of incense (Exodus 30:2: "You shall make its horns on its four corners; its horns shall be of one piece with it"). In Leviticus 4:7, 18, the priest put blood of the sin offering "on the horns of the altar of fragrant incense" as part of atonement.

The voice issues from the altar where the prayers of the saints were offered and where the fire of judgment was taken (8:3-5). The connection is theologically significant: the judgment announced by this voice is a response to the prayers. The martyrs' cry — "How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood?" (6:10) — was offered on this altar, and now the altar itself issues the command for a new phase of judgment. The prayers of the suffering faithful are being answered.

"Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates" (Lyson tous tessaras angelous tous dedemenous epi to potamo to megalo Euphrate). The command is direct: "Release" (lyson, aorist imperative of lyo, "to loose, to release"). Four angels are held bound (dedemenous, perfect passive participle — they have been bound and remain bound until this moment) at the Euphrates. The binding indicates that these are hostile forces that have been restrained — their destructive capacity has been held in check by divine decree, and only now, at the precise appointed moment, are they let loose. The concept of angels bound and awaiting release has precedent in 1 Enoch 18:14-16 and Jude 6, where angels who transgressed their boundaries are kept "in eternal bonds under darkness for the judgment of the great day."

The "great river Euphrates" (to potamo to megalo Euphrate) is the most geographically and historically charged boundary in Israel's scriptures. In Genesis 15:18, God defined the eastern limit of the promised land: "To your descendants I have given this land, from the river of Egypt as far as the great river, the river Euphrates." In Deuteronomy 1:7 and Joshua 1:4, the Euphrates marks the far eastern boundary. Throughout Israel's history, the great military threats came from beyond the Euphrates: Assyria, which destroyed the northern kingdom in 722 BCE; Babylon, which destroyed Jerusalem and the temple in 586 BCE; Persia, which conquered Babylon. The Euphrates was the line beyond which hostile empires gathered their strength.

For a first-century audience under Roman rule, the Euphrates carried a more immediate resonance. The Euphrates was the eastern frontier of the Roman Empire, beyond which lay the Parthian Empire — Rome's most feared and unconquered rival. The Parthians had inflicted humiliating defeats on Roman armies, most notably the annihilation of Crassus's legions at Carrhae in 53 BCE. Parthian cavalry — mounted archers and armored horsemen — were legendary for their speed, ferocity, and tactical ingenuity, including the famous "Parthian shot," firing arrows while appearing to retreat. The fear of a Parthian invasion from beyond the Euphrates was a persistent anxiety in the Roman world, particularly in the eastern provinces. The description that follows — a cavalry of inconceivable numbers bearing fire, smoke, and brimstone — would have resonated with this fear while transcending it: the reality the author describes surpasses any earthly army.

"The four angels, who had been prepared for the hour and day and month and year, were released, so that they would kill a third of mankind" (hoi hetoimasmenoi eis ten horan kai hemeran kai mena kai eniauton, hina apokteinousin to triton ton anthropon). The phrase "prepared for the hour and day and month and year" (hetoimasmenoi eis ten horan kai hemeran kai mena kai eniauton) expresses divine foreordination with extraordinary precision. The perfect passive participle hetoimasmenoi ("having been prepared") indicates that the preparation was completed in the past and its result endures. These angels were prepared for a specific moment — not merely a general season but an exact hour, day, month, and year. The quadruple temporal specification (hour, day, month, year, moving from smallest to largest unit) conveys absolute precision. Nothing about this event is improvised, accidental, or contingent. The timing is as fixed as the identity of the agents.

The purpose is stated: "so that they would kill a third of mankind" (hina apokteinousin to triton ton anthropon). The escalation from the fifth trumpet is severe. The locusts were prohibited from killing; the sixth trumpet's forces are commissioned to kill. And the scale is staggering: a third of humanity. The fraction "a third" (to triton) maintains the proportion that has governed the entire trumpet sequence (8:7-12). A third — not all, not half, not everything. The judgment is devastating but still partial, still leaving a surviving remainder. The partial character of the destruction is itself significant: the judgment leaves survivors, and the text will address the response of those survivors in verses 20-21.

div.title: Verses 16-19: The Cavalry of Fire, Smoke, and Brimstone
div.p: "The number of the armies of the horsemen was two hundred million; I heard the number of them. And this is how I saw in the vision the horses and those who sat on them: the riders had breastplates the color of fire and of hyacinth and of brimstone; and the heads of the horses are like the heads of lions; and out of their mouths proceed fire and smoke and brimstone. A third of mankind was killed by these three plagues, by the fire and the smoke and the brimstone which proceeded out of their mouths. For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails; for their tails are like serpents and have heads, and with them they do harm."

"The number of the armies of the horsemen was two hundred million" (ho arithmos ton strateumaton tou hippikou dismyriades myriadon). The Greek is dismyriades myriadon — literally "two ten-thousands of ten-thousands," which calculates to 200,000,000. The number is beyond any military force in human history. For reference, the entire population of the Roman Empire at its height is estimated at fifty to seventy million. An army of two hundred million exceeds the population of the ancient world. The number signifies an innumerable, overwhelming force — a military reality that no human power could resist or even comprehend. In Daniel 7:10, "a thousand thousands served him, and ten thousand times ten thousand stood before him" — a description of the heavenly court's attendants. The author's number surpasses even Daniel's multitude. The phrase "I heard the number of them" (ekousa ton arithmon auton) parallels 7:4, "I heard the number of those who were sealed." In both cases, John hears a number he could not have counted by sight.

"The riders had breastplates the color of fire and of hyacinth and of brimstone" (echontas thorakas pyrinous kai hyakinthinous kai theiodeis). The breastplates (thorakas) of the riders are described in three colors, each corresponding to one of the three plagues that will kill a third of humanity. "Fiery" (pyrinous, from pyr, "fire") corresponds to fire; "hyacinth-colored" (hyakinthinous — a deep blue or dark blue-purple, the color of the hyakinthos flower) corresponds to smoke; "brimstone-colored" (theiodeis — sulfurous yellow) corresponds to brimstone. The riders wear on their bodies the colors of the destruction they bring. The visual description encodes the nature of the judgment: the army is fire, smoke, and brimstone made mobile and militant.

"The heads of the horses are like the heads of lions" (hai kephalai ton hippon hos kephalai leonton). As with the locusts (9:8), lion imagery characterizes the destructive power of these creatures. Joel 1:6, describing the locust invasion: "Its teeth are the teeth of a lion." The lion's head on a horse's body creates another composite creature — a being that combines the strength and speed of a war horse with the ferocity and devouring power of a lion.

"Out of their mouths proceed fire and smoke and brimstone" (ek ton stomaton auton ekporeuetai pyr kai kapnos kai theion). The three substances that proceed from the horses' mouths are the traditional instruments of divine judgment associated with the destruction of Sodom and Gomorrah. Genesis 19:24-25: "Then the LORD rained on Sodom and on Gomorrah brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven. And he overthrew those cities and all the valley and all the inhabitants of the cities." The phrase "brimstone and fire" (theion kai pyr, LXX) is the signature of God's judgment on a civilization that had reached the limit of its wickedness. In Psalm 11:6 (LXX 10:6): "Upon the wicked he shall rain snares, fire and brimstone and a burning wind will be the portion of their cup." In Isaiah 30:33: "Its pyre is made deep and large, a burning heap of fire and wood; the breath of the LORD, like a stream of brimstone, kindles it." In Ezekiel 38:22, the judgment on Gog includes "fire and brimstone." The trio of fire, smoke, and brimstone connects the sixth trumpet's judgment to the entire prophetic tradition of divine destruction of the wicked.

"A third of mankind was killed by these three plagues, by the fire and the smoke and the brimstone" (apo ton trion plegon touton apektanthesan to triton ton anthropon, ek tou pyros kai tou kapnou kai tou theiou tou ekporeuomenou ek ton stomaton auton). The word plegon ("plagues") is the same word used in the LXX for the plagues of Egypt (Exodus 11:1, LXX: eti mian plegen). The author explicitly categorizes the three substances as "plagues" — placing them within the exodus-plague framework that has governed the trumpet sequence from the beginning. The fire, the smoke, and the brimstone are three distinct plagues, each contributing to the killing of a third of humanity. The fraction "a third" is maintained: the destruction is massive but not total.

"For the power of the horses is in their mouths and in their tails; for their tails are like serpents and have heads, and with them they do harm" (hai gar exousiai ton hippon en to stomati auton eisin kai en tais ourais auton; hai gar ourai auton homoiai ophesin, echousai kephalas, kai en autais adikousin). The horses inflict harm from both ends: their mouths breathe fire, smoke, and brimstone, and their tails are serpent-like, with heads of their own that do harm. The serpent (ophis) has been a figure of danger and deception since Genesis 3:1. In Numbers 21:6, the LORD sent "fiery serpents" (tous opheis tous thanatountas, LXX) among the people as punishment for their complaining, and the serpents bit the people and many died. In this document, the serpent will be identified explicitly as "the serpent of old who is called the devil and Satan" (12:9; 20:2). The serpent-tails suggest that the destructive power of this cavalry operates through both direct assault (fire from the mouths) and insidious harm (the serpent-tails that strike from behind). The double source of power — mouths and tails — creates a force from which there is no safe approach.

The verb adikousin ("they do harm, they act unjustly") is the same verb used throughout the chapter for the locusts' power to hurt (9:4, 10). The word links the two woe-visions: both the locusts and the cavalry are agents of adikia — harm, injustice, destructive action — operating under divine authorization against those who dwell on the earth.

div.title: Verses 20-21: The Refusal to Repent
div.p: "The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands, so as not to worship demons, and the idols of gold and of silver and of brass and of stone and of wood, which can neither see nor hear nor walk; and they did not repent of their murders nor of their sorceries nor of their immorality nor of their thefts."

"The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent" (hoi loipoi ton anthropon, hoi ouk apektanthesan en tais plegais tautais, ou metenoesan). These two verses are the theological climax of the chapter. Everything that precedes — the opening of the abyss, the locust torment, the cavalry of fire and brimstone, the killing of a third of humanity — leads to this moment. The question implicit in the entire trumpet sequence is: will the judgments produce repentance? The answer is stated with devastating brevity: ou metenoesan — "they did not repent."

The word metanoeo ("to repent, to change one's mind, to turn") is a key word in this document. In the seven messages, the risen Christ repeatedly called the assemblies to repent: Ephesus must repent or lose its lampstand (2:5); Pergamum must repent of tolerating false teaching (2:16); Thyatira is given time to repent (2:21); Sardis must repent (3:3); Laodicea must repent (3:19). Repentance is the appropriate response to divine warning and judgment. The earth-dwellers' refusal to repent stands in direct contrast to the repentance demanded of the assemblies. The assemblies are called to repent of specific failures of faithfulness; the earth-dwellers refuse to repent despite the most severe conceivable warning.

The parallel to the Egyptian plagues is exact. In Exodus 7-12, God sent plague after escalating plague upon Egypt, and after each plague Pharaoh's heart was hardened. The Hebrew text alternates between Pharaoh hardening his own heart (Exodus 8:15, 32; 9:34) and God hardening Pharaoh's heart (Exodus 9:12; 10:20, 27; 11:10). The result was the same: despite the devastating evidence of God's power and judgment, Pharaoh refused to yield. In Exodus 10:3, God asks through Moses: "How long will you refuse to humble yourself before me?" The survivors of the trumpet plagues face the same question. The judgments are, in effect, God's demand that the earth-dwellers humble themselves and abandon their idolatry. The refusal mirrors Pharaoh's: obstinate, persistent, irrational in the face of overwhelming evidence.

"Did not repent of the works of their hands" (ou metenoesan ek ton ergon ton cheiron auton). The phrase "the works of their hands" (ta erga ton cheiron auton) is the standard prophetic designation for idols in the Hebrew scriptures. Deuteronomy 4:28: "There you will serve gods, the work of human hands (erga cheiron anthropon, LXX), wood and stone, which neither see nor hear nor eat nor smell." 2 Kings 19:18 (LXX 4 Kingdoms 19:18): "They have cast their gods into the fire, for they were not gods but the work of human hands (erga cheiron anthropon), wood and stone." Psalm 115:4 (LXX 113:12): "Their idols are silver and gold, the work of human hands (erga cheiron anthropon)." Psalm 135:15 (LXX 134:15): "The idols of the nations are silver and gold, the work of human hands (erga cheiron anthropon)." Isaiah 2:8: "Their land has also been filled with idols; they worship the work of their hands (ta erga ton cheiron auton), that which their fingers have made." Jeremiah 1:16: "I will pronounce my judgments on them concerning all their wickedness in forsaking me, and in burning incense to other gods and in worshipping the works of their own hands (tois ergois ton cheiron auton)."

The phrase is prophetic shorthand for idolatry — the worship of things humans have manufactured. The prophetic critique is consistent and devastating: the idol is the product of the worshipper's own labor, yet the worshipper treats it as a power greater than himself. The inversion is absurd: the maker worships the made thing.

"So as not to worship demons, and the idols of gold and of silver and of brass and of stone and of wood" (hina me proskynesousin ta daimonia kai ta eidola ta chrysa kai ta argyra kai ta chalka kai ta lithina kai ta xylina). The author adds an interpretive layer that the Hebrew prophets occasionally made explicit: behind the idols stand demons. Deuteronomy 32:17: "They sacrificed to demons (daimoniois, LXX) who were not God, to gods whom they have not known." Psalm 106:37 (LXX 105:37): "They sacrificed their sons and their daughters to the demons (tois daimoniois)." 1 Corinthians 10:20, in a text likely known to the assemblies: "The things which the Gentiles sacrifice, they sacrifice to demons (daimoniois) and not to God." The worship of idols is not merely a cognitive error — a mistake about the nature of the statue. It involves actual spiritual engagement with hostile powers. The earth-dwellers are not simply confused; they are entangled with demonic forces.

The catalogue of idol materials — gold, silver, brass, stone, and wood — follows a descending order from most precious to least valuable. A nearly identical list appears in Daniel 5:4, 23, describing the idolatrous feast of Belshazzar: "They drank the wine and praised the gods of gold and silver, of bronze, iron, wood, and stone." In Daniel 5, Belshazzar's feast ended with the handwriting on the wall and his kingdom's fall that very night. The echo of Belshazzar's materials reinforces the Danielic framework: like Belshazzar, the earth-dwellers persist in idolatry even as divine judgment closes in.

"Which can neither see nor hear nor walk" (ha oute blepein dynantai oute akouein oute peripatein). This phrase recapitulates the prophetic polemic against idols with devastating precision. Psalm 115:5-7 (LXX 113:13-15): "They have mouths, but they do not speak; they have eyes, but they do not see. They have ears, but they do not hear; they have noses, but they do not smell. They have hands, but they do not feel; they have feet, but they do not walk; they make no sound in their throat." Deuteronomy 4:28: "gods... which neither see nor hear nor eat nor smell." Isaiah 46:7: "They lift it to their shoulders and carry it; they set it in its place, and it stands there; it does not move from its place. Though one cries out to it, it does not answer; it cannot deliver him from his distress." The idols cannot see the worshipper's need, cannot hear the worshipper's prayer, cannot walk to the worshipper's aid. They are inert, powerless, dead things worshipped by those who refuse to worship the living God.

The contrast with the God who sits on the throne in chapters 4-5 is total. The God of this document has eyes "like a flame of fire" (1:14; 2:18) that see everything. He has ears that receive the prayers of the saints (5:8; 8:3-4). He acts — he comes, he judges, he rewards, he creates anew. The idols can do none of these things. The absurdity of the earth-dwellers' choice is exposed: they have witnessed the power of the living God displayed in plague after plague and still cling to objects that are incapable of any response whatsoever.

"And they did not repent of their murders nor of their sorceries nor of their immorality nor of their thefts" (kai ou metenoesan ek ton phonon auton oute ek ton pharmakon auton oute ek tes porneias auton oute ek ton klemmaton auton). The double refusal to repent — stated in verse 20 regarding idolatry and restated in verse 21 regarding moral conduct — creates a comprehensive catalogue of the earth-dwellers' sins. The four sins listed in verse 21 — murders (phonoi), sorceries (pharmaka), immorality (porneia), and thefts (klemmata) — correspond roughly to violations of the second table of the Decalogue: "You shall not murder" (Exodus 20:13), the prohibition of sorcery (Exodus 22:18; Deuteronomy 18:10-11), "You shall not commit adultery" (Exodus 20:14), and "You shall not steal" (Exodus 20:15).

The word pharmaka ("sorceries") derives from pharmakon, which means "drug, potion, poison" and by extension "sorcery, magic." In the LXX, pharmakon and its cognates are associated with magical practices, potions, and occult manipulation. In Exodus 7:11, 22; 8:7 (LXX 8:3), Pharaoh's magicians (pharmakoi, LXX of Exodus 7:11) replicated Moses's signs through their "secret arts." In Galatians 5:20, pharmakeia appears in a list of "works of the flesh." In Revelation 18:23, Babylon's sorcery (pharmakeia) is the means by which "all the nations were deceived." The word carries associations of deception, manipulation, and the use of substances and rituals to access or manipulate spiritual powers apart from God.

The word porneia ("immorality, sexual immorality, fornication") functions throughout this document on two levels. Literally, it refers to sexual conduct outside the boundaries established by the Torah. Figuratively, it represents idolatrous unfaithfulness — the metaphor used by Hosea, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel for Israel's unfaithfulness to God (Hosea 1-3; Jeremiah 3:1-10; Ezekiel 16, 23). In this document, the two senses merge: the "great harlot" of chapters 17-18 embodies both literal sexual exploitation and idolatrous seduction. The earth-dwellers' porneia is their comprehensive unfaithfulness — sexual, spiritual, and political — to the one who sits on the throne.

The structure of verses 20-21 is chiastic in theme: the outer frame is religious (idolatry, verse 20; sorcery, included in verse 21 as a religious practice), and the inner core is ethical (murders, immorality, thefts). The two dimensions — worship and conduct — are presented as inseparable. Wrong worship produces wrong behavior. The refusal to repent of idolatry is bound to the refusal to repent of violence, sexual exploitation, and theft. The prophetic tradition consistently linked these: Hosea 4:1-2: "There is no faithfulness or steadfast love, and no knowledge of God in the land; there is swearing, deception, murder, stealing, and adultery. They employ violence, and bloodshed follows bloodshed." Jeremiah 7:9: "Will you steal, murder, commit adultery, swear falsely, offer sacrifices to Baal, and walk after other gods that you have not known?" The pairing of idolatry with ethical violation is not a secondary observation but the prophets' central diagnosis: the root sin (wrong worship) produces the fruit of sin (wrong conduct).

div.title: Summary of the Chapter's Argument

list.item: Chapter 9 delivers the first two of the three woes announced by the eagle in 8:13. The shift from the first four trumpets (which struck the natural world) to the fifth and sixth trumpets (which strike humanity directly) represents a deliberate escalation. God's preliminary judgments on creation did not produce repentance; the woe-trumpets now fall on the earth-dwellers themselves. The fifth trumpet torments without killing; the sixth trumpet kills a third of humanity. The intensification is purposeful, moving from warning to devastation.

The divine passive edothe ("was given") continues to govern every destructive action in the chapter. The key to the abyss was given to the star (9:1). Power was given to the locusts (9:3). They were told what they could and could not do (9:4-5). The four angels were released by a command from the golden altar (9:13-14). The four angels were prepared for an exact moment (9:15). Every agent of destruction in this chapter operates under divine authorization, within divine limits, and according to divine timing. The chain of authority running from the throne through the Lamb through the scroll through the trumpets to the agents of judgment remains unbroken.

The fifth trumpet draws extensively on the locust-army imagery of Joel 1-2 and the plague of locusts in Exodus 10. Joel described a locust invasion as the Day of the LORD and identified the locust horde as God's own army: "The LORD utters his voice before his army" (Joel 2:11); "My great army which I sent among you" (Joel 2:25). The author of Revelation transforms Joel's imagery: the locusts emerge not from the natural world but from the abyss, they are forbidden from harming vegetation (their natural target) and instead torment humans, and they are equipped with scorpion stings rather than devouring mouths. The transformation elevates the vision from natural disaster to supernatural judgment while maintaining the Joeline framework of the locust army as a divine instrument.

The protection of the sealed (9:4) connects the trumpet judgments directly to the sealing vision of chapter 7. The 144,000 sealed servants of God were marked before the judgments began; now, the locusts are explicitly prohibited from harming those who bear God's seal. The pattern replicates the exodus: as the blood on the doorposts protected Israel's firstborn from the destroyer (Exodus 12:13), and as the mark on the foreheads protected the righteous from the destroying angels in Ezekiel 9:4-6, so the seal of God protects the faithful through the trumpet judgments. The sealed are not removed from the scene of judgment; they are protected within it.

The five-month duration (9:5, 10) reinforces the bounded, temporary nature of the judgment. The five months correspond to the natural life cycle of locusts in the Mediterranean world. The judgment is severe but has a divinely imposed expiration. The prohibition against killing (9:5) further limits the torment: it afflicts but does not destroy. The sufferers desire death but are denied it (9:6), suggesting that the purpose of the torment is not annihilation but the creation of conditions under which repentance might occur.

The composite description of the locusts (9:7-10) defies literal interpretation and demands symbolic reading. The creatures combine features of horses, humans, women, lions, scorpions, and insects into a single form that violates every natural category. The accumulation of fearsome attributes — armor, lion teeth, scorpion stings, cavalry sound — constructs a vision of overwhelming, inescapable spiritual torment. The author signals through the genre (esemanen, 1:1 — the revelation is "signified," communicated through signs) that these are symbolic representations of realities that exceed the capacity of literal description.

The name Abaddon/Apollyon (9:11) identifies the king of the locust army as "Destruction" personified. In the Hebrew scriptures, Abaddon is a synonym for Sheol — the realm of the dead (Job 26:6; 28:22; Psalm 88:11; Proverbs 15:11; 27:20). The Greek name Apollyon ("Destroyer") carries a phonetic echo of Apollo (Apollon), the patron deity of the Roman emperors and a god associated with plagues in Greek tradition. For an audience in the Roman province of Asia, where Apollo was prominently worshipped, the resonance would suggest that the divine patron of the imperial order is, in truth, the ruler of the abyss — the king of destructive forces, not a heavenly protector.

The sixth trumpet's command originates from the golden altar (9:13), linking it directly to the prayers of the saints (8:3-5) and the martyrs' cry (6:9-10). The same altar that received the prayers now issues the command for judgment. The prayers of the suffering faithful are not decorative but operative: they participate in the heavenly process that produces earthly judgment. The cry "How long?" is being answered through the trumpet sequence.

The Euphrates (9:14) activates the full weight of Israel's historical memory and the first-century geopolitical imagination. In Israel's scriptures, the Euphrates marks the boundary beyond which the great destroying empires gathered: Assyria, Babylon, Persia (Genesis 15:18; Isaiah 7:20; 8:7-8). For a first-century audience, the Euphrates was the Roman Empire's eastern frontier, beyond which lay the Parthian threat. The four angels bound at the Euphrates represent destructive forces held in check at the boundary of the known world, now released by divine command. The imagery is simultaneously scriptural and contemporary: the author deploys Israel's historical geography to describe a judgment that transcends any single historical moment.

The cavalry of 200 million (9:16-19) exceeds any conceivable human army. The number surpasses the population of the ancient world. The horses breathe fire, smoke, and brimstone — the traditional instruments of divine judgment associated with Sodom's destruction (Genesis 19:24). The riders wear the colors of the destruction they carry: fire-red, smoke-blue, brimstone-yellow. The serpent-tails echo the serpent of Genesis 3 and the fiery serpents of Numbers 21:6. The imagery combines military terror with the full vocabulary of divine wrath, producing a vision of judgment that is both militaristic and supernatural.

The refusal to repent (9:20-21) is the theological center of the chapter. Everything that precedes it — the torment of the locusts, the killing of a third of humanity — serves a purpose that is now revealed by its failure. The judgments were designed to produce repentance, and the survivors refuse to repent. The pattern replicates Pharaoh's response to the Egyptian plagues: escalating judgment met by unyielding obstinacy. The sins the survivors cling to are comprehensive: idolatry (the root) and murders, sorceries, immorality, and thefts (the fruit). The prophetic tradition (Hosea 4:1-2; Jeremiah 7:9) consistently presented wrong worship and wrong conduct as inseparable. The catalogue of idol materials (gold, silver, brass, stone, wood) echoes Daniel 5:4, 23 — the feast of Belshazzar, who praised dead idols on the night his kingdom fell. The idols "can neither see nor hear nor walk" (Psalm 115:5-7; Deuteronomy 4:28), a withering prophetic polemic that exposes the absurdity of preferring inert objects to the living God whose power has just been demonstrated in plague after plague.

The chapter's position within the document's larger argument reinforces the conditional and urgent nature of the assemblies' situation. The earth-dwellers refuse to repent despite the most severe judgments. The assemblies, by contrast, are called to repent (2:5, 16, 21-22; 3:3, 19) while the opportunity exists. The contrast between the two groups — those who hear and repent, those who experience judgment and do not — is the document's central pastoral concern. The assemblies are being shown what happens to those who persist in idolatry and unfaithfulness, and the vision functions as both warning and exhortation: repent now, while the risen Christ still walks among the lampstands and offers the promise to those who conquer. The refusal to repent in 9:20-21 is the dark counterpart to the repentance the messages demand. The document does not assume that its audience will automatically be among the saved; it places the choice before them with unflinching clarity.

div.title: Revelation 10 — First-Century Reading
Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (Revelation 9): The fifth and sixth trumpets delivered the first two of the three woes announced by the eagle in 8:13. The fifth trumpet (9:1-12) released the locusts of the abyss — supernatural agents of torment, forbidden from killing but authorized to afflict "the men who do not have the seal of God on their foreheads" (9:4) for five months. The sixth trumpet (9:13-19) released four angels bound at the Euphrates along with a cavalry of two hundred million whose horses breathed fire, smoke, and brimstone, killing a third of humanity. The chapter's theological climax came in its final two verses (9:20-21): "The rest of mankind, who were not killed by these plagues, did not repent of the works of their hands, so as not to worship demons, and the idols of gold and of silver and of brass and of stone and of wood, which can neither see nor hear nor walk; and they did not repent of their murders nor of their sorceries nor of their immorality nor of their thefts." Despite the escalating severity of six trumpet judgments — from partial destruction of the natural world (trumpets 1-4, chapter 8) to agonizing torment (trumpet 5) to the killing of a third of humanity (trumpet 6) — the survivors refused to repent. The refusal replicated the pattern of Pharaoh during the Egyptian plagues: escalating judgment met by unyielding obstinacy. The trumpet sequence, which began as the divine response to the prayers of the saints offered on the golden altar (8:3-5), had reached its penultimate stage and produced no change in the earth-dwellers.

What the author argues immediately after (Revelation 11): The interlude that begins at 10:1 continues through 11:13. In 11:1-2, John is given a measuring rod and told to measure the temple of God, the altar, and those who worship in it — but to exclude the outer courtyard, which "has been given to the nations" who "will trample the holy city for forty-two months." In 11:3-13, two witnesses prophesy for 1,260 days, are killed by "the beast that comes up out of the abyss" (11:7 — the same abyss opened in 9:1-2), lie dead in the street for three and a half days, are raised to life by "the breath of life from God" (11:11), and ascend to heaven. An earthquake destroys a tenth of the city and kills seven thousand people, and then — in a crucial turn — "the rest were terrified and gave glory to the God of heaven" (11:13). This response contrasts sharply with 9:20-21: where the survivors of the sixth trumpet refused to repent, the survivors of the earthquake give glory to God. The interlude thus shows a different outcome: faithful prophetic witness, even unto death, producing in some the acknowledgment of God that the trumpet judgments alone did not produce.

After the interlude, the announcement comes: "The second woe is past; behold, the third woe is coming quickly" (11:14). Then the seventh angel sounds (11:15), and loud voices in heaven declare: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ; and He will reign forever and ever." The twenty-four elders worship, declaring that God has "taken Your great power and have begun to reign" (11:17). This is the culmination that 10:7 announced: "the mystery of God is finished."

How chapter 10 connects the surrounding argument: Between the sixth and seventh seals, the author inserted an interlude (chapter 7) that addressed the question raised by the sixth seal's cosmic upheaval — "Who is able to stand?" (6:17) — by showing the sealed servants of God and the innumerable multitude who had come through the great tribulation. Between the sixth and seventh trumpets, the author inserts a parallel interlude (10:1-11:13) that addresses the crisis raised by the sixth trumpet's aftermath — the earth-dwellers' refusal to repent (9:20-21). The crisis is not merely military or cosmic; it is spiritual. If escalating judgment does not produce repentance, what will? The interlude answers: the prophetic word, internalized and proclaimed even at the cost of the prophets' lives.

Chapter 10 thus occupies a pivotal structural position. It stands between the failed response of 9:20-21 and the successful response of 11:13, and it addresses the mechanism by which the transition occurs. The prophet must eat the scroll — internalize the divine word — and prophesy again to all peoples, nations, languages, and kings. The prophetic witness of the two witnesses in 11:3-13 enacts what 10:11 commissions. The interlude is not a digression from the trumpet sequence but its interpretive key: the judgments are not self-sufficient; they require the prophetic word to accomplish God's purpose.

The chapter also answers the question that has been building since 6:10, when the souls under the altar cried, "How long, O Lord, holy and true, will You refrain from judging and avenging our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" They were told to wait "a little while longer" (6:11). Now, six trumpets later, the angel swears: "there will be no more delay" (10:6). The waiting is over. The mystery of God will be completed when the seventh angel sounds.

div.title: Verses 1-2: The Strong Angel Descends with the Open Scroll
div.p: "I saw another strong angel coming down from heaven, clothed with a cloud; and the rainbow was on his head, and his face was like the sun, and his feet like pillars of fire; and he had in his hand a little scroll, which was open. He placed his right foot on the sea and his left on the land."

"Another strong angel" (allon angelon ischyron). The phrase echoes 5:2, where John saw "a strong angel proclaiming with a loud voice, 'Who is worthy to open the scroll and to break its seals?'" The word allon ("another") connects this figure to the strong angel of chapter 5 while distinguishing him from that figure. The strong angel of 5:2 posed the question that drove the heavenly drama: who can open the sealed scroll? Now, another strong angel appears holding a scroll that is already open. The question has been answered. The seals have been broken. The content is accessible. The cycle that began with the sealed scroll on the throne (5:1) has advanced to the point where a scroll stands open in an angel's hand.

"Coming down from heaven" (katabainonta ek tou ouranou). The angel descends — his movement is from the heavenly realm to the earthly. The same verb (katabaino, "to come down, to descend") describes the descent of the new Jerusalem (3:12; 21:2, 10) and of fire from heaven (13:13; 20:9). The angel's descent signals that the heavenly initiative is now reaching into the earthly sphere. Until this point in the trumpet sequence, the judgments have been dispatched from heaven; now a heavenly figure physically enters the earthly scene where John stands.

"Clothed with a cloud" (peribeblemenon nephelen). The cloud is not incidental decoration. In Israel's scriptures and in this document, the cloud is the signature of divine presence. The pillar of cloud led Israel through the wilderness (Exodus 13:21-22). The cloud covered Mount Sinai when God descended to give the Torah (Exodus 19:9, 16; 24:15-18). The cloud filled the tabernacle so that Moses could not enter (Exodus 40:34-35). The cloud filled Solomon's temple at its dedication so that the priests could not stand to minister (1 Kings 8:10-11). In Ezekiel 1:4, the prophet's throne-chariot vision begins with "a great cloud" (nephele megale, LXX). In Daniel 7:13, "one like a son of man was coming with the clouds of heaven" (meta ton nephelon tou ouranou, LXX). In this document, the risen Christ is introduced in 1:7 with the declaration: "Behold, He is coming with the clouds" (meta ton nephelon). The cloud is not merely weather but theophany — the visible sign that God is present and acting.

The verb periballo ("to clothe, to wrap around") is used throughout this document for what figures are wearing: the twenty-four elders are "clothed in white garments" (4:4), the great multitude is "clothed in white robes" (7:9, 13), the woman of chapter 12 is "clothed with the sun" (12:1). This angel is clothed with a cloud in the same way others are clothed with garments. The cloud is not above him or around him but on him — he wears the divine presence the way others wear robes.

"The rainbow was on his head" (he iris epi ten kephalen autou). The rainbow (iris) appeared previously in this document at 4:3, where "there was a rainbow around the throne, like an emerald in appearance." The rainbow in 4:3 encircled the throne of God himself. Its scriptural root is Genesis 9:12-17, where God established the rainbow as the sign of his covenant with Noah and all flesh: "I have set My rainbow in the cloud, and it shall serve as a sign of a covenant between Me and the earth... and never again shall the water become a flood to destroy all flesh" (Genesis 9:13, 15). The rainbow is the visible marker of God's commitment not to destroy the earth by water — a promise made in the context of judgment (the flood had just occurred) and mercy (the promise restrains future total destruction).

In Ezekiel 1:28, the prophet saw the glory of the LORD on the throne-chariot and described it: "Like the appearance of the rainbow in the clouds on a rainy day, so was the appearance of the surrounding radiance. Such was the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the LORD." For Ezekiel, the rainbow-radiance was the visible form of God's glory. The angel in Revelation 10 bears on his head the same sign that encircled God's throne in chapter 4 and that constituted the appearance of God's glory in Ezekiel 1. He carries the covenant sign — the reminder that God's judgments, however severe, operate within the bounds of his promises.

"His face was like the sun" (to prosopon autou hos ho helios). This is the same language used to describe the risen Christ in 1:16: "His face was like the sun shining in its strength." The parallel is precise: the same simile, the same noun, the same comparison. In the Hebrew scriptures, the association between a face and the sun appears in Judges 5:31: "Let all Your enemies perish, O LORD; but let those who love Him be like the rising of the sun in its might." Moses's face shone when he came down from Sinai after speaking with God (Exodus 34:29-30, 35) — the reflected glory of the divine presence made his face radiant. In Daniel 10:6, the man in linen had a "face with the appearance of lightning" — a different but related image of overwhelming luminosity.

"His feet like pillars of fire" (hoi podes autou hos styloi pyros). The image combines two elements from Israel's foundational narrative. First, the pillar of fire (stylos pyros) that led Israel through the wilderness by night: "The LORD was going before them in a pillar of cloud by day to lead them on the way, and in a pillar of fire by night to give them light" (Exodus 13:21). The pillar of fire was the visible manifestation of God's guiding, protecting presence during the exodus journey. Second, the feet of the risen Christ in 1:15: "His feet were like burnished bronze when it has been heated to a glow in a furnace." In Daniel 10:6, the man in linen had "arms and feet like the gleam of polished bronze." The angel's feet are not merely fiery but pillar-like — they suggest the solidity and permanence of the architectural pillars in the temple (cf. the promise to the overcomer in 3:12: "I will make him a pillar in the temple of My God") combined with the fire of the exodus theophany.

The accumulation of divine attributes. The angel bears the cloud of God's presence, the rainbow of God's covenant, the sun-face of the risen Christ, and the fire-pillar feet of the exodus theophany. Each attribute, taken individually, belongs to either God or Christ elsewhere in this document and in the Hebrew scriptures. The question naturally arises: is this angel the risen Christ himself?

The text does not support that identification. The word angelos ("angel, messenger") is used without qualification, and the qualifier allon ("another") places this figure in a series with the strong angel of 5:2, who was plainly an angelic being distinct from both God and the Lamb. In the Hebrew scriptures, angelic figures sometimes bear the attributes of divine presence without being identified as God himself. The angel of the LORD who appeared to Moses in the burning bush was surrounded by fire and spoke God's words, yet was distinguished from the LORD who spoke from within the bush (Exodus 3:2-4). In Daniel 10:5-6, the man in linen bore attributes — face like lightning, eyes like flaming torches, arms and feet like polished bronze — that closely parallel the description of the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7:9 and the divine figure in Ezekiel 1:26-28. The pattern is consistent: angelic messengers who carry out the divine commission bear the marks of the one who sends them. This angel comes clothed in the insignia of divine authority because he speaks and acts on behalf of the God who sits on the throne and the Lamb who opened the seals. His attributes indicate the weight of his commission, not his personal identity.

"He had in his hand a little scroll, which was open" (echon en te cheiri autou biblaridion eneogmenon). The word biblaridion is a diminutive form, meaning "little scroll" or "small book." The full-sized scroll (biblion) introduced in 5:1 was "written inside and on the back, sealed up with seven seals." That scroll could not be opened until the Lamb was found worthy (5:5-7). Its opening through the seven seals constituted the judgments of chapters 6-8. Now a different scroll appears — smaller, and critically, already open (eneogmenon, perfect passive participle of anoigo: "having been opened" — the opening was completed in the past, and the scroll remains in its opened state).

The relationship between the two scrolls has been debated, but the text provides internal guidance. The great scroll of chapter 5 was sealed; this little scroll is open. The great scroll's contents were progressively revealed through the seals and trumpets; the little scroll is ready to be consumed and proclaimed. The diminutive form (biblaridion rather than biblion) need not mean the content is less important — diminutives in Greek frequently express endearment or specificity rather than insignificance. What the text makes clear is that this scroll is accessible. Its content is not hidden behind seals that must be broken but is available to be taken, eaten, and proclaimed. In the logic of the document's narrative, the progressive unsealing of the great scroll through seals and trumpets has reached the point where the content is now ready for direct prophetic engagement. The little scroll is the content that the prophet must internalize before he can prophesy again.

"He placed his right foot on the sea and his left on the land" (etheken ton poda autou ton dexion epi tes thalasses ton de euonymon epi tes ges). The posture is one of comprehensive dominion. Sea and land together constitute the entire created surface of the earth (Genesis 1:9-10). To plant a foot on something is to claim authority over it — as God told Joshua: "Every place on which the sole of your foot treads, I have given it to you" (Joshua 1:3). The angel's stance claims the full extent of the earthly domain for the message he is about to deliver.

The positioning also anticipates a development later in the document. In 13:1, a beast rises "out of the sea" (ek tes thalasses), and in 13:11, another beast comes up "out of the earth" (ek tes ges). The two domains from which the beasts will emerge are the same two domains over which the angel now plants his feet. Before the beasts arise from sea and land, the angel has already claimed both domains. The divine authority over sea and land is asserted before any counterfeit authority attempts to occupy those same territories.

div.title: Verses 3-4: The Lion-Roar, the Seven Thunders, and the Sealed Words
div.p: "And he cried out with a loud voice, as when a lion roars; and when he had cried out, the seven peals of thunder uttered their voices. When the seven peals of thunder had spoken, I was about to write; and I heard a voice from heaven, saying, 'Seal up the things which the seven peals of thunder have spoken, and do not write them.'"

"He cried out with a loud voice, as when a lion roars" (ekraxen phone megale hosper leon mykatai). The verb krazo ("to cry out, to shout") describes an authoritative, powerful utterance — not ordinary speech but proclamation. The comparison to a lion's roar has specific prophetic resonance. In Amos 3:7-8, the connection between the lion's roar and prophetic compulsion is explicit: "Surely the Lord GOD does nothing unless He reveals His secret plan to His servants the prophets. A lion has roared! Who will not fear? The Lord GOD has spoken! Who can do anything but prophesy?" In Amos, the lion's roar is God's voice, and the roar compels prophetic response. The linkage is: God roars (acts, speaks), the prophet must prophesy. The angel's lion-roar in Revelation 10:3 initiates the same sequence that will culminate in the command: "You must prophesy again" (10:11).

The lion association also connects backward within this document. In 5:5, one of the elders identified the Lamb as "the Lion that is from the tribe of Judah, the Root of David," who has overcome and is worthy to open the scroll. The lion roar of the angel in 10:3 carries the resonance of that identification: the authority behind the angel's cry is the authority of the Lion-Lamb who opened the seals.

In Hosea 11:10, God himself is the roaring lion: "They will walk after the LORD; He will roar like a lion; indeed He will roar, and His sons will come trembling from the west." In Joel 3:16 (LXX 4:16): "The LORD roars from Zion and utters His voice from Jerusalem, and the heavens and the earth tremble." The lion-roar in prophetic tradition is the voice of God speaking in power, demanding attention and obedience.

"The seven peals of thunder uttered their voices" (elalesan hai hepta brontai tas heauton phonas). The "seven thunders" (hai hepta brontai) appear with the definite article — "the seven thunders," as if they are a known entity, not introduced for the first time. The definite article suggests that the original audience would have recognized the reference. The most likely source is Psalm 29, which contains exactly seven occurrences of "the voice of the LORD" (qol YHWH, LXX phone kyriou), each associated with thunder and its effects:

list.item: "The voice of the LORD is on the waters; the God of glory thunders" (29:3)
"The voice of the LORD is powerful" (29:4a)
"The voice of the LORD is majestic" (29:4b)
"The voice of the LORD breaks the cedars" (29:5)
"The voice of the LORD divides flames of fire" (29:7)
"The voice of the LORD shakes the wilderness" (29:8)
"The voice of the LORD makes the deer give birth" (29:9)

div.p: In Psalm 29, the sevenfold "voice of the LORD" is the complete expression of divine power over the created order — over waters, cedars, fire, wilderness, and all living things. The psalm concludes: "The LORD sat as King at the flood; yes, the LORD sits as King forever" (29:10). The seven thunders in Revelation 10 appear to be the same phenomenon: the full, sevenfold divine voice — God's complete word spoken with the authority of the King who reigns over all creation.

Thunder in Israel's scriptures is consistently the voice of God in action. At Sinai, "God answered him with thunder" (Exodus 19:19). In 1 Samuel 7:10, "the LORD thundered with a great thunder on that day against the Philistines." In Job 37:2-5: "Listen closely to the thunder of His voice... God thunders with His voice wondrously." In this document, thunder emanates from the throne (4:5; 8:5; 11:19; 16:18) — it is part of the Sinai-theophany formula that marks climactic moments of divine disclosure.

The seven thunders speak with their own voices (tas heauton phonas — "their own voices," the reflexive pronoun emphasizing that the thunders are not echoing someone else's speech but articulating their own content). The thunders deliver intelligible speech — they "spoke" (elalesan, from laleo, "to speak, to utter words"), and John understood enough to begin writing.

"I was about to write" (emellon graphein). John's instinct to write what the thunders said follows from his commission in 1:11: "Write what you see in a scroll and send it to the seven churches." He has been writing down what he sees and hears throughout the vision. The fact that he was about to write confirms that the thunders' speech was comprehensible — it contained specific content that could be recorded.

"Seal up the things which the seven peals of thunder have spoken, and do not write them" (sphragison ha elalesan hai hepta brontai, kai me auta grapses). The command to seal (sphragizo) what the thunders said is a deliberate withholding of revelation. John heard the content, understood it well enough to write it, and was prohibited from recording it. The voice from heaven — not the angel, but a separate heavenly voice — intervenes to restrict the scope of John's written prophecy.

The primary scriptural parallel is Daniel 12:4, 9, where Daniel was commanded: "Keep these words secret and seal up the book until the end of time" (12:4) and "Go your way, Daniel, for these words will be kept secret and sealed up until the end time" (12:9). In Daniel, the sealing was temporal — the content was sealed because the end had not yet arrived. The revelation would become accessible when the time came.

The contrast between Daniel's sealing and Revelation's treatment of the rest of its content is significant. In 22:10, John is told: "Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near." The book as a whole is explicitly not sealed — the time has arrived, and the revelation is to be proclaimed openly. But the thunders' words are sealed within the unsealed book. The author creates a category of divine communication that exists — it was spoken, it was heard — but is not disclosed. Not all of God's counsel is made available to the audience. The revelation is genuine and extensive, but it has boundaries. The prophet is authorized to deliver what he is given, not everything that exists to be known.

The sealing of the thunders' words also functions within the document's literary architecture. Throughout the seal and trumpet sequences, the audience has been given detailed descriptions of each judgment. The seven thunders interrupt this pattern: here is a divine communication that the audience is told occurred but whose content is withheld. The effect is to remind the audience that the vision they are receiving, however comprehensive it may seem, does not exhaust the totality of God's purposes. There is more than what is written.

div.title: Verses 5-7: The Angel's Oath — No More Delay, the Mystery Finished
div.p: "Then the angel whom I saw standing on the sea and on the land raised his right hand to heaven, and swore by Him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and the things in it, and the earth and the things in it, and the sea and the things in it, that there will no longer be a delay, but in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he is about to sound, then the mystery of God is finished, as He announced to His servants the prophets."

"Raised his right hand to heaven" (eren ten cheira autou ten dexian eis ton ouranon). The gesture is the standard oath-taking posture in the ancient world. It has a precise scriptural parallel in Daniel 12:7: the man dressed in linen, "who was above the waters of the stream," raised "his right hand and his left toward heaven, and swore by Him who lives forever." The verbal and gestural parallels between Revelation 10:5-6 and Daniel 12:7 are too exact to be coincidental. The author is deliberately reenacting the Danielic scene.

In Daniel 12:7, the man in linen raised both hands; here the angel raises only his right hand. The variation may be significant: the right hand is the hand of authority and power throughout the scriptures (Exodus 15:6: "Your right hand, O LORD, is majestic in power"; Psalm 110:1: "Sit at My right hand"). The angel raises the hand of authority to heaven — toward the one by whom he swears.

In Deuteronomy 32:40, God himself makes the oath-gesture: "Indeed, I raise My hand to heaven, and say, as I live forever." The same gesture, the same oath formula. In Genesis 14:22, Abraham told the king of Sodom: "I have raised my hand to the LORD God Most High, Possessor of heaven and earth." The raised hand toward heaven is the solemn, binding gesture by which the most consequential commitments are made.

"Swore by Him who lives forever and ever, who created heaven and the things in it, and the earth and the things in it, and the sea and the things in it" (omosen en to zonti eis tous aionas ton aionon, hos ektisen ton ouranon kai ta en auto kai ten gen kai ta en aute kai ten thalassan kai ta en aute). The oath formula has two components: the identity of the one by whom the angel swears, and the content of the oath.

The one by whom the oath is sworn is identified by two attributes. First, he is the one "who lives forever and ever" (ho zon eis tous aionas ton aionon). This title appeared in Daniel 12:7, where the man in linen "swore by Him who lives forever" (LXX: omosen en to zonti eis ton aiona). It identifies God as the eternal one whose life has no end and whose word therefore cannot be revoked. It also appears in this document at 4:9-10, where the living creatures give "glory and honor and thanks to Him who sits on the throne, to Him who lives forever and ever," and the elders fall down and worship. The title places the oath on the most unshakeable foundation: the life of the God who cannot die and whose purposes cannot be frustrated.

Second, he is the Creator "who created heaven and the things in it, and the earth and the things in it, and the sea and the things in it." This threefold Creator formula echoes Exodus 20:11, the rationale for the Sabbath commandment: "For in six days the LORD made the heavens and the earth, the sea, and all that is in them." It also echoes Psalm 146:6: "Who made heaven and earth, the sea and everything in them." And Nehemiah 9:6: "You alone are the LORD. You made the heavens, the heaven of heavens with all their hosts, the earth and all that is on it, the seas and all that is in them." The threefold formula (heaven, earth, sea) comprehensively covers all of creation. The angel swears by the God who made everything on which the angel is standing. The three domains — heaven, earth, sea — correspond to the three zones the angel occupies: he has descended from heaven, stands on the earth and the sea, and swears toward heaven. The Creator's authority over every domain is the guarantee of the oath.

"That there will no longer be a delay" (hoti chronos ouketi estai). The word chronos means "time, delay, period of time." The phrase can be translated either "there will be no more time" or "there will be no more delay." The context favors "no more delay," because the next clause specifies when the culmination will occur: "in the days of the voice of the seventh angel." Time itself is not ending; rather, the waiting period is ending. The interval between the promise and its fulfillment is being declared closed.

This announcement directly answers the martyrs' cry in 6:10: "How long, O Lord, holy and true, will You refrain from judging and avenging our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" In 6:11, they were told to wait "a little while longer" (eti chronon mikron — note the same word chronon). The delay (chronos) that was imposed in 6:11 is now removed in 10:6 (chronos ouketi estai). The waiting that the martyrs endured is over. The vindication they cried for is imminent. The arc from 6:10-11 to 10:6 is one of the document's most carefully constructed trajectories: the question "How long?" receives the answer "No longer."

"But in the days of the voice of the seventh angel, when he is about to sound" (all' en tais hemerais tes phones tou hebdomou angelou, hotan melle salpizein). The culmination is assigned a specific temporal marker: the sounding of the seventh trumpet. The seventh trumpet will sound in 11:15, and when it does, the voices in heaven will declare: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ; and He will reign forever and ever." The angel's oath thus points forward to 11:15 as the moment of fulfillment. The phrase "the days of the voice" (en tais hemerais tes phones) — not merely "the moment" but "the days" — suggests that the seventh trumpet's sounding inaugurates a period during which its effects unfold, not an instantaneous event.

"Then the mystery of God is finished" (etelesthen to mysterion tou theou). The word mysterion ("mystery") in Jewish apocalyptic literature refers to God's hidden plan — the divine purpose that is concealed from human understanding but revealed to chosen recipients. In Daniel 2:28-29, 47, the Aramaic equivalent raz describes Nebuchadnezzar's dream: "There is a God in heaven who reveals mysteries" (Daniel 2:28). The "mystery of God" in Revelation 10:7 is God's total redemptive and judicial purpose — the full plan by which he brings creation to its intended end. This mystery has been partially disclosed throughout Israel's prophetic tradition, progressively unveiled through the seals and trumpets, and will be "finished" (etelesthen, from teleo, "to complete, to bring to an end, to accomplish") when the seventh trumpet sounds.

The verb teleo carries the sense of completion and accomplishment. In John 19:30, Jesus on the cross said tetelestai ("it is finished") — the same root, signifying the completion of the work assigned. The mystery of God will be fully accomplished, not merely stopped or interrupted but brought to its designed completion.

"As He announced to His servants the prophets" (hos euengelisen tous autou doulous tous prophetas). The verb euengelizo means "to announce good news, to proclaim the gospel." Its use here is striking: the completion of the mystery — which includes judgment and wrath — is called "good news." The judgments that have unfolded through seals and trumpets are not mere destruction but the working out of a purpose that was announced as good news to the prophets. The establishment of God's kingdom, the vindication of the righteous, the overthrow of evil — these constitute good news even though they involve devastating judgment on those who refuse to repent.

The phrase "His servants the prophets" (tous autou doulous tous prophetas) echoes Amos 3:7 directly: "Surely the Lord GOD does nothing unless He reveals His secret plan to His servants the prophets." The connection is precise: Amos says God reveals his plan (sod, "secret counsel") to the prophets; Revelation says God announced (euengelisen) the mystery to the prophets. The same relationship, the same vocabulary. God does not act without prior announcement through the prophetic tradition. The judgments of Revelation are not innovations but the fulfillment of what the prophets declared.

The identity of "the prophets" here is broad. It includes the Hebrew prophets who foretold the Day of the LORD (Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Joel, Amos, Zechariah, Malachi), Daniel who received visions of the end, and the prophetic tradition as a whole that anticipated God's ultimate assertion of sovereignty over the nations. The mystery now being completed is the same reality they glimpsed and proclaimed.

div.title: Verses 8-10: John Eats the Scroll — Sweet and Bitter
div.p: "Then the voice which I heard from heaven, I heard again speaking with me, and saying, 'Go, take the scroll which is open in the hand of the angel who stands on the sea and on the land.' And I went to the angel, telling him to give me the little scroll. And he said to me, 'Take it and eat it; it will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey.' I took the little scroll from the angel's hand and ate it, and in my mouth it was sweet as honey; and when I had eaten it, my stomach was made bitter."

"The voice which I heard from heaven, I heard again speaking with me" (he phone hen ekousa ek tou ouranou, palin lalousan met' emou). The voice that speaks is the same heavenly voice that commanded John to seal the thunders' words (v. 4). This voice operates independently of the angel — it is a distinct authority, speaking from heaven, directing John's actions. The voice acts as a mediator between the heavenly realm and the prophet, issuing the commands that govern what John may and must do. It told him what not to write (v. 4); now it tells him what to do (take the scroll).

"Go, take the scroll which is open in the hand of the angel" (hypage labe to biblion to eneogmenon en te cheiri tou angelou). The command uses hypage ("go") — John must physically approach the angel. In the vision, John moves. He is not a passive recipient but an active participant who must go, take, eat, and then prophesy. The description of the scroll as "open" (eneogmenon) is repeated from verse 2, emphasizing its accessibility. The content is available. The scroll is no longer sealed, no longer beyond reach.

"Take it and eat it" (labe kai kataphage auto). The command to eat the scroll draws directly on Ezekiel 2:8-3:3, the closest Old Testament parallel. In Ezekiel's commissioning, God said: "Son of man, eat what you find; eat this scroll, and go, speak to the house of Israel" (Ezekiel 3:1). Ezekiel obeyed: "So I opened my mouth, and He fed me this scroll. And He said to me, 'Son of man, feed your stomach and fill your body with this scroll which I am giving you.' Then I ate it, and it was sweet as honey in my mouth" (Ezekiel 3:2-3). The scroll Ezekiel ate was "written on the front and back, and written on it were songs of mourning, sighing, and woe" (Ezekiel 2:10).

The eating of a scroll is a prophetic act of internalization. The prophet does not merely hear the message or read it externally; he consumes it, takes it into his body, makes it part of himself. The prophetic word is not information to be relayed but substance to be embodied. What the prophet speaks will come from within him, not from a text held at arm's length. Jeremiah described the same reality in different terms: "Your words were found and I ate them, and Your words became a joy to me and the delight of my heart" (Jeremiah 15:16). Psalm 119:103: "How sweet are Your words to my taste! Yes, sweeter than honey to my mouth!" The metaphor of eating/tasting God's word is deeply embedded in the prophetic and wisdom traditions.

The verb kataphage (from katesthio, "to eat up, to devour, to consume completely") is more intensive than the simple phage ("eat"). John is to devour the scroll entirely — to take in every word, leaving nothing unconsumed.

"It will make your stomach bitter, but in your mouth it will be sweet as honey" (pikranei sou ten koilian, all' en to stomati sou estai glyky hos meli). The angel reverses the expected order: he mentions the bitterness first (the ultimate effect) and the sweetness second (the immediate experience). The sweetness is real — God's word is inherently good, desirable, nourishing. The psalms and prophets consistently describe God's word as sweet. But the content of this particular word produces bitterness when fully digested.

The sweetness and bitterness represent two dimensions of the same prophetic message. God's word is sweet because it comes from God — it reveals his purposes, discloses his plan, establishes his sovereignty. The word of God is always a gift, always an act of grace toward the one who receives it. Psalm 19:10: the LORD's ordinances are "sweeter than honey and the drippings of the honeycomb." But the specific content of this word — what John must proclaim "concerning many peoples, nations, languages, and kings" (v. 11) — is devastating. It includes judgment, destruction, suffering, and the consequences of the earth-dwellers' refusal to repent. The prophet who internalizes this message experiences both realities: the sweetness of being entrusted with God's word and the bitterness of knowing what that word contains.

"In my mouth it was sweet as honey; and when I had eaten it, my stomach was made bitter" (en to stomati mou hos meli glyky, kai hote ephagon auto epikranthe he koilia mou). John's experience confirms the angel's prediction exactly. The sweetness is immediate and real; the bitterness follows upon full consumption. The sequence mirrors Ezekiel's experience, though with a difference. Ezekiel reported the sweetness explicitly: "it was sweet as honey in my mouth" (Ezekiel 3:3). He did not report stomach bitterness directly. But in Ezekiel 3:14, after the Spirit carried him away, he described his state: "I went embittered in the rage of my spirit, and the hand of the LORD was strong on me." Ezekiel's bitterness came after the eating, as the weight of his prophetic commission pressed upon him. The author of Revelation makes the bitterness an immediate, physical part of the eating itself — the prophetic burden is inseparable from the prophetic gift.

The verb pikraino ("to make bitter, to embitter") appears elsewhere in the document only at 8:11, where the waters were made bitter (epikranthesan) by the star called Wormwood. The word links John's internal experience to the external judgment: the same bitterness that fell on the waters of the world now fills the prophet's stomach. The prophet carries within himself the weight of the judgment he must proclaim.

div.title: Verse 11: The Re-Commissioning — Prophesy Again
div.p: "And they said to me, 'You must prophesy again concerning many peoples, nations, languages, and kings.'"

"They said to me" (legousin moi). The verb is plural — "they say" — but no specific speaker is identified. The plural is striking after the singular "voice from heaven" (v. 8) and the singular angel (v. 9). Who are "they"? The text does not specify. The effect of the indefinite plural is to give the commission the weight of the entire heavenly council rather than a single speaker. The command comes from above, from the collective authority of the heavenly realm. The unidentified "they" may include the heavenly voice, the angel, and other unnamed heavenly figures. The lack of a specific attribution makes the commission feel comprehensive and inescapable.

"You must prophesy again" (dei se palin propheteusai). The word dei ("it is necessary, one must") expresses divine compulsion — not suggestion, not invitation, but necessity.
