The verb etelesthē ("was finished, was completed, was brought to its end") is from teleō, the same root as telos ("end, completion, fulfillment"). In this author's literary tradition, the cognate verb teleiōo appears in the Gospel's final cry from the cross: "It is finished" (tetelestai, John 19:30). There, the word signals the completion of the work the Father gave the Son to do. Here, etelesthē signals the completion of the wrath the Father has stored up against those who worship the beast. Both uses indicate not mere cessation but purposeful completion — the accomplishment of everything that needed to be done. The wrath of God is not an ongoing, indefinite phenomenon; it is a finite act with a beginning and an end, and these seven plagues bring it to its appointed conclusion.

The word thymos ("wrath, fury, passionate anger") is distinct from orgē, the other word for divine anger used in this document (cf. 6:16-17, "the wrath [orgē] of the Lamb... the great day of their wrath [orgēs] has come"). Thymos suggests the burning intensity of anger at its peak; orgē suggests the settled, judicial disposition of anger. Both appear in 16:19 together: "the cup of the wine of the fierceness [thymou] of his wrath [orgēs]." The seven plagues express the thymos — the full, fierce, undiluted intensity of God's response to the beast system and those who have given themselves to it.

div.title: Verses 2-4: The Conquerors and Their Song
div.p: "And I saw something like a sea of glass mixed with fire, and those who were victorious over the beast and his image and the number of his name, standing on the sea of glass, holding harps of God. And they sang the song of Moses, the bond-servant of God, and the song of the Lamb, saying, 'Great and marvelous are Your works, Lord God, the Almighty; Righteous and true are Your ways, King of the nations! Who will not fear You, Lord, and glorify Your name? For You alone are holy; For all the nations will come and worship before You, For Your righteous acts have been revealed.'"
div.title: The Sea of Glass Mixed with Fire
div.p: "And I saw something like a sea of glass mixed with fire" (kai eidon hōs thalassan hyalinēn memigmenēn pyri). The sea of glass first appeared in the throne-room vision of chapter 4: "Before the throne there was something like a sea of glass, like crystal" (4:6). There it was calm, transparent, crystalline — a vast, luminous expanse before God's throne suggesting both the separation between Creator and creation and the majesty of the heavenly court. Now the same sea of glass reappears, but it has changed. It is "mixed with fire" (memigmenēn pyri). The perfect participle memigmenēn ("having been mixed") indicates a completed transformation — the sea is not being set on fire; it already contains fire within it.

The combination of sea and fire evokes the Red Sea crossing with extraordinary precision. At the Red Sea, Israel stood on one side and Egypt on the other. The Lord went before Israel in a pillar of fire and cloud (Exodus 14:24). The waters divided, Israel passed through on dry ground, and the waters returned to destroy the Egyptian army (Exodus 14:21-28). The sea was the instrument of both salvation and judgment simultaneously: passage for the faithful, destruction for the enemy. Fire and water were both present at the crossing: the pillar of fire by night, the sea by day, and both were instruments of God's power.

The sea of glass mixed with fire in Revelation 15 compresses the entire Exodus deliverance into a single image. The conquerors stand on the far side of this sea, just as Israel stood on the far shore of the Red Sea after crossing. They have passed through the ordeal — the fire of tribulation, the sea of the beast's oppression — and they stand now in safety before God's throne. The fire in the sea represents both the trials they endured and the judgment that fell on their oppressors. The sea that was once an obstacle has become a platform of victory.

The qualifying phrase "something like" (hōs) appears here as it did in 4:6, signaling that what John sees is analogous to a sea of glass but is not literally one. The author consistently uses hōs to indicate visionary symbols that communicate through resemblance rather than exact correspondence.
div.title: The Conquerors
div.p: "And those who were victorious over the beast and his image and the number of his name" (kai tous nikōntas ek tou thēriou kai ek tēs eikonos autou kai ek tou arithmou tou onomatos autou). The participle nikōntas ("conquering, being victorious") is from nikaō, one of the most important verbs in this document. It appears in every letter to the seven churches, always in connection with promises to "the one who overcomes" (ho nikōn): the right to eat from the tree of life (2:7), immunity from the second death (2:11), hidden manna and a new name (2:17), authority over the nations (2:26), white garments and a name in the book of life (3:5), becoming a pillar in God's temple (3:12), sitting with Christ on his throne (3:21). In 12:11, the brothers "overcame" (enikēsan) the accuser "because of the blood of the Lamb and because of the word of their testimony, and they did not love their life even when faced with death."

The conquerors of 15:2 are the embodiment of everything promised to "the one who overcomes" in the letters. They have conquered. The question that the seven letters posed — will the churches endure? — is here answered: yes, these did. They are standing on the sea of glass. They are holding harps. They are singing.

What they conquered is specified with a threefold preposition: ek tou thēriou ("from the beast"), ek tēs eikonos autou ("from his image"), ek tou arithmou tou onomatos autou ("from the number of his name"). The preposition ek ("out of, away from") indicates separation and victory over each element. These are the three instruments of coercion described in chapter 13: the beast demanded worship (13:4, 8), its image was given breath and power to kill those who refused to worship it (13:15), and its number/mark was required for all economic activity (13:16-17). The threefold description in 15:2 mirrors the threefold threat in chapter 13. Each form of coercion — political worship, idolatrous image, economic mark — was faced and overcome. Those who stand on the sea of glass refused all three.

The verb nikōntas is present tense, which in Greek can indicate either ongoing action or a characteristic quality. These are people defined by their conquering. The present participle may also point to the fact that their victory is not a past event only but an abiding identity: they are conquerors. This is who they are.

The nature of their victory requires attention. In 12:11, the means of overcoming were stated: "the blood of the Lamb," "the word of their testimony," and the willingness to die rather than recant. In 13:7, the beast "was given to make war with the saints and to overcome them" (nikēsai autous). The beast "overcame" the saints in the earthly, physical sense — it killed them (13:15), excluded them economically (13:17), and exercised authority over every tribe, people, tongue, and nation (13:7). Yet the same people the beast "overcame" are now described as "those who were victorious over the beast." This is the paradox that runs through the entire document: the faithful conquer by refusing to yield, even at the cost of their lives. The beast's victory was physical; the saints' victory is ultimate. The sea of glass is the other side of death.
div.title: The Song of Moses and the Song of the Lamb
div.p: "Holding harps of God" (echontas tas kitharas tou theou). The kithara ("harp, lyre") appeared earlier in 5:8, where the twenty-four elders held harps along with golden bowls of incense (the prayers of the saints), and in 14:2, where a sound from heaven was "like the sound of harpists playing on their harps." The harps are called "of God" (tou theou) — belonging to God, given by God, dedicated to God. These are not the conquerors' own instruments but instruments from God's presence, provided for this very purpose: to sing in the heavenly court.

"And they sang the song of Moses, the bond-servant of God, and the song of the Lamb" (kai adousin tēn ōdēn Mōyseōs tou doulou tou theou kai tēn ōdēn tou arniou). The identification of this song requires careful attention. It is called both "the song of Moses" and "the song of the Lamb." These are not two separate songs but a single song with a dual identity, as indicated by the conjunction kai ("and") linking two descriptions of the same ōdēn ("song"). The conquerors are not singing one song and then another; they are singing a song that is simultaneously Mosaic and belongs to the Lamb.

Moses is called "the bond-servant of God" (tou doulou tou theou), a title used in the LXX for Moses at key moments. In Joshua 1:1-2, after Moses' death, Joshua is identified as the successor of "Moses, the servant of the Lord" (Mōysēs ho doulos kyriou). In Numbers 12:7, God distinguishes Moses from all other prophets: "Not so, with my servant Moses, he is faithful in all my household." The title places Moses in his covenantal role — not as a lawgiver in the abstract but as God's trusted servant who led Israel through the sea and who sang the victory song on the far shore.

There are two songs of Moses in the Torah. The first is in Exodus 15:1-18, sung after the crossing of the Red Sea. The second is in Deuteronomy 32:1-43, which God commanded Moses to write "as a witness against the sons of Israel" (Deuteronomy 31:19) — a prophetic song that recounts God's faithfulness, Israel's unfaithfulness, God's judgment, and his ultimate vindication. Both songs are relevant to Revelation 15, but the actual lyrics sung in verses 3-4 draw more heavily from Deuteronomy 32 and the Psalms than from Exodus 15.

The Exodus 15 connection lies in the dramatic situation: the conquerors stand on the far side of the sea, having passed through the ordeal, and sing of God's victory over the oppressor. This is the same posture as Israel on the shore of the Red Sea, watching Pharaoh's army destroyed, singing "I will sing to the LORD, for he is highly exalted; the horse and his rider he has hurled into the sea" (Exodus 15:1). The setting recapitulates the Exodus.

The Deuteronomy 32 connection lies in the song's function and content. God told Moses to write that song "so that this song may be a witness for me against the sons of Israel" (Deuteronomy 31:19). It was a song about God's righteous character, his just ways, and the certainty that he would vindicate his servants and render judgment against their adversaries: "Vengeance is mine, and retribution" (Deuteronomy 32:35); "Rejoice, O nations, with his people; for he will avenge the blood of his servants, and will render vengeance on his adversaries, and will atone for his land and his people" (Deuteronomy 32:43). The lyrics in Revelation 15:3-4 echo this theme of God's righteous character being revealed to the nations.

The song is also "the song of the Lamb" (tēn ōdēn tou arniou). The Lamb is the slaughtered-yet-standing figure of 5:6 who alone was worthy to open the scroll. The song of Moses celebrated deliverance through the Red Sea; the song of the Lamb celebrates deliverance through the Lamb's sacrificial death and the faithfulness of those who followed him through death. The dual title indicates that the new Exodus deliverance — the Lamb's victory over the beast — fulfills and completes what the first Exodus began. The conquerors' song is simultaneously about what God did through Moses (delivering Israel from Pharaoh through the sea) and what God did through the Lamb (delivering the faithful from the beast through death and resurrection). The pattern is the same; the fulfillment is greater.
div.title: The Lyrics of the Song
div.p: "Great and marvelous are Your works, Lord God, the Almighty" (megala kai thaumasta ta erga sou, kyrie ho theos ho pantokratōr). The opening line echoes multiple psalms. Psalm 111:2 (LXX 110:2): "Great are the works of the LORD" (megala ta erga tou kyriou). Psalm 139:14 (LXX 138:14): "Wonderful are your works" (thaumasia ta erga sou). The combination "great and marvelous" (megala kai thaumasta) also appears in the LXX of Psalm 98:1 (LXX 97:1), where God "has done wonderful things" (thaumasia). The works praised here are not abstract attributes but concrete actions — the same acts of judgment and deliverance that the plagues will execute. For the conquerors, the seven plagues are not terror; they are "great and marvelous works."

The title "Lord God, the Almighty" (kyrie ho theos ho pantokratōr) appears throughout this document as a characteristic divine name (1:8, 4:8, 11:17, 16:7, 19:6, 21:22). The word pantokratōr ("Almighty, ruler of all, the one who holds all things") is the LXX's standard rendering of the Hebrew Shaddai or of YHWH Tsevaoth ("LORD of hosts"). It is the title used when the emphasis falls on God's sovereign power over all competing powers. In a context where the beast has been "given authority over every tribe, people, tongue, and nation" (13:7), the title pantokratōr asserts that behind and above the beast's temporary, delegated authority stands the one who actually rules everything.

"Righteous and true are Your ways, King of the nations" (dikaiai kai alēthinai hai hodoi sou, ho basileus tōn ethnōn). The phrase "righteous and true" (dikaiai kai alēthinai) describes God's "ways" (hodoi) — his paths, his courses of action, the manner in which he conducts his governance. Deuteronomy 32:4: "The Rock! His work is perfect, for all his ways are just (dikaiai)" — the opening declaration of the Song of Moses. Psalm 145:17: "The LORD is righteous in all his ways" (dikaios kyrios en pasais tais hodois autou). The word alēthinai ("true, genuine, reliable") adds the dimension of faithfulness and trustworthiness: God's actions correspond to his character. His ways are not merely powerful (the first line established that); they are just and reliable.

The title "King of the nations" (ho basileus tōn ethnōn) draws directly from Jeremiah 10:7 (LXX): "Who would not fear you, O King of the nations (basileu tōn ethnōn)?" — which is echoed in the very next line of the song. Some manuscripts read "King of the ages" (basileus tōn aiōnōn), but the reading "King of the nations" fits the context: the song's climax in verse 4 is that "all the nations will come and worship before you," and the title "King of the nations" prepares for that climax. God is king not only of Israel but of all peoples. The beast claimed authority over "every tribe, people, tongue, and nation" (13:7); the song asserts that this authority belongs to God, who is the true King of the nations.

"Who will not fear You, Lord, and glorify Your name?" (tis ou mē phobēthē, kyrie, kai doxasei to onoma sou;) This line is drawn almost verbatim from Jeremiah 10:7 (LXX): "Who would not fear you, O King of the nations? For it is your due." The rhetorical question anticipates a universal answer: no one will fail to fear the Lord. The word phobēthē ("fear") carries the sense of reverent awe before overwhelming power and holiness, the recognition that one stands before the sovereign of all things. In this document, the call to "fear God" appeared in the first angel's proclamation in 14:7: "Fear God and give him glory, because the hour of his judgment has come." The conquerors' song answers the first angel's call: yes, all will fear God. The question is whether that fear comes as willing worship or as the terror of judgment.

"And glorify your name" (kai doxasei to onoma sou) — the glorification of God's name is the proper response to his revealed character. In the bowl judgments of chapter 16, the opposite response will be described: those afflicted by the plagues "blasphemed the name of God" (16:9) rather than glorifying it. The contrast between the conquerors who glorify and the beast-worshipers who blaspheme runs through the entire sequence.

"For You alone are holy" (hoti monos hosios). The word hosios ("holy, devout, pious") is distinct from hagios, the more common word for "holy" in this document (as in the Trisagion of 4:8: "Holy, holy, holy"). Hosios in the LXX carries the sense of covenant faithfulness, of one who keeps his commitments, who is loyal and trustworthy. In Deuteronomy 32:4 (LXX), God is described as "faithful" (pistos) and "there is no unrighteousness in him" — the same cluster of attributes. In Psalm 145:17 (LXX 144:17): "The LORD is righteous in all his ways and hosios in all his works." The conquerors declare that God alone possesses this character. No other power — not the beast, not the dragon, not any earthly kingdom — is hosios. God alone is faithful, trustworthy, and covenant-keeping.

"For all the nations will come and worship before You" (hoti panta ta ethnē hēxousin kai proskunēsousin enōpion sou). This line draws from Psalm 86:9 (LXX 85:9): "All nations whom you have made will come and worship before you, Lord, and they will glorify your name." The vision is not of the nations being merely destroyed but of the nations acknowledging God's sovereignty and rendering worship. The word proskunēsousin ("will worship, will bow down") is the same verb used for the worship the beast demands (13:4, 8, 12, 15). Throughout chapters 13-14, the central conflict was about worship: whom will the nations worship? The beast demands it; God deserves it. The song declares the outcome: the nations will come and worship before God. The beast's claim to worship was temporary and coerced; God's worship is the final reality to which all history moves.

The statement "all the nations will come" (panta ta ethnē hēxousin) raises the question of whether this envisions the conversion of the nations or their enforced submission. The verb hēxousin ("will come") suggests voluntary movement, and the context of Psalm 86:9 describes nations who come freely to worship. Isaiah 2:2-3 uses similar language: "All the nations will stream to it. And many peoples will come and say, 'Come, let us go up to the mountain of the LORD.'" The song envisions a time when the nations recognize what is true and respond accordingly. This aligns with the vision of 21:24-26, where "the nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it."

"For Your righteous acts have been revealed" (hoti ta dikaiōmata sou ephanerōthēsan). The word dikaiōmata ("righteous acts, righteous judgments, ordinances") is the crucial term. In the LXX, dikaiōma refers both to God's statutes or ordinances (Deuteronomy 4:1, 5, 8, 14: "the statutes [dikaiōmata] and the judgments") and to his righteous deeds or acts of justice (Judges 5:11: "the righteous acts [dikaiōmata] of the LORD"). Both senses are operative here. God's righteous judgments — the seven plagues — are about to be poured out, and these judgments are themselves acts of justice that vindicate the oppressed and punish the oppressor. The verb ephanerōthēsan ("were revealed, were made manifest") indicates that what was hidden is now visible. God's justice, which may have seemed absent during the time of the beast's authority over the saints (13:7), is now revealed in the plagues. The cries of the martyrs under the altar — "How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood?" (6:10) — receive their answer in the bowls. God's righteous acts have been revealed.

The entire song, considered as a unit, is a mosaic of scriptural phrases drawn from the Torah, the Psalms, and the Prophets. It is not a quotation of any single passage but a tapestry woven from the common liturgical vocabulary of Israel's worship: Deuteronomy 32:4 (God's perfect, just ways), Psalm 111:2 (great works), Psalm 86:9 (nations coming to worship), Psalm 145:17 (righteous in all his ways), Jeremiah 10:7 (who will not fear the King of the nations). The song's composite nature is itself significant. The conquerors do not sing a new, unprecedented text; they sing the scriptures of Israel. Their experience of deliverance from the beast is interpreted through the same categories that Israel used to understand deliverance from Egypt. The God who acted in the Exodus is the same God who acts in the bowls. The pattern is the same; the scope is cosmic.

div.title: Verses 5-8: The Heavenly Temple Opens and the Angels Emerge
div.p: "After these things I looked, and the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened, and the seven angels who had the seven plagues came out of the temple, clothed in linen, clean and bright, and their chests wrapped with golden sashes. And one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever. And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from His power; and no one was able to enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished."
div.title: The Temple of the Tabernacle of Testimony
div.p: "After these things I looked, and the temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven was opened" (meta tauta eidon, kai ēnoigē ho naos tēs skēnēs tou martyriou en tō ouranō). The phrase ho naos tēs skēnēs tou martyriou ("the temple of the tabernacle of testimony") is a dense, deliberately constructed expression that combines multiple elements of Israel's sacred architecture.

The word naos ("temple, sanctuary, inner shrine") refers not to the entire temple complex (hieron) but to the inner sanctuary where God's presence dwells. Throughout this document, naos is the word used for the heavenly temple (7:15, 11:19, 14:15, 17, 16:1, 17). It is the holy of holies, the place of God's actual presence.

The word skēnē ("tent, tabernacle") refers to the wilderness tabernacle — the portable dwelling of God that traveled with Israel from Sinai through the wilderness wandering. The Greek phrase skēnē tou martyriou ("tent of testimony" or "tabernacle of witness") is the LXX's characteristic designation for this structure (Numbers 1:50, 53; 17:7-8; Acts 7:44). The word martyriou ("of testimony, of witness") derives from the same root as martyria ("testimony, witness"), the word that defines the identity of the faithful in this document (1:2, 9; 6:9; 11:7; 12:11, 17; 19:10; 20:4). The tabernacle was called the "tent of testimony" because it housed the ark containing the tablets of the covenant — the stone tablets that were God's testimony, his witness, his authoritative declaration of who he is and what he requires. The ark was also called "the ark of the testimony" (Exodus 25:22; 26:33-34).

In 11:19, the heavenly temple was opened and "the ark of his covenant appeared in his temple." Now the temple opens again, but this time what emerges is not the ark but the seven angels carrying the final plagues. The two openings are related: the ark of the covenant in 11:19 signaled that the judgments to follow are covenant-based, rooted in God's character as revealed in his testimony. The opening of the "temple of the tabernacle of testimony" in 15:5 reinforces the same point with even greater emphasis. The plagues that emerge from this temple are not arbitrary acts of power; they proceed from the place where God's testimony is kept. They are the covenantal consequences of rebellion against the God who has made himself known.

Stephen's speech in Acts 7:44 provides the hermeneutical framework for this image: "Our fathers had the tabernacle of testimony in the wilderness, just as He who spoke to Moses directed him to make it according to the pattern which he had seen." The earthly tabernacle was a copy of a heavenly original. The author of Revelation now shows the heavenly original itself. The bowls of wrath come from the ultimate reality of which the earthly tabernacle was only a shadow.

The verb ēnoigē ("was opened") is the same verb used in 11:19 for the opening of the temple. The passive voice indicates divine action: the temple does not open by itself or at human initiative. God opens it. The opening signals that God is now acting from the innermost center of his being, from the place of his covenant presence.
div.title: The Seven Angels in Priestly Garments
div.p: "And the seven angels who had the seven plagues came out of the temple, clothed in linen, clean and bright, and their chests wrapped with golden sashes" (kai exēlthon hoi hepta angeloi hoi echontes tas hepta plēgas ek tou naou, endedymenoi linon katharon lampron kai periezōsmenoi peri ta stēthē zōnas chrysas). The angels emerge from the naos — from the inner sanctuary, from the very presence of God. Their clothing is described with deliberate care.

"Clothed in linen, clean and bright" (endedymenoi linon katharon lampron). The word linon ("linen") is the material of priestly garments. In Exodus 28:39-42 and Leviticus 16:4, the high priest's garments for the Day of Atonement are specified as linen: "He shall put on the holy linen tunic, and the linen undergarments shall be next to his body, and he shall be girded with the linen sash." The adjective katharon ("clean, pure") describes both ritual and moral purity. The word lampron ("bright, shining, radiant") adds the dimension of heavenly glory. The angels' garments combine the priestly purity of the Day of Atonement liturgy with the radiance of heavenly beings. They are priests emerging from the sanctuary to execute God's decree.

In Ezekiel 9:2-3, a parallel scene occurs: six men come with "destroying weapons" in their hands, and "the man clothed in linen" accompanies them. They emerge to execute judgment on Jerusalem, beginning at the sanctuary (Ezekiel 9:6). In Daniel 10:5-6, the angelic figure who appears to Daniel is "dressed in linen, and his waist was girded with a belt of pure gold of Uphaz." The linen-and-gold combination in Revelation 15:6 draws on this same tradition of angelic figures who serve as agents of God's direct action.

"And their chests wrapped with golden sashes" (kai periezōsmenoi peri ta stēthē zōnas chrysas). The golden sash or belt across the chest recalls the description of the risen Christ in 1:13: "clothed in a robe reaching to the feet, and girded across his chest with a golden sash" (periezōsmenon pros tois mastois zōnēn chrysan). The angels' attire mirrors the attire of the risen Christ himself. They are his representatives, dressed as he is dressed, acting on his authority. The golden sash across the chest (rather than at the waist, where a working servant would wear it) indicates the dignity of office. These angels are not servants performing menial tasks; they are royal-priestly agents executing a sovereign decree.
div.title: The Golden Bowls
div.p: "And one of the four living creatures gave the seven angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God, who lives forever and ever" (kai hen ek tōn tessarōn zōōn edōken tois hepta angelois hepta phialas chrysas gemousas tou thymou tou theou tou zōntos eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn). The four living creatures (zōa) appeared first in the throne-room vision of chapter 4, stationed around and in the center of the throne (4:6-8), ceaselessly declaring "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty" (4:8). In 5:8, they fell down before the Lamb when he took the scroll. In 6:1-7, each of the first four living creatures called out "Come!" as the first four seals were opened. They are the innermost attendants of God's throne, the closest beings to his presence.

That one of these living creatures gives the bowls to the angels connects the bowl judgments directly to the throne of God. The bowls do not originate from a secondary source; they are handed over from the center of the divine court. The act of giving (edōken) indicates deliberate transfer of a prepared instrument. The bowls have been filled; the wrath has been measured; the living creature delivers them to the executing agents.

The word phialas ("bowls, shallow cups") refers to a wide, flat bowl used for libations in temple worship. In the LXX, the cognate term appears in descriptions of temple vessels used for offerings and libations (Numbers 7:13-14, 84-85). In 5:8, the twenty-four elders held "golden bowls full of incense, which are the prayers of the saints" (phialas chrysas gemousas thymimatōn). There, the golden bowls held the prayers of God's people ascending to God. Now the golden bowls hold the wrath of God descending upon the earth. The correspondence is deliberate: the saints' prayers for justice (5:8) and the martyrs' cries for vindication (6:9-10) have been received, and the bowls that once carried prayers upward now carry the divine response downward. The prayers have been answered; the answer is the bowls.

The phrase "full of the wrath of God" (gemousas tou thymou tou theou) uses the word gemousas ("full, filled to capacity"). The bowls are not partially filled; they contain the entirety of the wrath that has been stored. The modifier "who lives forever and ever" (tou zōntos eis tous aiōnas tōn aiōnōn) is added to the divine name not as a mere epithet but as a theological assertion: the God whose wrath fills these bowls is the living God, the eternal one. The beast system, for all its apparent power, is temporary — it has forty-two months (13:5). The God who opposes it lives forever. The contrast between the beast's limited time and God's eternal life underscores the inevitability of the bowls' fulfillment. The wrath of the eternal God will outlast the temporary power of any earthly regime.
div.title: The Smoke of Glory
div.p: "And the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and from His power" (kai egemisthē ho naos kapnou ek tēs doxēs tou theou kai ek tēs dynameōs autou). This is one of the most important images in the chapter, drawing on three foundational moments in Israel's history when God's presence overwhelmed the sacred space:

First, Exodus 40:34-35: "Then the cloud covered the tent of meeting, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle. And Moses was not able to enter the tent of meeting because the cloud had settled on it, and the glory of the LORD filled the tabernacle." At the completion of the wilderness tabernacle, God's glory (kabod in Hebrew, doxa in the LXX) filled the structure so completely that even Moses — the servant who spoke with God face to face (Exodus 33:11) — could not enter.

Second, 1 Kings 8:10-11: "And it happened that when the priests came from the holy place, the cloud filled the house of the LORD, so that the priests could not stand to minister because of the cloud, for the glory of the LORD filled the house of the LORD." At the dedication of Solomon's temple, the same phenomenon occurred. The glory was so overwhelming that the priests — those specifically authorized to serve in God's presence — could not continue their ministry. The cloud stopped all human activity in the sanctuary.

Third, Isaiah 6:4: "And the foundations of the thresholds trembled at the voice of him who called out, while the temple was filling with smoke." In Isaiah's vision of the Lord enthroned, smoke filled the temple while the seraphim declared God's holiness. The smoke accompanied the declaration of God's absolute holiness and Isaiah's overwhelming awareness of human inadequacy before it.

In each of these precedents, the pattern is the same: God's glory manifests with such intensity that the sacred space becomes inaccessible to all creatures, even those authorized to serve there. The glory is not a gentle presence but an overwhelming one. It stops all activity. No one can enter, minister, or function in its presence.

In Revelation 15:8, the heavenly temple fills with smoke from two sources: "from the glory of God" (ek tēs doxēs tou theou) and "from his power" (ek tēs dynameōs autou). The doxa ("glory") is God's manifest presence; the dynamis ("power") is his active force. The combination indicates that God's presence is not passive or contemplative but active and operative. The smoke signals that God is acting — that the power behind the bowls is being unleashed from the innermost sanctuary.

"And no one was able to enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished" (kai oudeis edynato eiselthein eis ton naon achri telesthōsin hai hepta plēgai tōn hepta angelōn). The clause "no one was able to enter" (oudeis edynato eiselthein) parallels Moses' inability to enter the tabernacle (Exodus 40:35) and the priests' inability to minister in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 8:11). But in those precedents, the inaccessibility was temporary: Moses eventually entered, and the priests eventually resumed their ministry. Here the inaccessibility has a defined endpoint: "until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished" (achri telesthōsin hai hepta plēgai). The verb telesthōsin ("are finished, are completed") is from teleō, the same verb used in verse 1 (etelesthē, "is finished"). The completion of the plagues is the condition for the temple's reopening.

The theological significance is profound. As long as the plagues are being poured out, the temple is inaccessible. No one — not angels, not elders, not living creatures, not saints — can enter to intercede, to offer prayers, to make atonement, or to request mercy. The time for intercession has passed. The process is irrevocable. Once the bowls begin, they will be completed without interruption or mitigation. This is the corollary of the word "last" (eschatas) in verse 1: these are the final plagues, and once they begin, they run their course to completion.

The image also indicates that the judgments are not being carried out reluctantly or with the possibility of divine reconsideration. The smoke of glory filling the temple is not a sign of divine anguish but of divine majesty in action. God's glory and power are so fully engaged in the act of judgment that the sanctuary is completely occupied. There is no room for any other business. The entire heavenly temple is given over to this single purpose.

The word achri ("until") is the temporal marker that connects the present inaccessibility to a future restoration. The plagues will end. The smoke will clear. The temple will be accessible again. And indeed, by Revelation 21:3-4, the ultimate vision is of God dwelling with his people: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is among the people, and he will dwell among them." In 21:22, John sees "no temple" in the new Jerusalem, "for the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple." The smoke-filled, inaccessible temple of 15:8 is the penultimate reality; the final reality is unmediated presence, with no temple needed because God himself is the temple. But between the penultimate and the ultimate lies the completion of the bowls — the finishing of the wrath that must run its course before the new creation can emerge.

div.title: Summary of the Chapter's Argument
div.p: Revelation 15 is the shortest chapter in the document, only eight verses, but it functions as the theological preamble to the seven bowls of wrath. It answers three questions that the preceding chapters have raised:

First, what happens to those who conquered the beast? They stand on the far side of the sea of glass mixed with fire, in the presence of God, holding harps and singing. The threefold pressure of the beast system — political worship, idolatrous image, economic mark — has been faced and overcome. The faithful who were "given over" to the beast's authority (13:7) are now revealed as the true conquerors. Their victory was won not by military force or political resistance but by the blood of the Lamb, the word of their testimony, and their refusal to love their lives even unto death (12:11). The sea of glass mixed with fire is the Red Sea of the new Exodus: they have passed through, and they stand on the far shore.

Second, what is the character of the coming judgment? The conquerors' song answers this definitively: God's works are great and marvelous, his ways are righteous and true, he alone is holy, and his righteous acts have been revealed. The judgment is not an eruption of arbitrary power but the manifestation of God's covenant faithfulness. The song is composed entirely of scriptural language drawn from the Torah, the Psalms, and the Prophets, indicating that the bowls fulfill what Israel's scriptures have always declared about God's justice. The song of Moses and the song of the Lamb are one song because the new Exodus completes the pattern of the first: deliverance for the faithful, judgment for the oppressor, and the vindication of God's righteous character before all nations.

Third, what is the source and authority of the bowls? They emerge from the temple of the tabernacle of testimony — the heavenly original of which the earthly tabernacle was a copy. The angels who carry them are clothed in priestly garments that mirror the attire of the risen Christ himself. The bowls are given to them by one of the four living creatures from the innermost circle of God's presence. The smoke of God's glory fills the temple so completely that no one can enter until the plagues are finished. Every element of the preparation scene — the temple, the priestly garments, the golden bowls, the living creatures, the glory-cloud — declares that what is about to happen proceeds from the deepest center of God's being, from his covenant testimony, and from his manifest glory. The bowls are not the work of subordinate agents acting independently; they are the direct expression of God's own presence and power, authorized from his throne, executed by his priestly ministers, and irreversible until completed.

The chapter's placement between the harvest preview of chapter 14 and the bowl outpouring of chapter 16 is deliberate. The author pauses at the moment of maximum tension — judgment has been announced but not yet executed — to show the hearers two things simultaneously: the safety of the conquerors and the certainty of the wrath. Those who belong to the Lamb are on the far side of the sea, singing. Those who belong to the beast are about to receive the bowls. The conquerors' song is the theological interpretation of the bowls before they are poured: everything that follows in chapter 16 must be read through the lens of "Great and marvelous are your works... righteous and true are your ways." The judgments are not random catastrophes; they are the righteous acts of the King of the nations, revealed at last.

div.title: Revelation 16 — First-Century Reading
Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (Revelation 15): Chapter 15 served as the theological preamble to the seven bowls of wrath. It opened with the third great sign in heaven: seven angels carrying seven plagues, "which are the last, because in them the wrath of God is finished" (15:1). The verb etelesthē ("was finished, was completed") signaled that these plagues are not preliminary or partial but terminal — the conclusion of the sequence of divine judgment that began with the seals and continued through the trumpets. Before the bowls were poured, the author showed the conquerors — those who had been victorious over the beast, his image, and the number of his name — standing on the sea of glass mixed with fire, holding harps of God and singing "the song of Moses, the bond-servant of God, and the song of the Lamb" (15:2-4). Their song was a mosaic of scriptural phrases drawn from Deuteronomy 32, the Psalms, and the Prophets, declaring God's works "great and marvelous," his ways "righteous and true," and affirming that "all the nations will come and worship before you, for your righteous acts have been revealed" (15:3-4). The conquerors' position on the far side of the sea of glass recapitulated Israel's position on the far shore of the Red Sea after the crossing: they had passed through the ordeal; the judgment was not for them but for their oppressors.

The temple of the tabernacle of testimony in heaven then opened, and the seven angels emerged clothed in priestly linen with golden sashes — garments that mirrored the attire of the risen Christ in 1:13. One of the four living creatures gave the angels seven golden bowls full of the wrath of God (15:7), connecting the bowls directly to God's throne. The golden bowls corresponded to the golden bowls of incense "which are the prayers of the saints" in 5:8 — the saints' prayers for justice ascending to God now answered by bowls of wrath descending on the earth. The temple filled with smoke from God's glory and power, and "no one was able to enter the temple until the seven plagues of the seven angels were finished" (15:8). The inaccessibility of the temple meant that the time for intercession had passed. Once the bowls began, they would run their course to completion without interruption or mitigation.

What the author argues immediately after (Revelation 17): Chapter 17 returns to one element introduced during the bowls: Babylon. After the seventh bowl declared "It is done" and described the splitting of "the great city" into three parts and the giving of "Babylon the great" the cup of the wine of the fury of God's wrath (16:19), one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls approaches John and says: "Come, I will show you the judgment of the great harlot who sits on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed acts of immorality" (17:1-2). The angel carries John to a wilderness (17:3), where he sees a woman seated on a scarlet beast with seven heads and ten horns, full of blasphemous names — the same beast described in chapter 13. The woman is arrayed in purple and scarlet, adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls, holding a golden cup "full of abominations and of the unclean things of her immorality" (17:4). On her forehead is written "BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH" (17:5). She is "drunk with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the witnesses of Jesus" (17:6). The chapter then provides an interpretive key for the beast (17:7-18): the seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings; the ten horns are ten kings who will give their authority to the beast; the beast "was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss and go to destruction" (17:8); and the ten horns will turn against the harlot and destroy her (17:16-17), because "God has put it in their hearts to execute his purpose" (17:17). Chapter 17 thus unfolds the identity and judgment of Babylon that the seventh bowl announced but did not narrate in detail.

How chapter 16 connects the surrounding argument: Chapter 16 is the execution of what chapter 15 prepared. The structural pattern is now familiar from the author's prior sequences: a preparation scene in heaven (chapters 4-5 before the seals; 8:2-5 before the trumpets; chapter 15 before the bowls) followed by the sequential outpouring of judgments on earth. The conquerors sang that God's works are "great and marvelous" and his ways "righteous and true" (15:3); the bowl judgments demonstrate this by enacting justice that is explicitly declared righteous by angelic voices within the narrative itself (16:5-7). The song's affirmation that "your righteous acts have been revealed" (15:4) receives its concrete fulfillment as each bowl makes those righteous acts visible.

The bowls are also the final answer to the martyrs' cry under the altar in 6:9-10: "How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" The seals partially answered that cry. The trumpets intensified the answer. The bowls complete it. The angel of the waters explicitly makes this connection: "They poured out the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. They deserve it" (16:6). The altar itself responds: "Yes, Lord God, the Almighty, true and righteous are your judgments" (16:7) — the same altar under which the martyrs' souls waited, now confirming that justice has come.

The chapter also maintains the Exodus pattern that has governed the entire document's judgment sequences. The seals echoed certain Exodus plagues partially; the trumpets intensified them (affecting a third of the earth, sea, rivers, and heavenly bodies). The bowls now bring the Exodus pattern to its fullest expression: the plagues are total, not fractional, and they recapitulate the Egyptian plagues with unmistakable directness. The author has been building toward this climax since the conquerors sang "the song of Moses" on the far side of the sea of glass. The bowls are the new Exodus plagues, poured out on the new Pharaoh (the beast) and his followers, to complete the deliverance of God's people.

Between the sixth and seventh bowls, the author inserts a parenthetical warning and a brief narrative about the gathering at Armageddon (16:12-16), following the same structural pattern used between the sixth and seventh seals (chapter 7) and between the sixth and seventh trumpets (chapters 10-11:13). In each sequence, the pause between six and seven provides interpretive comment, exhortation, or additional vision before the climactic seventh event.

div.title: Verse 1: The Command from the Temple
div.p: "Then I heard a loud voice from the temple, saying to the seven angels, 'Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God.'"

"Then I heard a loud voice from the temple" (kai ekousa megalēs phōnēs ek tou naou). The voice comes from the naos — the inner sanctuary, the holy of holies. In 15:8, the temple was filled with smoke from the glory of God and his power, and "no one was able to enter the temple." Since no angel, elder, living creature, or any other being can enter the temple during the outpouring, the voice that issues the command from within the temple can only be God's own voice. No intermediary delivers this command. The bowls are not released by angelic initiative or by the delegation of authority through a chain of command; they are commanded directly by the voice of God from the place of his manifest presence.

The phrase "loud voice" (megalēs phōnēs) characterizes divine speech throughout this document. The risen Christ spoke with "a loud voice" (phōnē megalē, 1:10). The heavenly declarations consistently use this phrase (5:2, 12; 6:10; 7:2, 10; 10:3; 11:12, 15; 12:10; 14:7, 9, 15, 18; 16:1, 17; 19:1, 17; 21:3). The loudness is not a matter of volume but of authority and urgency: what is spoken with a great voice is a definitive divine pronouncement.

"Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God" (hypagete kai ekcheete tas hepta phialas tou thymou tou theou eis tēn gēn). The verb ekcheete ("pour out") is the characteristic verb for the outpouring of libations and of blood. In the LXX, ekcheo is used for the pouring out of drink offerings (Exodus 30:9; Numbers 28:7), for the pouring out of blood at the base of the altar (Leviticus 4:7, 18, 25, 30, 34), and critically, for the pouring out of God's wrath (Psalm 69:24 [LXX 68:25]: "Pour out [ekcheon] your indignation upon them"; Jeremiah 10:25: "Pour out [ekcheon] your wrath on the nations"; Ezekiel 7:8: "I will pour out [ekcheo] my wrath on you"; Ezekiel 14:19: "I pour out [ekcheo] my wrath upon it in blood"; Ezekiel 20:8, 13, 21: "I will pour out [ekcheo] my wrath on them"; Zephaniah 3:8: "to pour out [ekcheo] on them my indignation, all my burning anger"). The pouring-out language is deeply embedded in Israel's prophetic vocabulary for divine judgment. What the prophets announced, the bowls execute.

The command "go" (hypagete) sends the angels forth from the heavenly temple into the earth. The movement is from God's presence outward into the domain where the beast exercises authority. The earth (gē) is the same earth over which the beast was given authority (13:7-8, 12) and on which the beast's worshipers dwell (13:14). The bowls descend on the beast's territory.

div.title: Verse 2: The First Bowl — Sores on the Beast's Worshipers
div.p: "So the first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth; and it became a loathsome and malignant sore on the people who had the mark of the beast and who worshiped his image."

"The first angel went and poured out his bowl on the earth" (kai apēlthen ho prōtos kai execheen tēn phialēn autou eis tēn gēn). The first bowl is poured "on the earth" (eis tēn gēn), the same domain from which the second beast arose (13:11) and where the beast's mark was imposed (13:16). The verb execheen ("poured out") is the aorist of ekcheo, the same word used in the command of verse 1.

"And it became a loathsome and malignant sore on the people who had the mark of the beast and who worshiped his image" (kai egeneto helkos kakon kai ponēron epi tous anthrōpous tous echontas to charagma tou thēriou kai tous proskunountas tē eikoni autou). The word helkos ("sore, ulcer, boil") is the LXX term for the sixth plague of Egypt. Exodus 9:9-11 (LXX): "It will become fine dust over all the land of Egypt and will become boils (helkē) breaking out in sores (phlyktides) on man and beast throughout the land of Egypt." Exodus 9:10: "And it became boils (helkē) breaking out in sores on man and beast." Exodus 9:11: "And the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils (tōn helkōn), for the boils (ta helkē) were on the magicians and on all the Egyptians." The verbal parallel is precise: helkos in Revelation 16:2 directly recapitulates the helkē of Exodus 9. The first bowl plague corresponds to the sixth Egyptian plague.

A critical detail from the Exodus account illuminates the author's point: "the magicians could not stand before Moses because of the boils" (Exodus 9:11). The magicians — Egypt's equivalent of the second beast's false prophets, who had replicated Moses' signs up to a point (Exodus 7:11, 22; 8:7) — were themselves struck by the plague and rendered unable to function. The boils incapacitated the very agents of Pharaoh's opposition. The first bowl's sores fall specifically on "the people who had the mark of the beast and who worshiped his image" — the beast's own people, the participants in the beast's system. Just as the boils struck Egypt's magicians, the first bowl strikes the beast's devotees.

The adjectives kakon kai ponēron ("loathsome and malignant" or "evil and painful") intensify the description. The word ponēron ("painful, grievous, malignant") appears again in 16:11 when the beast-worshipers "blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores (helkōn)." The sores persist through the subsequent bowls — they are still present at the fifth bowl (16:11), indicating that the effects of the bowls are cumulative, not sequential replacements. Each plague adds to the burden of the preceding ones.

The Deuteronomic covenant curses provide additional background. Deuteronomy 28:27 (LXX): "The LORD will smite you with the boils (helkei) of Egypt and with tumors and with the scab and with the itch, from which you cannot be healed." Deuteronomy 28:35: "The LORD will strike you on the knees and legs with sore boils (helkei ponēro), from which you cannot be healed, from the sole of your foot to the crown of your head." The phrase helkei ponēro ("sore/malignant boil") in Deuteronomy 28:35 is nearly identical to helkos kakon kai ponēron in Revelation 16:2. In Deuteronomy, these boils are covenant curses — the consequences of Israel's unfaithfulness to God's covenant. The author of Revelation applies the covenant-curse language not to unfaithful Israel but to those who have given their allegiance to the beast. The beast's worshipers, having entered a covenant of sorts with the beast (receiving his mark, worshiping his image), now receive the covenant curses that attend unfaithfulness to the true God. They chose the wrong covenant partner, and the consequences follow.

The targeting of the plague is precise: only those with the mark of the beast and those who worship his image are struck. This selectivity recapitulates the Exodus pattern in which the plagues fell on Egypt but not on Israel. Exodus 8:22-23 (LXX): "I will set apart (diastelo) the land of Goshen, where my people are dwelling... I will put a division (lytrōsin, 'redemption/distinction') between my people and your people." Exodus 9:4: "The LORD will make a distinction (diastele) between the livestock of Israel and the livestock of Egypt." Exodus 9:26: "Only in the land of Goshen, where the sons of Israel were, there was no hail." Exodus 10:23: "But all the sons of Israel had light in their dwellings." The God who distinguished between Egypt and Israel in the first Exodus distinguishes between the beast's worshipers and his own people in the new Exodus. The sores fall on those who bear the beast's mark, not on those who bear the seal of God (7:3; 9:4; 14:1).

div.title: Verse 3: The Second Bowl — The Sea Becomes Blood
div.p: "The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became blood like that of a dead man; and every living thing in the sea died."

"The second angel poured out his bowl into the sea, and it became blood like that of a dead man" (kai ho deuteros execheen tēn phialēn autou eis tēn thalassan, kai egeneto haima hōs nekrou). The second bowl targets the sea (thalassa), the same domain from which the first beast arose (13:1). The sea becomes "blood like that of a dead man" (haima hōs nekrou) — not merely reddened water but the thick, coagulated blood of a corpse. The simile "like that of a dead man" distinguishes this from fresh, flowing blood; it evokes death in its most visceral, physical form. The water is not merely contaminated but transformed into something repulsive and lifeless.

The Exodus parallel is the first plague: the Nile turned to blood. Exodus 7:20-21 (LXX): "He lifted up the staff and struck the water that was in the Nile, in the sight of Pharaoh and in the sight of his servants, and all the water that was in the Nile was turned to blood (eis haima). The fish that were in the Nile died, and the Nile became foul (epōzesen), and the Egyptians could not drink water from the Nile, and the blood was through all the land of Egypt."

The second trumpet had a partial parallel: "something like a great mountain burning with fire was thrown into the sea; and a third of the sea became blood, and a third of the creatures which were in the sea and had life, died, and a third of the ships were destroyed" (8:8-9). The trumpet affected one-third; the bowl affects the totality. The escalation from trumpet to bowl follows the same intensification pattern visible throughout the three judgment sequences. The seals affected one-fourth (6:8); the trumpets affected one-third (8:7-12); the bowls affect the whole. The plagues have been building toward this comprehensive judgment.

"And every living thing in the sea died" (kai pasa psychē zōēs apethanen ta en tē thalassē). The phrase pasa psychē zōēs ("every living soul/thing") echoes Genesis 1:20-21 (LXX), where God created the sea creatures: "Let the waters teem with swarms of living creatures (psychōn zōsōn)" and "God created the great sea monsters and every living creature (pasan psychēn zōōn) that moves, with which the waters swarmed." The creation language is inverted: what God created in the sea is now destroyed. The bowl undoes the work of the third day of creation (Genesis 1:9-10 separating the waters) and the fifth day (Genesis 1:20-23 filling the seas with life). The judgment is a partial un-creation — a reversal of the creative acts that established the ordered world. This theme of un-creation runs through the entire bowl sequence and echoes the prophetic tradition where cosmic dissolution accompanies divine judgment (Isaiah 34:4; Jeremiah 4:23-26; Joel 2:10, 30-31).

div.title: Verses 4-7: The Third Bowl — Rivers Become Blood, and the Declaration of Divine Justice
div.p: "Then the third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of waters; and they became blood. And I heard the angel of the waters saying, 'Righteous are You, who are and who were, O Holy One, because You judged these things; for they poured out the blood of saints and prophets, and You have given them blood to drink. They deserve it.' And I heard the altar saying, 'Yes, O Lord God, the Almighty, true and righteous are Your judgments.'"
div.title: The Third Plague
div.p: "The third angel poured out his bowl into the rivers and the springs of waters; and they became blood" (kai ho tritos execheen tēn phialēn autou eis tous potamous kai tas pēgas tōn hydatōn, kai egeneto haima). The third bowl continues the first plague of Egypt but extends it from the sea (bowl two) to the inland waters — the rivers (potamous) and springs (pēgas). All water sources are now affected. The Exodus account similarly describes the blood-contamination extending to all water: "the blood was throughout all the land of Egypt" (Exodus 7:21), including "their rivers and their ponds and all their pools of water" (Exodus 7:19). The first angel's proclamation in 14:7 called the earth to "worship him who made the heaven and the earth and sea and springs of waters (pēgas hydatōn)." The springs of waters that God created are now turned to blood as instruments of his judgment.

The third trumpet had a partial parallel: a burning star called Wormwood fell on "a third of the rivers and on the springs of waters," making the waters bitter and causing many to die (8:10-11). Again, the trumpet was partial (one-third); the bowl is total. And whereas the trumpet made the waters bitter and poisonous, the bowl makes them blood — a more direct and visceral transformation.
div.title: The Angel of the Waters and the Declaration of Justice
div.p: "And I heard the angel of the waters saying" (kai ekousa tou angelou tōn hydatōn legontos). The phrase "the angel of the waters" (tou angelou tōn hydatōn) indicates an angelic being assigned to or responsible for the waters. The concept of angels governing elements of creation appears in Jewish tradition of this period. In this document, an angel has "authority over fire" (14:18); the four angels at the Euphrates (9:14-15) govern a specific geographical feature; the angel of the abyss rules that domain (9:11). In 1 Enoch 60:16-22, angels are assigned to various natural phenomena: "the spirit of the sea," "the spirit of the hoar-frost," "the spirit of the hail," "the spirit of the snow," "the spirit of the wind." The angel of the waters speaks not in protest against the contamination of his domain but in affirmation of the justice that requires it. Even the guardian of the element being destroyed acknowledges the righteousness of the judgment.

"Righteous are You, who are and who were, O Holy One, because You judged these things" (dikaios ei, ho ōn kai ho ēn, ho hosios, hoti tauta ekrinas). The declaration begins with an assertion of God's righteousness (dikaios, "righteous, just"). The word dikaios is judicial: it means that God's verdict is correct, fair, and in accordance with what is due. The phrase addresses God directly in the second person: "You are righteous."

The divine title "who are and who were" (ho ōn kai ho ēn) is a shortened form of the three-part title used at the opening of the document: "who is and who was and who is to come" (ho ōn kai ho ēn kai ho erchomenos, 1:4, 8; 4:8). The conspicuous absence of the third element — "who is to come" (ho erchomenos) — is significant. In 1:4, 1:8, and 4:8, God's identity was described as spanning past, present, and future: the one who is, who was, and who is coming. Now, at the pouring of the bowls, the "coming" has arrived. God is no longer described as "the one who is to come" because he has come — his coming is enacted in the bowls. The future element has become present. This same shortened title appeared in 11:17, where the twenty-four elders praised God after the seventh trumpet: "We give you thanks, O Lord God, the Almighty, who are and who were" — again omitting "who is to come" because the kingdom had arrived (11:15). The shortened title is a literary signal that the author's eschatological expectation is being realized within the narrative: God's "coming" is no longer anticipated but actualized.

The word hosios ("Holy One") is the same word used in the conquerors' song of 15:4: "For you alone are holy (hosios)." As noted in the analysis of chapter 15, hosios in the LXX carries the sense of covenant faithfulness, trustworthiness, and loyalty — the character of one who keeps his commitments. God's holiness (hosiotes) is not abstract purity but demonstrated faithfulness: he does what he said he would do. The bowls are acts of a hosios God — a God who is faithful to his promises, including his promise to avenge the blood of his servants.

The conjunction hoti ("because") introduces the reason for the declaration of righteousness: "because you judged these things" (hoti tauta ekrinas). The verb ekrinas ("you judged") is aorist: the judgment is accomplished, not hypothetical. God's righteousness is demonstrated by his judgment, not merely by his character in the abstract. He is righteous because he acts righteously — because he responds to injustice with justice.

"For they poured out the blood of saints and prophets, and You have given them blood to drink. They deserve it" (hoti haima hagiōn kai prophētōn exechean, kai haima autois dedōkas piein; axioi eisin). The angel now states the specific ground of justice: the principle of proportional requital. The verb exechean ("they poured out") uses the same word (ekcheo) that describes the pouring of the bowls themselves. The beast's followers "poured out" (exechean) the blood of saints and prophets; God "poured out" (execheen, v. 4) the bowl that turned their waters to blood. The same verb connects the crime and its punishment. The punishment mirrors the offense: those who shed blood are given blood to drink.

The phrase "saints and prophets" (hagiōn kai prophētōn) identifies the victims whose blood was poured out. The "saints" (hagioi) are the covenant community — the same "saints" against whom the beast made war (13:7). The "prophets" (prophētai) are the witnesses who spoke God's word — the two witnesses of chapter 11 (11:10: "these two prophets tormented those who dwell on the earth"), and more broadly, the prophetic line extending back through Israel's history. Jesus' warning about the blood of the prophets is echoed: "so that upon you may fall the guilt of all the righteous blood shed on earth, from the blood of righteous Abel to the blood of Zechariah, the son of Berechiah" (Matthew 23:35). In 18:24, Babylon will be found guilty of "the blood of prophets and of saints and of all who have been slain on the earth." The shedding of prophetic and saintly blood is the specific injustice that the bowls address.

The phrase "they deserve it" (axioi eisin, literally "they are worthy/deserving") uses the word axios, which elsewhere in this document describes the Lamb's worthiness: "Worthy (axios) is the Lamb that was slain" (5:12). The word axios indicates that what is received corresponds exactly to what is due. In 5:12, the Lamb is worthy of honor and power because of his sacrificial death. In 16:6, the beast-worshipers are worthy of blood-to-drink because of their shedding of blood. The word operates with exact justice in both directions: the worthy Lamb receives what is due to the worthy Lamb; the blood-shedders receive what is due to blood-shedders.

The principle of proportional justice has deep roots in the Torah. Genesis 9:6: "Whoever sheds man's blood, by man his blood shall be shed." Exodus 21:23-25: "life for life, eye for eye, tooth for tooth." The same principle operates in the prophets. Isaiah 49:26: "I will feed your oppressors with their own flesh, and they will become drunk with their own blood as with sweet wine." Obadiah 15: "As you have done, it will be done to you. Your dealings will return on your own head." The angel's declaration places the third bowl squarely within this tradition: the judgment is not arbitrary but proportional, not vindictive but just. Blood for blood.
div.title: The Altar's Confirmation
div.p: "And I heard the altar saying, 'Yes, O Lord God, the Almighty, true and righteous are Your judgments'" (kai ekousa tou thysiastēriou legontos, Nai, kyrie ho theos ho pantokratōr, alēthinai kai dikaiai hai kriseis sou). The altar (to thysiastērion) speaks. This is the same altar under which the souls of the martyrs cried out in 6:9-10: "How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" The altar's confirmation in 16:7 is the answer to the martyrs' cry. The question "How long?" is now answered: the time has come; the judgment is underway; the blood is being avenged.

The altar speaks as a personified witness. In the document's structure, the altar has been consistently associated with the martyrs and their prayers. In 6:9, the souls were under the altar. In 8:3-5, the angel offered incense with the saints' prayers on the golden altar, and fire from the altar was thrown to earth, inaugurating the trumpet judgments. In 9:13, the sixth trumpet's command came from the golden altar's horns. In 14:18, the angel from the altar (who had authority over fire) directed the grape harvest. The altar is the location where the martyrs' blood and prayers accumulated, and it now validates the judgment that answers those prayers.

The words "true and righteous" (alēthinai kai dikaiai) directly echo the conquerors' song of 15:3: "Righteous and true are your ways" (dikaiai kai alēthinai hai hodoi sou). The same pair of adjectives describes God's ways in the song and God's judgments in the altar's confirmation. The bowls are the concrete manifestation of the "righteous and true ways" that the conquerors praised. The language of the song and the language of the altar's confirmation form an inclusio around the first three bowls: the theological interpretation (the song) precedes the events, and the theological confirmation (the altar) follows them. The hearers are not left to evaluate the bowls on their own; they are told, by the conquerors before and by the altar after, that these judgments are righteous.

The title "Lord God, the Almighty" (kyrie ho theos ho pantokratōr) is the same title used in the conquerors' song (15:3) and throughout the document (1:8; 4:8; 11:17; 19:6; 21:22). The word pantokratōr ("Almighty, ruler of all") asserts God's sovereignty over all competing powers. The altar affirms not only the justice but the sovereignty behind the judgments: the Almighty is acting, and his actions are both true (corresponding to reality) and righteous (corresponding to justice).

div.title: Verses 8-9: The Fourth Bowl — Scorching Heat from the Sun
div.p: "The fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was given to it to scorch men with fire. Men were scorched with fierce heat; and they blasphemed the name of God who has the power over these plagues, and they did not repent so as to give Him glory."

"The fourth angel poured out his bowl upon the sun, and it was given to it to scorch men with fire" (kai ho tetartos execheen tēn phialēn autou epi ton hēlion, kai edothē autō kaumatisai tous anthrōpous en pyri). The fourth bowl targets the sun. Unlike the previous bowls, which contaminate creation (sores on people, sea and rivers turned to blood), this bowl weaponizes a created element by intensifying its normal function. The sun, which God created to give light and warmth (Genesis 1:14-18), is now given permission to scorch with fire. The passive edothē ("it was given") is the divine passive: the sun's intensified burning is permitted by God, not an autonomous action. The same passive governed the beast's authority (13:5, 7, 14, 15) and now governs the instrument of judgment. God grants the sun the capacity to burn men with fire.

The fourth trumpet had affected the sun partially: "a third of the sun and a third of the moon and a third of the stars were struck, so that a third of them would be darkened" (8:12). The trumpet diminished the sun's light; the bowl intensifies its heat. The two judgments are not contradictory but represent different modes of cosmic disruption: the trumpet reduced illumination; the bowl increases scorching. Both demonstrate God's authority over the celestial bodies that were created to serve human life.

The verb kaumatisai ("to scorch, to burn with intense heat") and the related noun kauma appear in the eschatological promises as conditions from which the redeemed are protected. In 7:16, those before the throne are promised: "They will hunger no longer, nor thirst anymore; nor will the sun beat down on them (oude mē pesē ep' autous ho hēlios), nor any heat (kauma)" — a quotation of Isaiah 49:10 (LXX): "They will not hunger or thirst, nor will the scorching heat (kauma) or the sun strike them." The promise of protection from the sun's heat for the faithful is the counterpart of the sun's intensified heat on the unfaithful. The bowls fall on the beast's worshipers; the promises of protection cover those who stand with the Lamb.

"Men were scorched with fierce heat" (ekaumatisthēsan hoi anthrōpoi kauma mega). The noun kauma mega ("fierce/great heat") emphasizes the intensity of the scorching. This is not ordinary discomfort but extreme, burning affliction.

"And they blasphemed the name of God who has the power over these plagues, and they did not repent so as to give Him glory" (kai eblasphēmēsan to onoma tou theou tou echontos tēn exousian epi tas plēgas tautas, kai ou metenōēsan dounai autō doxan). The response of the afflicted is not repentance but blasphemy. The verb eblasphēmēsan ("they blasphemed") describes the same activity that characterized the beast: "He opened his mouth in blasphemies against God, to blaspheme his name" (13:6). The beast's worshipers have become like their master — speaking against God's name, which is the very thing the beast trained them to do. Having chosen the beast's way, they respond to affliction not with the recognition of God's sovereignty but with defiance.

The phrase "the name of God who has the power over these plagues" (to onoma tou theou tou echontos tēn exousian epi tas plēgas tautas) is significant in two ways. First, the afflicted recognize that these plagues come from God. They know who is responsible. Their blasphemy is not the cry of those who do not understand but the defiance of those who understand and refuse to submit. Second, the word exousia ("power, authority") is the same word used for the beast's authority (13:2, 4, 5, 7, 12). The beast received authority from the dragon; God has authority over the plagues. The beast's authority was delegated, temporary, and bounded (forty-two months); God's authority over the plagues is intrinsic and final.

"And they did not repent so as to give him glory" (kai ou metenōēsan dounai autō doxan). The verb metanoeō ("to repent, to change one's mind, to turn") is the word the risen Christ used in his messages to the assemblies: "repent" (metanoēson) was commanded to Ephesus (2:5), Pergamum (2:16), Thyatira (2:21-22), Sardis (3:3), and Laodicea (3:19). Repentance was the appropriate response to divine correction. The beast's worshipers refuse this response. The phrase dounai autō doxan ("to give him glory") echoes the first angel's proclamation in 14:7: "Fear God, and give him glory (dote autō doxan), because the hour of his judgment has come." The angel called the earth to give God glory; the beast-worshipers refuse. The conquerors' song asked: "Who will not fear you, Lord, and glorify your name?" (15:4). The answer, in the bowls, is: the beast's worshipers will not.

This refusal to repent despite clear evidence of God's power recalls the Exodus pattern. Pharaoh's heart was hardened through the plagues: Exodus 7:13 ("Pharaoh's heart was hardened"), 7:22, 8:15, 8:19, 8:32, 9:7, 9:12, 9:34-35, 10:20, 10:27, 11:10. The plagues were designed to demonstrate God's power and produce the acknowledgment "that I am the LORD" (Exodus 7:5, 17; 8:10, 22; 9:14, 29; 10:2; 14:4, 18). Pharaoh saw the demonstrations and refused to acknowledge. The beast's worshipers see the plagues and refuse to repent. The hardening pattern of the Exodus is replicated in the bowls.

div.title: Verses 10-11: The Fifth Bowl — Darkness on the Beast's Throne
div.p: "Then the fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and his kingdom became darkened; and they gnawed their tongues because of pain, and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores; and they did not repent of their deeds."

"The fifth angel poured out his bowl on the throne of the beast, and his kingdom became darkened" (kai ho pemptos execheen tēn phialēn autou epi ton thronon tou thēriou, kai egeneto hē basileia autou eskotōmenē). The fifth bowl is the most targeted of the sequence: it strikes the throne of the beast directly. The word thronos ("throne") connects to the dragon's bestowal in 13:2: "The dragon gave him his power and his throne (thronon) and great authority." The throne that the dragon gave, God now attacks. The seat of the beast's power, the center of its authority, becomes the specific target of divine judgment.

The result is darkness: "his kingdom became darkened" (hē basileia autou eskotōmenē). The word basileia ("kingdom") is used for the beast's domain — the realm over which the beast exercises authority. The darkness that descends upon the beast's kingdom recapitulates the ninth plague of Egypt. Exodus 10:21-23 (LXX): "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'Stretch out your hand toward the sky, that there may be darkness (skotos) over the land of Egypt, a darkness which may be felt.' So Moses stretched out his hand toward the sky, and there was thick darkness (skotos gnophos) in all the land of Egypt for three days. They did not see one another, nor did anyone rise from his place for three days, but all the sons of Israel had light in their dwellings."

The Exodus darkness plague is especially relevant because of its selectivity: Egypt was dark; Israel had light. The darkness fell on Pharaoh's domain specifically. So too the fifth bowl falls on the beast's throne and his kingdom — the darkness is not universal but targeted at the beast's realm. This selectivity reinforces the Exodus typology: just as God distinguished between Egypt and Israel in the darkness plague, so God distinguishes between the beast's kingdom and his own people. The beast's followers experience darkness; those sealed with God's name are not in view.

The fifth trumpet also involved darkening: "the sun and the air were darkened by the smoke of the pit" (9:2). But the trumpet's darkness came from the abyss (the opened pit), while the bowl's darkness is poured directly on the beast's throne. The trumpet darkened through an intermediary (smoke); the bowl darkens the seat of power itself.

The theological resonance of darkness in the prophetic tradition is extensive. Joel 2:2: "A day of darkness (skotous) and gloom." Amos 5:18, 20: "The day of the LORD is darkness (skotos) and not light... will not the day of the LORD be darkness (skotos) instead of light?" Isaiah 8:22: "Then they will look to the earth, and behold, distress and darkness (skotos), the gloom of anguish." In the prophets, darkness is the characteristic condition of the day of the LORD — the day when God acts in judgment. The beast's kingdom experiencing darkness is the beast's kingdom experiencing the day of the LORD.

"And they gnawed their tongues because of pain" (kai emasōnto tas glōssas autōn ek tou ponou). The verb emasōnto ("they gnawed, they chewed") is vivid and visceral. The pain (ponos) drives them to gnaw their own tongues — an image of extreme, unrelieved suffering. This is the accumulated effect of all the preceding bowls: the sores from the first bowl (16:2), combined with the scorching heat from the fourth bowl (16:8-9), combined now with the darkness of the fifth bowl. The plagues are cumulative. Each new bowl does not replace the previous afflictions but adds to them.

"And they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores; and they did not repent of their deeds" (kai eblasphēmēsan ton theon tou ouranou ek tōn ponōn autōn kai ek tōn helkōn autōn, kai ou metenōēsan ek tōn ergōn autōn). The response is identical to that after the fourth bowl: blasphemy rather than repentance. The title "the God of heaven" (ton theon tou ouranou) is a title used in the LXX for God in contexts of pagan recognition of God's sovereignty. Daniel 2:44: "The God of heaven (ho theos tou ouranou) will set up a kingdom." Jonah 1:9: "I fear the LORD God of heaven (ton theon tou ouranou) who made the sea and the dry land." The title acknowledges God's heavenly authority — the beast's worshipers blaspheme a God they know is in heaven and in authority.

The mention of "their sores" (tōn helkōn autōn) confirms that the first bowl's sores are still present. Five bowls have now been poured, and the accumulated affliction includes sores (bowl one), blood-water (bowls two and three), scorching heat (bowl four), and darkness with pain (bowl five). Yet the phrase "they did not repent of their deeds" (ou metenōēsan ek tōn ergōn autōn) repeats the verdict of verse 9. The word ergōn ("deeds, works") refers to the specific actions that constitute their rebellion: receiving the mark, worshiping the image, participating in the beast's system, shedding the blood of saints. The opportunity for repentance is present — the author notes its absence, which implies its possibility — but it is refused. The pattern of hardening deepens with each bowl, just as Pharaoh's hardening deepened through the ten plagues.

div.title: Verse 12: The Sixth Bowl — The Euphrates Dried Up
div.p: "The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river, the Euphrates; and its water was dried up, so that the way would be prepared for the kings from the east."

"The sixth angel poured out his bowl on the great river, the Euphrates" (kai ho hektos execheen tēn phialēn autou epi ton potamon ton megan ton Euphratēn). The Euphrates (Euphratēs) is identified as "the great river" (ton potamon ton megan), a designation drawn directly from Israel's scriptures. Genesis 15:18 (LXX): "To your seed I will give this land, from the river of Egypt to the great river (tou potamou tou megalou), the river Euphrates (potamou Euphratou)." Deuteronomy 1:7: "Turn and set your journey... as far as the great river (tou potamou tou megalou), the river Euphrates." Joshua 1:4: "From the wilderness and this Lebanon, even as far as the great river (tou potamou tou megalou), the river Euphrates." The Euphrates was the boundary of the promised land — the northeastern limit of the territory God covenanted to Abraham. It was also the border beyond which Israel's great enemies lay: Assyria, Babylon, and Persia all originated from beyond the Euphrates. The river was the barrier between Israel and the eastern empires.

In this document, the Euphrates has already appeared at the sixth trumpet: "Release the four angels who are bound at the great river Euphrates" (9:14). The release of those angels produced a vast cavalry army of two hundred million (9:16) that killed "a third of mankind" (9:18). The sixth trumpet's Euphrates event was a partial judgment; the sixth bowl's Euphrates event is its completion.

"And its water was dried up, so that the way would be prepared for the kings from the east" (kai exēranthē to hydōr autou, hina hetoimasthē hē hodos tōn basileōn tōn apo anatolēs hēliou). The verb exēranthē ("was dried up") recalls several acts of God in Israel's history where the drying of waters signified divine power and served as a means of deliverance or judgment.
