First, the crossing of the Red Sea. Exodus 14:21-22: "The LORD swept the sea back by a strong east wind all night and turned the sea into dry land, and the waters were divided." Isaiah 51:10 (LXX) commemorates this: "Was it not you who dried up (xēranasa) the sea, the water of the great deep; who made the depths of the sea a way (hodon) for the redeemed to cross over?" The drying of the Red Sea was a way (hodos) for the redeemed; the drying of the Euphrates is "the way" (hē hodos) for the kings from the east. The verbal echo is precise: the same vocabulary (drying, way, water) is applied, but the purpose is inverted. At the Red Sea, the drying made a path for God's people to escape; at the Euphrates, the drying makes a path for hostile kings to advance.

Second, the crossing of the Jordan. Joshua 3:13, 16-17: "The waters which are flowing down from above will stand in one heap... the waters which were flowing down toward the sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off... all Israel crossed on dry ground." The drying of the Jordan repeated the Red Sea miracle and enabled Israel's entry into the promised land. The pattern of God drying waters to accomplish his purposes is now applied to a new situation.

Third, the prophetic tradition about Babylon's fall. Isaiah 44:27-28: "It is I who says to the watery deep (tē abyssō), 'Be dried up! (xēranthēti)' And I will make your rivers dry (tous potamous sou xēranō). It is I who says of Cyrus, 'He is my shepherd! And he will perform all my desire.'" Jeremiah 50:38: "A drought on her waters, and they will be dried up!" The historical fall of Babylon was traditionally associated with the drying or diversion of the Euphrates. According to Herodotus (Histories 1.191), Cyrus conquered Babylon by diverting the Euphrates, allowing his troops to enter the city along the dried riverbed. Isaiah explicitly connects the drying of waters with Cyrus's role as God's instrument against Babylon. In Revelation 16:12, the drying of the Euphrates to prepare the way for "the kings from the east" recapitulates the pattern: God removes the water barrier to allow the advance of those who will accomplish his purposes.

The phrase "the kings from the east" (tōn basileōn tōn apo anatolēs hēliou, literally "the kings from the rising of the sun") carries historical resonance. Cyrus came from the east. The Parthian Empire, Rome's great eastern rival in the first century, lay beyond the Euphrates. The fear of eastern invasion — specifically Parthian cavalry crossing the Euphrates — was a persistent anxiety in the Roman world. The author draws on this geopolitical reality and the prophetic precedent of Cyrus to depict the drying of the Euphrates as the removal of the barrier that protects the beast's domain from eastern invasion. The beast's kingdom, like Babylon before it, is laid open to assault from beyond the river.

The phrase hina hetoimasthē hē hodos ("so that the way would be prepared") uses the language of Isaiah 40:3 (LXX): "Prepare the way (hetoimasate tēn hodon) of the Lord, make straight in the wilderness the paths of our God." The verbal echo may carry ironic force: in Isaiah, the way was prepared for God's redemptive coming; here, the way is prepared for the advance of destructive kings. God's purposes operate through both salvation and judgment, and both require a "prepared way."

div.title: Verses 13-14: The Three Unclean Spirits
div.p: "And I saw coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs; for they are spirits of demons, performing signs, which go out to the kings of the whole world, to gather them together for the war of the great day of God, the Almighty."

"And I saw coming out of the mouth of the dragon and out of the mouth of the beast and out of the mouth of the false prophet, three unclean spirits like frogs" (kai eidon ek tou stomatos tou drakontos kai ek tou stomatos tou thēriou kai ek tou stomatos tou pseudoprophētou pneumata tria akatharta hōs batrachoi). This is the first appearance in the document of the term "the false prophet" (tou pseudoprophētou) as a title for the second beast. The identification is not new in substance — the second beast of 13:11-17 performed signs, spoke with deceptive authority, and directed worship toward the first beast, all characteristic functions of a false prophet. But the explicit designation pseudoprophētēs appears here for the first time and will recur in 19:20 and 20:10. The title connects the second beast to the tradition of false prophets throughout Israel's history: Deuteronomy 13:1-5 (the prophet who leads Israel after other gods), 1 Kings 22:22-23 (the lying spirit in the mouths of Ahab's prophets), Jeremiah 14:14 (prophets who prophesy lies), Ezekiel 13:1-16 (prophets who prophesy out of their own imagination).

The three figures — the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet — now act together as a counterfeit trinity. The dragon parodies the Father (granting authority, 13:2). The beast parodies the Son (appearing slain yet alive, receiving worship, 13:3-4). The false prophet parodies the Spirit (performing signs, giving breath/pneuma to the image, directing worship, 13:13-15). The three unclean spirits emerge from the mouths of all three, indicating that the deception is a collaborative enterprise of the entire anti-God system.

The spirits come from "the mouth" (ek tou stomatos) of each figure. The mouth is the organ of speech, and in this document, the mouth has been consistently associated with the beast's blasphemous speech (13:5-6: "there was given to him a mouth speaking arrogant words and blasphemies") and with the witnesses' prophetic fire (11:5: "fire proceeds out of their mouth"). What comes from the dragon's mouth is deception (12:15: the serpent "poured water like a river out of his mouth after the woman"). The unclean spirits emerging from the mouths of the counterfeit trinity are the concentrated expression of their deceptive speech — speech that leads to destruction.

The spirits are described as "like frogs" (hōs batrachoi). The frog is the animal of the second Egyptian plague. Exodus 8:2-6 (LXX): "I will smite all your territory with frogs (batrachois). The Nile will swarm with frogs (batrachous) which will come up and go into your house and into your bedroom and on your bed and into the houses of your servants and on your people and into your ovens and into your kneading bowls." The frog plague was one that Egypt's magicians were able to replicate (Exodus 8:7), but they could not remove it. The frogs were everywhere, inescapable, pervading every space. The simile "like frogs" thus evokes both the Exodus plague tradition and the quality of invasive, pervasive, inescapable influence. The unclean spirits, like the frogs, go everywhere and penetrate every domain.

The designation "unclean" (akatharta) places these spirits in the category of ritual impurity. In Israel's purity system, frogs themselves were among the swarming creatures considered unclean (Leviticus 11:10-12, 29-31 covers aquatic and swarming creatures). Unclean spirits (pneumata akatharta) appear throughout the Gospel tradition as demonic agents that inhabit and torment people (Mark 1:23, 26, 27; 3:11, 30; 5:2, 8, 13; 6:7; 7:25; 9:25; Matthew 10:1; 12:43; Luke 4:33, 36; 6:18; 8:29; 9:42; 11:24). The three unclean spirits are demonic agents whose impurity defiles everything they touch.

"For they are spirits of demons, performing signs" (eisin gar pneumata daimoniōn poiounta sēmeia). The author identifies the frog-like spirits explicitly as "spirits of demons" (pneumata daimoniōn). Their activity is "performing signs" (poiounta sēmeia) — the same activity attributed to the second beast/false prophet in 13:13-14 ("he performs great signs") and 19:20 ("the false prophet who performed the signs in his presence"). The signs deceive. The connection to Deuteronomy 13 is maintained: signs and wonders performed by a false prophet are not evidence of divine authorization but instruments of deception that test whether people love the true God.

"Which go out to the kings of the whole world, to gather them together for the war of the great day of God, the Almighty" (ha ekporeuetai epi tous basileis tēs oikoumenēs holēs, synagagein autous eis ton polemon tēs hēmeras tēs megalēs tou theou tou pantokratoros). The demonic spirits go out to "the kings of the whole world" (tous basileis tēs oikoumenēs holēs). The scope is universal: not merely the "kings from the east" (16:12) but the kings of the entire inhabited world (oikoumenē). The purpose is to "gather them together" (synagagein autous) for war.

The verb synagagein ("to gather, to assemble") echoes Psalm 2:2 (LXX): "The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers assembled together (synēchthēsan epi to auto) against the LORD and against his Anointed." Joel 3:2 (LXX 4:2): "I will gather (synaxō) all the nations and bring them down to the valley of Jehoshaphat." Zechariah 14:2: "I will gather (synaxō) all the nations against Jerusalem for battle." The gathering of nations for battle against God is a fixed element of the prophetic expectation of the final confrontation. In the prophetic tradition, it is God who gathers the nations — the kings assemble not because they have planned wisely but because God has brought them to the place of judgment. The irony is that the demonic spirits think they are gathering an army for victory, but the prophetic pattern shows that God is gathering the nations for their own destruction. Joel 3:2 makes this explicit: God gathers the nations to the valley of Jehoshaphat "to enter into judgment with them there."

The phrase "the war of the great day of God, the Almighty" (ton polemon tēs hēmeras tēs megalēs tou theou tou pantokratoros) identifies this gathering as the final eschatological battle. The concept of "the great day" (hē hēmera hē megalē) draws on the prophetic "day of the LORD" tradition. Joel 2:11: "The day of the LORD is great (megalē) and very terrible." Joel 2:31 (LXX 3:4): "The great (megalēn) and glorious day of the LORD." Malachi 4:5 (LXX 3:23): "The great (megalēn) and glorious day of the LORD." Zephaniah 1:14: "Near is the great day (hē hēmera hē megalē) of the LORD." In 6:17 of this document, the sixth seal produced the cry: "The great day (hē hēmera hē megalē) of their wrath has come, and who is able to stand?" The gathering of the kings is for this day — the day when the Almighty (pantokratōr) acts decisively against all opposing powers. The title pantokratōr ("ruler of all"), applied to God, makes the outcome of the battle clear before it is narrated: the Almighty cannot be defeated by any assembly of earthly kings. The gathering is for their destruction, not their triumph.

div.title: Verse 15: The Parenthetical Warning from Christ
div.p: "('Behold, I am coming like a thief. Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes, so that he will not walk about naked and men will not see his shame.')"

"Behold, I am coming like a thief" (idou, erchomai hōs kleptēs). This is a direct statement from Christ, inserted parenthetically into the narrative between the gathering of the kings (16:13-14) and the naming of the gathering place (16:16). The first person "I am coming" (erchomai) identifies the speaker as the risen Christ, who has spoken in the first person throughout the document (1:8, 17-18; 2:1-3:22; 22:7, 12, 20). The statement is addressed to the listening assemblies — a pastoral interjection amid the vision of cosmic conflict.

The simile "like a thief" (hōs kleptēs) has a specific tradition behind it in the early community's teaching. In 3:3, the risen Christ warned the assembly at Sardis: "If you do not wake up, I will come like a thief (hōs kleptēs), and you will not know at what hour I will come to you." The thief simile emphasizes unexpectedness: a thief does not announce the hour of his arrival. The simile appears in the broader tradition as well: 1 Thessalonians 5:2 ("the day of the Lord will come just as a thief in the night"); 2 Peter 3:10 ("the day of the Lord will come like a thief"); Matthew 24:43-44 ("if the head of the house had known at what time of the night the thief was coming, he would have been on the alert"; "for this reason you also must be ready; for the Son of Man is coming at an hour when you do not think he will"). The thief image does not characterize Christ as a criminal but as one whose arrival is sudden, unscheduled, and catching the unprepared off guard. The point is readiness, not morality.

"Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes" (makarios ho grēgorōn kai tērōn ta himatia autou). This is the third of the document's seven beatitudes (1:3; 14:13; 16:15; 19:9; 20:6; 22:7; 22:14). The word makarios ("blessed, fortunate, to be congratulated") declares the true condition of a person as God evaluates it. The one who is blessed is the one who "stays awake" (grēgorōn, from grēgoreō, "to be watchful, to be alert, to stay awake") and "keeps his clothes" (tērōn ta himatia autou).

The verb grēgoreō ("to be watchful") appeared in the warning to Sardis: "Wake up (grēgorēson), and strengthen the things that remain, which were about to die" (3:2). And in 3:3: "If you do not wake up (grēgorēsēs)..." The watching is not literal wakefulness but spiritual alertness — the sustained attention of one who knows that the decisive moment may come at any time and who refuses to be caught off guard. In the Gethsemane tradition, Jesus told the disciples: "Keep watching (grēgoreite) and praying" (Matthew 26:41; Mark 14:38). They fell asleep instead and were unprepared for the crisis.

"Keeps his clothes" (tērōn ta himatia autou) connects to the clothing imagery that runs through the document. In 3:4, the faithful at Sardis "have not soiled their garments." In 3:5, the overcomer "will be clothed in white garments." In 3:18, Laodicea is counseled to buy "white garments so that you may clothe yourself, and that the shame of your nakedness will not be revealed." In 7:14, the great multitude washed their robes "in the blood of the Lamb." In 19:8, the bride is clothed in "fine linen, bright and clean." Garments throughout the document represent covenant faithfulness, moral integrity, and the identity of one who belongs to the Lamb. To "keep one's clothes" is to maintain one's covenant standing — to remain faithful, to not strip off the identity that belongs to God's people.

"So that he will not walk about naked and men will not see his shame" (hina mē gymnos peripatē kai blepōsin tēn aschēmosynēn autou). Nakedness (gymnotēs) and shame (aschēmosynē) are linked in the prophetic tradition with judgment and exposure. Genesis 3:7: Adam and Eve "knew that they were naked" after the fall. Isaiah 47:3: Babylon is told, "Your nakedness will be uncovered, your shame (aischynē, LXX) also will be exposed." Ezekiel 16:36-37: Jerusalem's nakedness was "uncovered" through her harlotries. Nahum 3:5: "I will lift up your skirts over your face, and show to the nations your nakedness." Hosea 2:3 (LXX 2:5): "Otherwise I will strip her naked and expose her as on the day when she was born." The shame of nakedness in the prophetic tradition represents the exposure of unfaithfulness — being caught without the garments of covenant loyalty.

The Laodicea connection is particularly direct: "you do not know that you are wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked" (3:17). Laodicea's nakedness was its spiritual complacency — its false sense of self-sufficiency that left it without the garments of genuine faithfulness. The parenthetical warning in 16:15 addresses the same danger: even as the cosmic battle unfolds, the assemblies are warned not to be found naked — not to have abandoned their covenant faithfulness in the face of the beast's pressure or their own complacency.

The placement of this beatitude between the sixth and seventh bowls follows the established pattern. Between the sixth and seventh seals, the sealing of the 144,000 and the vision of the great multitude provided assurance and identification of the faithful (chapter 7). Between the sixth and seventh trumpets, the small scroll and the two witnesses provided prophetic recommissioning and testimony (chapters 10-11:13). Between the sixth and seventh bowls, the warning about readiness provides pastoral exhortation: even now, at the climactic moment, faithfulness must be maintained. The repeated pattern of inserting exhortation between six and seven shows that the author's purpose is not merely to narrate cosmic events but to form the character and sustain the faithfulness of the listening community.

div.title: Verse 16: The Gathering at Armageddon
div.p: "And they gathered them together to the place which in Hebrew is called Har-Magedon."

"And they gathered them together" (kai synēgagen autous). The verb synēgagen ("he/they gathered") completes the action begun in verse 14, where the demonic spirits went out to "gather" (synagagein) the kings. The gathering is accomplished. The kings of the whole world, deceived by the frog-like spirits, have assembled for battle. The subject of synēgagen is ambiguous — it could refer to the spirits who performed the gathering, or it could be a divine passive indicating that God has orchestrated the assembly for his own purposes (as in Joel 3:2, Zechariah 14:2).

"To the place which in Hebrew is called Har-Magedon" (eis ton topon ton kaloumenon Hebraisti Harmagedon). The author specifies that this name is "in Hebrew" (Hebraisti), indicating that the name carries meaning within the Hebrew linguistic tradition and that its significance lies in its Hebrew etymology rather than in a Greek equivalent.

The name Harmagedon (also written Armageddon) is most naturally understood as a transliteration of the Hebrew Har Megiddo — "the mountain of Megiddo." Megiddo was a city in the Jezreel Valley of northern Israel, situated on the ancient Via Maris trade route. It occupied a strategically critical position controlling the pass through the Carmel mountain range, and it was the site of numerous decisive battles in Israel's history.
The associations a first-century hearer familiar with Israel's scriptures would bring to Megiddo include:

Judges 5:19-20 (the Song of Deborah): "The kings came and fought; then fought the kings of Canaan at Taanach near the waters of Megiddo (Megeddō, LXX)... The stars fought from heaven, from their courses they fought against Sisera." The battle at Megiddo in Judges 5 was a battle in which the stars themselves participated — a cosmic dimension to an earthly conflict. The enemy (Sisera's army) was destroyed by divine intervention, including flood waters from the Kishon river (Judges 5:21). The defeat was total and was celebrated as God's victory over the kings of Canaan.

2 Kings 23:29-30: King Josiah, the last righteous king of Judah, was killed at Megiddo in a battle against Pharaoh Neco of Egypt. Josiah's death was a catastrophic turning point in Judah's history, leading directly to Babylonian domination and exile. 2 Chronicles 35:22-24 describes the mourning for Josiah, and Zechariah 12:11 references it: "In that day there will be great mourning in Jerusalem, like the mourning of Hadad-rimmon in the plain of Megiddo (tou Magedon, LXX)."

The Megiddo/Jezreel Valley was thus associated in Israel's memory with both the triumph of God over enemy kings (Deborah and Barak) and the tragedy of a righteous king's death (Josiah). Both associations are relevant to the author's use. The gathering at Armageddon is both a gathering of enemy kings for divine defeat (like Sisera's army) and a gathering that occurs in the context of the suffering of God's people (like Josiah's death).

The specification "mountain" (Har) is puzzling, since Megiddo itself sat in a valley, not on a mountain. Several explanations are possible. The Carmel mountain range overlooks the Megiddo valley, and the valley is bounded by hills. Alternatively, "mountain" may carry the symbolic weight it holds elsewhere in the prophets: the mountain of God's decisive action. Ezekiel 38:8, 21; 39:2, 4, 17 places the eschatological battle of Gog and Magog on "the mountains of Israel" — a mountain setting for the final conflict. The author may be combining the historical battle-site (Megiddo) with the prophetic mountain-of-judgment tradition (Ezekiel 38-39) to create a composite name for the place of the final confrontation.

What is notable is what the text does not describe: no battle is narrated here. The kings are gathered, but the combat does not occur in this verse. The actual confrontation will be narrated in 19:11-21, where the rider on the white horse meets the beast and the kings of the earth and their armies. The sixth bowl prepares the gathering; the seventh bowl concludes the series; the battle itself is deferred to the next major narrative sequence. The name Armageddon designates the gathering place, not the battle itself.

div.title: Verses 17-21: The Seventh Bowl — "It Is Done"
div.p: "Then the seventh angel poured out his bowl upon the air; and a loud voice came out of the temple from the throne, saying, 'It is done.' And there were flashes of lightning and sounds and peals of thunder; and there was a great earthquake, such as there had not been since man came to be upon the earth, so great an earthquake was it, and so mighty. The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell. Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of His fierce wrath. And every island fled away, and the mountains were not found. And huge hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, came down from heaven upon men; and men blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, because its plague was extremely severe."
div.title: The Bowl Poured on the Air
div.p: "The seventh angel poured out his bowl upon the air" (kai ho hebdomos execheen tēn phialēn autou epi ton aera). The seventh bowl is poured "upon the air" (epi ton aera). The first four bowls targeted specific elements: earth, sea, rivers, and sun. The fifth targeted the beast's throne. The sixth targeted the Euphrates. The seventh targets the air itself — the atmosphere, the medium through which all earthly life breathes and through which sound travels. The air encompasses everything; it is the most comprehensive of all the bowls' targets. The bowl poured on the air is a bowl poured on the entire domain of earthly existence.
div.title: The Voice from the Temple and the Throne
div.p: "And a loud voice came out of the temple from the throne, saying, 'It is done'" (kai exēlthen phōnē megalē ek tou naou apo tou thronou legousa, Gegonen). The voice comes from two locations simultaneously: "out of the temple" (ek tou naou) and "from the throne" (apo tou thronou). Since no one could enter the temple during the plagues (15:8), and since the throne is God's seat of authority, the voice is again God's own. The combination "temple" and "throne" merges the cultic/liturgical space (temple) with the political/sovereign space (throne): God speaks as both the holy one enthroned in his sanctuary and the sovereign ruler of all things.

The word gegonen ("it is done," or "it has come to pass") is the perfect tense of ginomai ("to become, to come into being, to happen"). The perfect tense indicates a completed action with abiding results: what has happened is done and remains done. This single word echoes and answers the declaration of 15:1, where the bowls were introduced as the plagues in which "the wrath of God is finished" (etelesthē). The completion announced in 15:1 is now confirmed in 16:17: "It is done." The wrath has been poured out. The last plagues are completed.

The word gegonen also resonates with the great declaration of 21:6, where the one seated on the throne says: "It is done (gegonan). I am the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end." The same word of completion that marks the end of the bowl judgments marks the inauguration of the new creation. The bowls' completion clears the way for what comes after: the destruction of Babylon (chapters 17-18), the final battle (chapter 19), the judgment (chapter 20), and the new heaven and new earth (chapters 21-22).
div.title: The Theophany
div.p: "And there were flashes of lightning and sounds and peals of thunder" (kai egenonto astrapai kai phōnai kai brontai). This theophanic formula — lightning, sounds, and thunder — has appeared at every major structural transition in the document. In 4:5, it accompanied the throne-room vision: "Out of the throne come flashes of lightning and sounds and peals of thunder." In 8:5, it accompanied the transition from the prayers of the saints to the trumpet judgments: "The angel took the censer and filled it with the fire of the altar, and threw it to the earth; and there followed peals of thunder and sounds and flashes of lightning and an earthquake." In 11:19, it accompanied the seventh trumpet and the opening of the heavenly temple: "There were flashes of lightning and sounds and peals of thunder and an earthquake and a great hailstorm." Now in 16:18, it accompanies the seventh bowl.

The formula intensifies at each occurrence. In 4:5: lightning, sounds, thunder. In 8:5: thunder, sounds, lightning, earthquake (added). In 11:19: lightning, sounds, thunder, earthquake, great hailstorm (added). In 16:18-21: lightning, sounds, thunder, great earthquake (intensified), and huge hailstones (intensified). Each repetition adds elements and increases the scale, building toward the climactic theophany of the seventh bowl. The accumulation communicates that this is not a mere repetition but the ultimate expression of God's manifest power.

The theophanic formula originates at Sinai. Exodus 19:16 (LXX): "And it happened on the third day, when morning came, there were thunders (brontai) and lightnings (astrapai) and a thick cloud on the mountain, and a very loud trumpet sound (phōnē tēs salpiggos)." The Sinai theophany was the foundational revelation of God's presence to Israel, and every recurrence of the lightning-thunder-voice formula in Revelation signals that God's presence is being manifested with the same intensity and authority as at Sinai.
div.title: The Great Earthquake
div.p: "And there was a great earthquake, such as there had not been since man came to be upon the earth, so great an earthquake was it, and so mighty" (kai seismos egeneto megas, hoios ouk egeneto aph' hou anthrōpoi egenonto epi tēs gēs, tēlikoutos seismos houtō megas). Earthquakes have accompanied divine action throughout the document: at the sixth seal (6:12, "a great earthquake"), at the seventh trumpet (11:13, "a great earthquake"), and now at the seventh bowl. Each earthquake has increased in intensity. The sixth seal's earthquake was "great" (megas). The seventh trumpet's earthquake caused a tenth of "the great city" to fall (11:13). The seventh bowl's earthquake is described with superlative language: "such as there had not been since man came to be upon the earth."

This superlative echoes Daniel 12:1: "There will be a time of distress such as never occurred since there was a nation until that time." Jesus used similar language in the Olivet discourse: "There will be a great tribulation, such as has not occurred since the beginning of the world until now, nor ever will" (Matthew 24:21; Mark 13:19). The superlative formula identifies this earthquake as the climactic event of history — the unprecedented, unrepeatable act of God that surpasses all prior demonstrations of power.

The earthquake is the instrument through which the restructuring described in the following verses occurs: the splitting of the great city, the falling of the nations' cities, the disappearance of islands and mountains.
div.title: The Great City Split and Babylon Remembered
div.p: "The great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell" (kai egeneto hē polis hē megalē eis tria merē, kai hai poleis tōn ethnōn epesan). The identity of "the great city" (hē polis hē megalē) must be determined from the author's own usage of this phrase within the document. In 11:8, "the great city" is the place "where also their Lord was crucified" — a reference to Jerusalem, but described in that verse as "mystically called Sodom and Egypt." In 14:8, the second angel announced: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great" (Babylōn hē megalē). In 16:19b (the next clause), "Babylon the great" (Babylōn hē megalē) is explicitly named. In 17:18, the angel explains: "The woman whom you saw is the great city (hē polis hē megalē), which reigns over the kings of the earth." In 18:10, 16, 18, 19, 21, "the great city" is Babylon.

The author uses "the great city" in two distinguishable ways: in 11:8, it designates the city where the Lord was crucified (Jerusalem in its fallen state, sharing the character of Sodom and Egypt); in the rest of the document (14:8; 16:19; 17:18; 18:10-21), it consistently designates Babylon. In 16:19, the immediate context resolves any ambiguity: the very next clause identifies "Babylon the great" as the object of divine wrath. Whether "the great city" in 16:19a is identical to Babylon or whether the splitting of "the great city" into three parts and the naming of Babylon are two related but distinct judgments, the focus of the verse is the destruction of the system that Babylon represents.

The splitting "into three parts" (eis tria merē) suggests catastrophic fragmentation — the total structural collapse of the city. Ezekiel 5:1-12 provides a prophetic precedent for a threefold division as a symbol of comprehensive judgment: Ezekiel was told to divide his shaved hair into three parts, each representing a different mode of destruction for Jerusalem (fire, sword, scattering to the wind). The threefold division represents exhaustive judgment: no part escapes; every portion receives its own form of destruction.

"And the cities of the nations fell" (kai hai poleis tōn ethnōn epesan). The judgment extends beyond the great city to include "the cities of the nations" — the entire network of earthly powers allied with the beast's system. The verb epesan ("fell") echoes the announcement of 14:8: "Fallen, fallen (epesen epesen) is Babylon the great." What was announced by the angel in 14:8 is now enacted in 16:19. The cities of the nations that participated in Babylon's system share in Babylon's fall.

"Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of His fierce wrath" (kai Babylōn hē megalē emnēsthē enōpion tou theou, dounai autē to potērion tou oinou tou thymou tēs orgēs autou). The verb emnēsthē ("was remembered") carries specific covenantal weight in the LXX. In Genesis 8:1: "God remembered (emnēsthē) Noah." In Exodus 2:24: "God heard their groaning; and God remembered (emnēsthē) his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob." In the LXX usage, when God "remembers," he acts on what he remembers. God's remembering is not the recovery of forgotten information but the activation of a commitment. When God remembered Noah, the waters receded. When God remembered his covenant, the Exodus began. When God remembers Babylon, Babylon receives judgment. The verb emnēsthē signals that God has not forgotten what Babylon has done — the blood of saints and prophets (16:6; 18:24), the seduction of the nations (14:8), the luxury built on exploitation (18:3, 11-19) — and now acts on that memory.

"The cup of the wine of his fierce wrath" (to potērion tou oinou tou thymou tēs orgēs autou) is the most intensified expression of divine anger in the document. It combines four nouns: cup (potērion), wine (oinos), fury (thymos), and wrath (orgē). Each successive genitive intensifies the preceding one: it is a cup containing wine, but the wine is the thymos (the burning fury) of God's orgē (settled, judicial wrath). This same phrase appeared in 14:10, where the third angel warned that the beast-worshiper "will drink of the wine of the wrath of God, which is mixed in full strength in the cup of his anger." What was threatened in 14:10 is now administered in 16:19. Babylon receives the cup she was promised.

The irony runs deep: in 17:4, the harlot Babylon herself holds "a golden cup full of abominations and of the unclean things of her immorality." In 14:8, she "made all the nations drink of the wine of the passion of her immorality." Babylon held a cup and made others drink from it; now God holds a cup and makes Babylon drink from it. The cup imagery reverses: the one who intoxicated the nations is now made to drink God's own undiluted wine.
div.title: Cosmic Dissolution
div.p: "And every island fled away, and the mountains were not found" (kai pasa nēsos ephygen, kai orē ouch heurethēsan). The disappearance of islands and mountains echoes the sixth seal: "Every mountain and island were moved out of their places" (6:14). The sixth seal described displacement; the seventh bowl describes elimination. The mountains and islands do not merely shift position; they vanish entirely. The phrase "were not found" (ouch heurethēsan) indicates total disappearance — a search for them would yield nothing.

The dissolution of the natural landscape represents the un-creation motif. Mountains and islands are the most stable, permanent features of the physical world. Their removal signals the dissolution of the present created order, preparing for the new creation of chapters 21-22, where "the first heaven and the first earth passed away, and there is no longer any sea" (21:1). The cosmic dissolution that the prophets anticipated — Isaiah 24:19-20 ("The earth is broken asunder, the earth is split through, the earth is shaken violently. The earth reels to and fro like a drunkard"); Isaiah 34:4 ("All the host of heaven will wear away, and the sky will be rolled up like a scroll"); Nahum 1:5 ("Mountains quake because of him, and the hills dissolve") — reaches its fulfillment in the seventh bowl.
div.title: The Hailstones
div.p: "And huge hailstones, about one hundred pounds each, came down from heaven upon men" (kai chalaza megalē hōs talantaia katabainei ek tou ouranou epi tous anthrōpous). The hailstones are described as "about the weight of a talent" (hōs talantaia). A talent (talanton) was approximately 75-100 pounds (34-45 kilograms). Hailstones of this magnitude are catastrophically destructive — not a weather event but a cataclysmic act of divine power.

The hail plague recapitulates the seventh plague of Egypt. Exodus 9:18-26 (LXX): "Behold, about this time tomorrow, I will send a very heavy hail (chalazan pollēn sphodra), such as has not been seen in Egypt from the day it was founded until now... The LORD sent thunder (brontēn) and hail (chalazan), and fire ran down to the earth... The hail struck all that was in the field through all the land of Egypt, both man and beast; the hail struck every plant of the field and broke every tree of the field. Only in the land of Goshen, where the sons of Israel were, there was no hail." The Egyptian hail was described in superlative terms ("such as has not been seen"); the bowl's hail is described in even more extreme terms, with each stone weighing a talent. The escalation from Exodus to Revelation continues the pattern of the bowls intensifying the Exodus plagues.

In the prophetic tradition, hail is a weapon of divine judgment. Isaiah 28:2: "The Lord has a strong and mighty agent; as a storm of hail (chalazēs)." Isaiah 30:30: "The LORD will cause his voice of authority to be heard, and the descending of his arm to be seen, in fierce anger, and in the flame of a consuming fire, in cloudburst, downpour, and hailstones (lithos chalazēs)." Ezekiel 13:11-13: "Tell those who plaster it over with whitewash, that it will fall. A flooding rain will come, and you, O hailstones (lithoi petraboloi), will fall; and a violent wind will break out... I will make a violent wind break out in my wrath. There will also be in my anger a flooding rain and hailstones (lithoi) to consume it in wrath." Ezekiel 38:22: "With pestilence and with blood I will enter into judgment with him; and I will rain on him and on his troops, and on the many peoples who are with him, a torrential rain, with hailstones (lithous chalazēs), fire and brimstone." The hailstone judgment in Ezekiel 38:22 is part of the Gog-Magog battle, which the author of Revelation draws on explicitly in 20:7-10. The hail of the seventh bowl belongs to the same prophetic tradition of God's weaponry against assembled enemies.

Joshua 10:11 provides a historical precedent: "The LORD threw large stones (lithous chalazēs, LXX "hailstones") from heaven on them as far as Azekah, and they died; there were more who died from the hailstones than those whom the sons of Israel killed with the sword." In Joshua, the hailstones were God's direct intervention in battle on behalf of Israel, killing more enemies than Israel's own army. The hail was God fighting for his people. The seventh bowl's hailstones serve the same function in the eschatological context: God fights against the gathered kings with weapons no army can resist.

"And men blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail, because its plague was extremely severe" (kai eblasphēmēsan hoi anthrōpoi ton theon ek tēs plēgēs tēs chalazēs, hoti megalē estin hē plēgē autēs sphodra). For the third time in the chapter (after verses 9 and 11), the response to divine judgment is blasphemy rather than repentance. The word plēgē ("plague") is the same word used for the plagues throughout the document and for the Egyptian plagues in the LXX (Exodus 9:14; 11:1; 12:13). The adjective sphodra ("extremely, exceedingly") emphasizes the severity. The plague is acknowledged as extreme — the men know what is happening and how devastating it is — but their response is to blaspheme rather than submit.

The threefold blasphemy (16:9, 11, 21) forms a pattern that runs through the entire bowl sequence. After the fourth bowl: "they blasphemed the name of God... and they did not repent." After the fifth bowl: "they blasphemed the God of heaven... and they did not repent." After the seventh bowl: "they blasphemed God because of the plague of the hail." The repetition establishes the moral character of the beast's worshipers as fixed. The plagues reveal not only God's justice but the depth of human rebellion: given every possible demonstration of God's power and every opportunity to turn, the beast's followers choose blasphemy. The hardening is complete.

div.title: Summary of the Chapter's Argument
div.p: Revelation 16 narrates the execution of the seven bowls of God's wrath, completing the sequence prepared in chapter 15 and bringing to fulfillment the judgments announced throughout the document. The chapter's structure moves from targeted plagues (bowls one through five) through eschatological preparation (bowl six) to cosmic climax (bowl seven), with a parenthetical warning to the assemblies inserted between the sixth and seventh bowls.

The Exodus pattern governs the entire sequence. The bowls recapitulate and intensify the plagues of Egypt: sores (the sixth Egyptian plague, Exodus 9:8-12), water turned to blood (the first Egyptian plague, Exodus 7:20-21), scorching heat (intensifying the natural elements), darkness (the ninth Egyptian plague, Exodus 10:21-23), and hail (the seventh Egyptian plague, Exodus 9:18-26). The pattern is not merely allusive but structural: just as the ten plagues fell on Egypt to liberate Israel, the seven bowls fall on the beast's domain to complete the liberation of God's people. The conquerors of 15:2-4 — standing on the far side of the sea of glass, singing the song of Moses and the Lamb — are the new Israel on the far shore; the bowl plagues are the new Exodus judgments on the new Pharaoh.
Three features of the chapter's theological argument deserve attention.

First, the justice of the bowls is explicitly declared within the narrative. The angel of the waters does not merely observe the judgment; he affirms its righteousness: "Righteous are you... because you judged these things; for they poured out the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink. They deserve it" (16:5-6). The altar confirms: "True and righteous are your judgments" (16:7). The bowls are not narrated as raw power but as adjudicated justice. The principle of proportional requital — blood for blood — is stated as the ground of God's action. The angel and the altar serve as witnesses in a judicial proceeding, certifying that the verdict is correct. The author does not allow the hearers to experience the bowls as arbitrary violence; he frames them as the righteous acts of the King of the nations, disclosed before the watching heavenly court.

Second, the response of the beast's worshipers reveals the depth of their commitment to the beast's system. Three times the text notes that the afflicted "blasphemed God" and "did not repent" (16:9, 11, 21). The plagues are not arbitrary torments inflicted on helpless victims; they are the consequences of a choice — the choice to worship the beast and receive his mark — and the recipients respond to the consequences not with reconsideration but with deeper rebellion. The hardening is the mirror of Pharaoh's hardening: the plagues that were intended to produce acknowledgment of God ("that you may know that I am the LORD," Exodus 7:17; 8:10, 22; 9:14, 29; 10:2) instead produced increased defiance. The author presents the beast-worshipers' blasphemy not as evidence that the plagues fail but as evidence that the choice for the beast is self-reinforcing: those who have given themselves to the beast's system respond to God's corrective action with the beast's own characteristic speech — blasphemy (13:5-6).

Third, the chapter maintains its pastoral address to the assemblies. The parenthetical beatitude of 16:15 — "Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes" — interrupts the cosmic narrative to speak directly to the listening community. Even as the kings of the world are being gathered for the final battle, the assemblies are called to watchfulness and faithfulness. The insertion is consistent with the author's method throughout the document: the visions of judgment and cosmic conflict are not ends in themselves but serve the formation of the community that hears them. The assemblies must remain awake, keep their garments, and refuse to be found naked and ashamed. The cosmic drama is the context; the community's faithfulness is the purpose.

The seventh bowl brings the sequence to its climax with the word gegonen — "It is done." The wrath of God, introduced as "finished" (etelesthē) in 15:1, is now completed. The earthquake, the splitting of the great city, the fall of the nations' cities, the remembering of Babylon, the disappearance of islands and mountains, and the devastating hail together constitute the most comprehensive act of divine judgment in the document. The created order itself is shaken and dissolved, preparing for the new creation that lies beyond. Babylon is remembered and judged. The kings are gathered and will be defeated. The way is cleared for the narrative that follows: the detailed judgment of Babylon (chapters 17-18), the final battle (chapter 19), the last judgment (chapter 20), and the new heaven and new earth (chapters 21-22).

The bowls complete the arc that began with the martyrs' cry in 6:9-10. "How long?" they asked. The answer has been unfolding through the seals, the trumpets, and now the bowls. The angel of the waters answers: "They poured out the blood of saints and prophets, and you have given them blood to drink." The altar confirms: "True and righteous are your judgments." The voice from the throne declares: "It is done." The martyrs' question has received its final answer. The blood has been avenged. The wrath is complete. What remains is the disclosure of the judgment's details (Babylon's fall), the final battle (the rider on the white horse), and the new world that emerges when every bowl has been emptied and every plague has run its course.

div.title: Revelation 17 — First-Century Reading
Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (Revelation 16): Chapter 16 narrated the pouring out of the seven bowls of wrath that chapter 15 had introduced and prepared. After the seven angels emerged from the heavenly temple clothed in priestly garments and received the golden bowls from one of the four living creatures (15:5-8), a loud voice from the temple commanded: "Go and pour out on the earth the seven bowls of the wrath of God" (16:1). The bowls replicated and intensified the Exodus plagues in systematic fashion: the first produced loathsome and malignant sores on those who bore the mark of the beast and worshiped his image (16:2; cf. Exodus 9:8-12, the plague of boils); the second turned the sea to blood "like that of a dead man," and every living thing in the sea died (16:3; cf. Exodus 7:20-21); the third turned the rivers and springs to blood (16:4), at which the angel of the waters declared God righteous: "because they poured out the blood of saints and prophets, you have given them blood to drink. They deserve it" (16:5-6), and the altar confirmed: "Yes, Lord God, the Almighty, true and righteous are your judgments" (16:7) — directly echoing the conquerors' song in 15:3-4; the fourth caused the sun to scorch people with fire, and they "blasphemed the name of God who has the power over these plagues, and they did not repent so as to give him glory" (16:8-9); the fifth was poured on the throne of the beast, and his kingdom became darkened, and people "gnawed their tongues because of pain, and they blasphemed the God of heaven because of their pains and their sores; and they did not repent of their deeds" (16:10-11; cf. Exodus 10:21-23, the plague of darkness); the sixth was poured on the great river Euphrates and its water dried up to prepare the way for the kings from the east (16:12), and three unclean spirits like frogs came from the mouths of the dragon, the beast, and the false prophet, performing signs and gathering the kings of the whole world to "the war of the great day of God, the Almighty" at "the place which in Hebrew is called Har-Magedon" (16:13-16); the seventh was poured into the air, and a loud voice from the throne declared "It is done" (Gegonen, 16:17), followed by flashes of lightning, sounds, thunder, and the greatest earthquake ever (16:18), at which "the great city was split into three parts, and the cities of the nations fell. Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of his fierce wrath" (16:19). Every island fled and every mountain vanished, and enormous hailstones fell from heaven, and people "blasphemed God because of the plague of hail" (16:20-21).

Two elements of chapter 16 are essential for understanding chapter 17. First, the consistent response of those under judgment was blasphemy and refusal to repent (16:9, 11, 21). The bowls did not produce repentance; they hardened those already committed to the beast's system, exactly as the Exodus plagues hardened Pharaoh. Second, the seventh bowl specifically named "Babylon the great" as the object of God's wrath (16:19): "Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of his fierce wrath." This mention of Babylon at the climax of the bowls is the trigger for what follows in chapters 17-18. The bowls have completed the execution of wrath (15:1: "in them the wrath of God is finished"), but the author has not yet explained who Babylon is or narrated her fall in detail. The second angel of 14:8 announced "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great," and 16:19 recorded that God "remembered" her. Chapters 17-18 now unpack this: who is Babylon, what is her relationship to the beast, and what does her fall mean?

What the author argues immediately after (Revelation 18): Chapter 18 narrates the detailed lamentation over Babylon's fall. An angel descends from heaven with great authority, the earth illuminated by his glory, and cries out: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!" (18:2) — repeating the announcement of 14:8 but now with elaboration: she has "become a dwelling place of demons and a prison of every unclean spirit" (18:2). Her sins are specified: "all the nations have drunk of the wine of the passion of her immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed acts of immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have become rich by the wealth of her sensuality" (18:3). A voice from heaven commands: "Come out of her, my people, so that you will not participate in her sins and receive of her plagues" (18:4). Three groups then mourn Babylon's destruction in succession: the kings of the earth who "committed acts of immorality and lived sensuously with her" weep and stand at a distance saying "Woe, woe, the great city, Babylon, the strong city!" (18:9-10); the merchants of the earth weep because "no one buys their cargoes any more" (18:11), and the lengthy inventory of luxury goods is listed (18:12-13) — gold, silver, precious stones, fine linen, purple, silk, scarlet, all kinds of citron wood, ivory, bronze, iron, marble, cinnamon, spice, incense, ointment, frankincense, wine, olive oil, fine flour, wheat, cattle, sheep, horses, chariots, and "bodies and souls of men" (18:13); and the shipmasters and sailors weep because "the great city, in which all who had ships at sea became rich by her wealth" has been laid waste "in one hour" (18:17-19). Then heaven, the saints, apostles, and prophets are commanded to "rejoice over her" because "God has pronounced judgment for you against her" (18:20). A strong angel picks up a stone like a great millstone and throws it into the sea, saying "So will Babylon, the great city, be thrown down with violence, and will not be found any longer" (18:21). The chapter ends with the final verdict: "in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints and of all who have been slain on the earth" (18:24).

How chapter 17 connects the surrounding argument: The connection is seamless. The seventh bowl (16:17-21) announced that "Babylon the great was remembered before God." The audience has heard the name "Babylon" since 14:8, has seen the bowls poured out, and has heard Babylon named at the climax of the seventh bowl. But the author has not yet shown who Babylon is, what she looks like, how she operates, or how her fall comes about. Chapter 17 is the interpretive unveiling of the entity that has been named but not yet fully seen. One of the seven bowl-angels — the very angels who poured out the wrath that "remembered" Babylon — now serves as John's guide to a vision that explains Babylon's identity, her relationship to the beast, and the mechanism of her destruction. Chapter 18 then narrates the consequences of that destruction in the form of a funeral dirge. The sequence is: the bowls execute wrath and name Babylon (chapter 16), the angel interprets who Babylon is and how she falls (chapter 17), and the earthly response to her fall is lamented and celebrated (chapter 18). Chapters 17 and 18 together are the expansion of the single phrase in 16:19: "Babylon the great was remembered before God, to give her the cup of the wine of his fierce wrath."

The subject has not changed. From the moment the second angel of 14:8 announced Babylon's fall, the author has been building toward this full narration. The bowls were the instruments; chapters 17-18 are the interpretation and dramatization.

div.title: Verses 1-2: The Bowl-Angel's Invitation
div.p: "Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me, saying, 'Come here, I will show you the judgment of the great harlot who sits on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed acts of immorality, and those who dwell on the earth were made drunk with the wine of her immorality.'"

"Then one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls came and spoke with me" (kai ēlthen heis ek tōn hepta angelōn tōn echontōn tas hepta phialas kai elalēsen met' emou). The guide-angel is not a new figure but one of the seven who poured out the bowls in chapter 16. The identification is deliberate: the same angel who participated in the execution of God's wrath now serves as the interpreter who explains what that wrath was directed against and why. The author creates a structural parallel that will become fully visible in 21:9, where again "one of the seven angels who had the seven bowls" comes to John and says "Come here, I will show you the bride, the wife of the Lamb." The two invitations form a mirror pair: one angel shows the harlot; a corresponding angel shows the bride. Babylon and the new Jerusalem are presented as deliberate counterparts, seen through the same angelic lens.

The verb elalēsen met' emou ("spoke with me") describes personal, conversational interaction. This is not a distant proclamation but an intimate exchange between the angel and the seer. The angel will explain the vision as it unfolds, providing interpretive commentary that the author presents as authoritative.

"Come here, I will show you the judgment of the great harlot who sits on many waters" (deuro, deixō soi to krima tēs pornēs tēs megalēs tēs kathēmenēs epi hydatōn pollōn). The invitation uses the imperative deuro ("come, come here") followed by the future deixō ("I will show"). The angel promises to show John the krima — the "judgment, verdict, sentence" — of the harlot. The word krima can denote both the judicial sentence itself and its execution. What follows in chapters 17-18 is both the verdict (why Babylon is condemned) and the sentence (how she is destroyed).

The figure is called hē pornē hē megalē — "the great harlot" or "the great prostitute." The word pornē ("prostitute, harlot") in prophetic usage designates a city or nation that has been unfaithful to God through idolatry, or a city that seduces others into spiritual-political corruption. The prophetic background is decisive for understanding this figure.

Isaiah 23:15-17 applies the harlot image to Tyre, the great commercial city: "At the end of seventy years the LORD will visit Tyre. Then she will go back to her harlot's wages (to pornikon) and will play the harlot (porneusei) with all the kingdoms on the face of the earth" (LXX). Tyre's "harlotry" is her commercial alliances and seductions — the way a trading city draws all nations into profitable but corrupting relationships.

Nahum 3:4 calls Nineveh, the capital of Assyria, "the charming one, the mistress of sorceries, who sells nations by her harlotries (tais porneiais autēs) and families by her sorceries." Nineveh's "harlotry" is her imperial seduction of the nations, drawing them into her political and religious orbit through attractive but ultimately destructive alliances.

Most significantly, Ezekiel 16 and 23 apply the harlot image to Jerusalem itself. In Ezekiel 16:15, God says to Jerusalem: "But you trusted in your beauty and played the harlot (eporneusen) because of your fame, and you poured out your harlotries (tēn porneian sou) on every passer-by." In Ezekiel 23, the two sisters Oholah (Samaria) and Oholibah (Jerusalem) both "played the harlot" with foreign nations. The prophetic tradition of the harlot-city is thus not limited to foreign oppressors; it can also designate God's own city when she has become unfaithful.

The phrase "who sits on many waters" (tēs kathēmenēs epi hydatōn pollōn) derives directly from Jeremiah 51:13 (LXX 28:13), where God addresses ancient Babylon: "O you who dwell by many waters (epi hydasi pollois), rich in treasures, your end has come, the measure of your covetousness." Historical Babylon was built on the Euphrates and surrounded by an elaborate canal system. The "many waters" in Jeremiah refer to the literal waterways that sustained Babylon's wealth and commerce. In verse 15, the angel will interpret the waters symbolically: "The waters which you saw where the harlot sits, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues" (17:15). The "many waters" are not geographical but demographic — the vast populations over which the harlot exercises her influence. She "sits on" them, meaning she is supported by, sustained by, and exercises dominion over the multitudes.

"With whom the kings of the earth committed acts of immorality" (meth' hēs eporneusan hoi basileis tēs gēs). The verb eporneusan ("committed sexual immorality") describes the political-religious alliances that the kings of the earth have formed with the harlot. In the prophetic framework, the "immorality" is not literal sexual behavior but the seductive entanglement of rulers with a corrupt system. The kings of the earth are drawn into the harlot's orbit, entering into relationships of mutual benefit and mutual corruption. They receive her luxuries; she receives their political support. The arrangement is presented in the language of prostitution: it is transactional, corrupting, and a betrayal of the allegiance that properly belongs to God alone.

Ezekiel 16:26-29 describes Jerusalem's "harlotry" with Egypt, Assyria, and Chaldea in similar terms: political alliances framed as sexual liaisons. The difference is that in Ezekiel, Jerusalem is the unfaithful wife of God who prostitutes herself with foreign powers. In Revelation 17, the harlot-city draws the kings of the earth to herself. She is not the unfaithful wife but the seductress who corrupts others.

"And those who dwell on the earth were made drunk with the wine of her immorality" (kai emethysthēsan hoi katoikountes tēn gēn ek tou oinou tēs porneias autēs). The earth-dwellers (hoi katoikountes tēn gēn) — the recurring designation in this document for those whose identity and allegiance are bound to the earthly order (3:10; 6:10; 8:13; 11:10; 13:8, 12, 14) — have been made drunk (emethysthēsan, aorist passive: "were made drunk," indicating the harlot's agency in intoxicating them). The wine of her immorality (ek tou oinou tēs porneias autēs) is the same phrase used in the second angel's announcement in 14:8: "she who has made all the nations drink of the wine of the passion of her immorality." The intoxication is the condition of those who have been seduced by the harlot's system — they are not thinking clearly, not perceiving reality accurately, not capable of the sober judgment that would lead them to "fear God and give him glory" (14:7). The harlot's wine is the opposite of the sober wakefulness that the document demands of the faithful (16:15: "Blessed is the one who stays awake and keeps his clothes").

Jeremiah 51:7 (LXX 28:7) again provides the source: "Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunk. The nations drank of her wine; therefore the nations went mad." The "madness" (emainonto) that follows drinking Babylon's wine is the inability to perceive reality — the nations cannot see that their alliance with the harlot is self-destructive, that her wealth is built on blood, and that her fall is inevitable.

div.title: Verse 3: The Woman on the Scarlet Beast in the Wilderness
div.p: "And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness; and I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast, full of blasphemous names, having seven heads and ten horns."

"And he carried me away in the Spirit into a wilderness" (kai apēnenken me eis erēmon en pneumati). The phrase en pneumati ("in the Spirit") marks a visionary transport. The same phrase appeared in 1:10 ("I was in the Spirit on the Lord's day"), 4:2 ("immediately I was in the Spirit, and behold, a throne was standing in heaven"), and will appear in 21:10 ("And he carried me away in the Spirit to a great and high mountain, and showed me the holy city, Jerusalem, coming down out of heaven from God"). Each use of en pneumati introduces a major visionary sequence. The transport here takes John to a wilderness (erēmon) — a detail whose significance should not be overlooked.

The wilderness (erēmos) has appeared already in this document. In 12:6, the woman (Israel/the covenant community) "fled into the wilderness (eis tēn erēmon) where she had a place prepared by God, so that there she would be nourished for one thousand two hundred and sixty days." In 12:14, the woman was given eagle's wings to fly "into the wilderness to her place, where she was nourished for a time and times and half a time, from the presence of the serpent." The wilderness in chapter 12 was a place of divine protection and nourishment — the same wilderness where Israel was sustained after the Exodus (Deuteronomy 8:2-3, 15-16). In the prophetic tradition, the wilderness can also be the place where God confronts a corrupt city. Isaiah 21:1 introduces the oracle against Babylon as "the oracle concerning the wilderness of the sea" (to horama tēs erēmou, LXX). Jeremiah 51:43 (LXX 28:43) describes Babylon's future: "Her cities have become an object of horror, a parched land and a wilderness (erēmos), a land in which no man lives."

There is an important contrast being drawn. In chapter 12, the faithful woman was nourished in the wilderness — the wilderness as refuge. In chapter 17, the harlot is shown to John in the wilderness — the wilderness as the place of desolation and judgment. The woman of chapter 12 fled to the wilderness for safety; the harlot of chapter 17 is found in the wilderness, the domain of her coming desolation. The author has constructed a deliberate counterpart: two women, both associated with the wilderness, but in opposite roles. The faithful woman is protected there; the harlot is exposed there. This woman-to-woman contrast will continue throughout the chapter and find its completion in the bride of chapters 21-22.

"And I saw a woman sitting on a scarlet beast, full of blasphemous names, having seven heads and ten horns" (kai eidon gynaika kathēmenēn epi thērion kokkinon, gemon onomatōn blasphēmias, echon kephalas hepta kai kerata deka). The woman and the beast are presented as distinct but intimately connected figures. The woman is riding the beast — she is seated upon it, supported by it, carried by it. Their relationship is one of mutual dependence: the beast gives the woman her position and mobility, while the woman presumably gives the beast a certain appearance of legitimacy and attractiveness.

The beast is immediately recognizable. It has "seven heads and ten horns" (kephalas hepta kai kerata deka) — the same configuration as the beast from the sea in 13:1 and the dragon in 12:3. The continuity is deliberate: this is the same beast system that the dragon empowered in chapter 13. The beast is described as kokkinon ("scarlet, crimson") — a color that connects it to the dragon of 12:3, who was pyrros ("fiery red"). The colors are in the same range: the dragon was red, the beast is scarlet. The beast's color also anticipates the woman's clothing in verse 4: she is dressed in purple and scarlet. The beast and the woman share the same color palette, visually linking them as parts of a single system.

The beast is gemon onomatōn blasphēmias — "full of blasphemous names." In 13:1, the beast had "blasphemous names" (onomata blasphēmias) on its heads. Here the blasphemous names cover the entire beast, not just the heads. The proliferation of blasphemous names indicates the intensification or comprehensive nature of the beast's self-deifying claims. Every surface of this creature declares what belongs to God alone. As discussed in the analysis of 13:1, the "blasphemous names" refer to the divine titles arrogated by imperial power — titles such as Sebastos/Augustus, Soter, Kyrios, and Theos that a first-century hearer in Roman Asia would associate with the emperor's official titulature.

div.title: Verses 4-5: The Woman's Appearance and Name
div.p: "The woman was clothed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls, having in her hand a gold cup full of abominations and of the unclean things of her immorality, and on her forehead a name was written, a mystery, 'BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH.'"

"The woman was clothed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls" (kai hē gynē ēn peribeblēmenē porphyroun kai kokkinon, kai kechrysōmenē chrysiō kai lithō timiō kai margaritais). The description of the harlot's appearance is deliberate and symbolically dense.

Purple (porphyroun) and scarlet (kokkinon) are the colors of imperial luxury and royal power. In the Roman world, purple-dyed cloth was extraordinarily expensive, produced from the mucus of the murex sea snail in a laborious process, and was associated with senatorial and imperial rank. The toga praetexta bordered in purple was a mark of Roman magistrates; the toga purpurea entirely of purple was reserved for triumphing generals and emperors. Scarlet (from the kermes insect) was similarly expensive and associated with military rank and royal display. Together, purple and scarlet communicate immense wealth, political power, and self-display.

These colors also have a significant scriptural resonance. In the construction of the tabernacle, purple (porphyra, LXX) and scarlet (kokkinon, LXX) were among the materials used for the curtains and priestly vestments (Exodus 25:4; 26:1, 31, 36; 28:5-6, 8, 15, 33). The tabernacle employed blue, purple, and scarlet thread together (Exodus 26:1). The harlot wears purple and scarlet — two of the three tabernacle colors — but without the blue (hyakinthos) that represents the heavenly dimension in the LXX tabernacle tradition. The omission of blue may be significant: the harlot possesses the outward appearance of sacred richness but lacks the heavenly component. Her adornment is a counterfeit of priestly splendor.

The gold, precious stones, and pearls further elaborate the display of extreme wealth. In 18:12, these items will appear in the catalogue of Babylon's trade goods: "cargoes of gold and silver and precious stones and pearls." In 18:16, the mourners will lament: "Woe, woe, the great city, she who was clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls." The harlot's personal adornment matches her commercial empire — she wears what she sells.

The contrast with the bride of the Lamb is pointed. In 19:8, the bride is given "fine linen, bright and clean" (byssinon lampron katharon), and the fine linen is identified as "the righteous acts of the saints" (ta dikaiōmata tōn hagiōn). The harlot's clothing is purchased luxury; the bride's clothing is earned righteousness. The harlot adorns herself with gold and stones; the bride is clothed in the pure deeds of the faithful. The two women are dressed in ways that reveal their respective characters.

"Having in her hand a gold cup full of abominations and of the unclean things of her immorality" (echousa potērion chrysoun en tē cheiri autēs gemon bdelygmatōn kai ta akatharta tēs porneias autēs). The golden cup (potērion chrysoun) recalls Jeremiah 51:7 (LXX 28:7): "Babylon was a golden cup (potērion chrysoun) in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunk." In Jeremiah, the cup is in God's hand — Babylon is the instrument through which God administers judgment on the nations. In Revelation 17, the cup is in the harlot's own hand — she drinks from it and gives it to others. The shift from God's hand to the harlot's hand indicates her autonomy in dispensing her intoxicating influence. She is not consciously serving as God's instrument; she is acting on her own behalf to seduce the nations.

The cup is "full of abominations" (gemon bdelygmatōn). The word bdelygma ("abomination, detestable thing") is the LXX's standard term for the idolatrous practices that God finds repulsive. Deuteronomy 7:25-26: "The graven images of their gods you are to burn with fire; you shall not covet the silver or the gold that is on them, nor take it for yourselves... you shall not bring an abomination (bdelygma) into your house." Deuteronomy 18:12: "whoever does these things is an abomination (bdelygma) to the LORD." Deuteronomy 29:17: "you have seen their abominations (bdelygmata) and their idols." The word appears in Daniel 9:27 and 11:31 and 12:11 in the phrase "the abomination of desolation" (bdelygma tēs erēmōseōs) — the desecrating object placed in the temple. The harlot's cup is filled with these abominations — the concentrated essence of everything that God's covenant people were commanded to destroy and avoid.

The phrase ta akatharta tēs porneias autēs ("the unclean things of her immorality") adds the language of ritual impurity. The word akathartos ("unclean, impure") is the opposite of katharos ("clean, pure") — the fundamental purity distinction of the Levitical system. The harlot's cup contains not merely what is offensive but what renders unclean, what defiles, what contaminates everything it touches. Those who drink from her cup are polluted by what they consume.

"And on her forehead a name was written, a mystery" (kai epi to metōpon autēs onoma gegrammenon, mystērion). The placement of a name on the forehead recalls the competing forehead inscriptions that have structured the document's imagery of allegiance. The 144,000 bear the Lamb's name and the Father's name on their foreheads (14:1). The servants of God are sealed on their foreheads (7:3). The beast's followers bear the mark on their foreheads (13:16). The high priest bore "Holy to the LORD" on his forehead (Exodus 28:36-38). The harlot bears her own name on her forehead — a self-identification that declares what she is.

The word mystērion ("mystery, secret, hidden meaning") functions here as a descriptor of the name that follows. In the author's usage, mystērion denotes something whose true meaning is hidden behind its surface appearance and requires revelation to understand. In 1:20, the "mystery of the seven stars" and the "seven golden lampstands" was explained: the stars are angels and the lampstands are churches. The term signals that what follows is symbolic — the name is not a literal label but a code that requires interpretation. The word may also be read as part of the inscription itself (i.e., the name written is "Mystery: Babylon the Great..."), but the author's use of mystērion elsewhere as a hermeneutical marker suggests it functions as a signal to the reader that the name that follows carries hidden significance.
"BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH" (BABYLŌN HĒ MEGALĒ, HĒ MĒTĒR TŌN PORNŌN KAI TŌN BDELYGMATŌN TĒS GĒS). The name has three elements.

First, "Babylon the Great" (Babylōn hē megalē) — the title already introduced in 14:8 and 16:19. As discussed in the analysis of 14:8, the epithet "the great" echoes Nebuchadnezzar's boast in Daniel 4:30. The name "Babylon" is typological: it identifies the present oppressive power with the archetypal oppressor of God's people from Israel's history.

Second, "the mother of harlots" (hē mētēr tōn pornōn). The harlot is not merely one prostitute among many but the origin, source, and exemplar of all harlotry. She is the mother — the one who generates and sustains the entire system of spiritual-political corruption. Every lesser instance of the nations' seduction proceeds from her. The cities, vassal kingdoms, and provincial authorities that imitate her ways are her offspring. The word mētēr ("mother") indicates generative power: the harlot does not merely corrupt; she reproduces her corruption.

Third, "the mother of the abominations of the earth" (hē mētēr tōn bdelygmatōn tēs gēs). She is the source not only of the harlotry but of the abominations — the idolatrous, defiling practices that constitute the content of her golden cup. The "abominations of the earth" encompass the entire range of false worship, blasphemous claims, and dehumanizing practices that the beast system has imposed.

Roman practice provides a first-century referent for this self-identification on the forehead. Prostitutes in the Roman world were sometimes identified by a label (titulus) worn on the forehead or displayed above their doors, advertising their trade name. Seneca (Controversiae 1.2) and Juvenal (Satires 6.122-123) attest to this practice. The harlot Babylon wears her name on her forehead as a prostitute would — openly displaying what she is. The irony is that despite this open display, the world does not recognize her for what she is (they are "drunk" with her wine, 17:2). Only the seer, guided by the angel, perceives the truth.

div.title: Verse 6: The Harlot Drunk with Blood
div.p: "And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the witnesses of Jesus. When I saw her, I wondered greatly."

"And I saw the woman drunk with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the witnesses of Jesus" (kai eidon tēn gynaika methyousan ek tou haimatos tōn hagiōn kai ek tou haimatos tōn martyrōn Iēsou). The image shifts from the harlot as one who intoxicates others (verse 2: she made the earth-dwellers drunk with her wine) to the harlot as one who is herself drunk — but not with wine. Her intoxicant is blood. The verb methyousan (present participle of methyō, "to be drunk, to be intoxicated") portrays the harlot in a state of ongoing, active inebriation. She is presently drunk, not merely stained. The present tense indicates that the bloodshed is not a past act she regrets but a continuing condition she enjoys. She is insatiable.

The blood is identified by two sources: "the blood of the saints" (tou haimatos tōn hagiōn) and "the blood of the witnesses of Jesus" (tou haimatos tōn martyrōn Iēsou). The saints (hagioi) are the consecrated people of God — the same community persecuted by the beast in 13:7 and commended for their perseverance in 13:10 and 14:12. The "witnesses of Jesus" (martyres Iēsou) are those whose testimony (martyria) about Jesus cost them their lives. The word martyrs (martyrōn) in this document carries the double weight of its first-century usage: a martys is one who testifies, a witness who declares what they have seen and known. But because the testimony these witnesses bear draws lethal opposition from the beast system, the word has already begun its semantic journey toward the later meaning of "martyr" — one who dies for testimony. In 6:9, the souls under the altar had been "slain because of the word of God, and because of the testimony (martyrian) which they had maintained." In 11:7, the beast "overcame and killed" the two witnesses (martyras). In 12:11, the brothers overcame the accuser "by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony (martyrias), and they did not love their life even when faced with death." The harlot is drunk with the blood of these people.

The two phrases — "blood of the saints" and "blood of the witnesses" — may describe the same group from two angles (the saints are the witnesses, and the witnesses are the saints), or they may distinguish two categories within the persecuted community (the holy ones in general and those specifically killed for bearing testimony to Jesus). The kai ("and") is most naturally read as epexegetical or additive: the harlot's victims are God's consecrated people who bore witness to Jesus.

The image of a city drunk on the blood of the righteous has prophetic precedent. In Jeremiah 51:49 (LXX 28:49): "As Babylon has caused the slain of Israel to fall, so at Babylon the slain of all the earth will fall." Isaiah 34:7 (on Edom): "the land will be soaked with blood" (LXX). The harlot's blood-drunkenness reveals the true nature of the luxury described in verse 4. Behind the gold, the pearls, the purple robes, and the golden cup lies violent persecution. The wealth and splendor are built on the murder of the faithful. The system sustains itself by eliminating those who refuse to participate. This will be stated definitively in 18:24: "And in her was found the blood of prophets and of saints and of all who have been slain on the earth."

"When I saw her, I wondered greatly" (kai ethaumasa idōn autēn thauma mega). The verb ethaumasa ("I marveled, I wondered, I was astonished") and the cognate noun thauma ("wonder, marvel, astonishment") describe John's visceral response to the vision. The word thaumazō in this document has a specific valence. In 13:3, "the whole earth was amazed (ethaumasthē) and followed after the beast" — the "wonder" of the earth-dwellers led them to worship. In 17:8, the earth-dwellers "will wonder (thaumasthēsontai) when they see the beast." Wondering/marveling in this document is typically the precursor to being deceived. John's reaction is significant: he is drawn in by what he sees, experiencing the same astonishment that leads the earth-dwellers astray. The angel's interpretation in the following verses serves to correct this response — to move John from astonishment to understanding, from wonder to discernment.

The content of John's wonder may be the jarring juxtaposition of splendor and horror: a woman dressed in royal finery, dripping with gold and jewels, holding a golden cup — but drunk with blood. The cognitive dissonance between her beauty and her violence is precisely what makes her effective as a seductress. The world sees the gold and pearls; John sees the blood. Or perhaps John marvels because the figure is simultaneously attractive and repulsive, and the tension between these qualities produces the vertigo of wonder. The angel will immediately address this: "Why do you wonder?" (17:7).

div.title: Verses 7-8: The Angel's Interpretation Begins — The Mystery of the Beast
div.p: "And the angel said to me, 'Why do you wonder? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her, which has the seven heads and the ten horns. The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss and go to destruction. And those who dwell on the earth, whose name has not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, will wonder when they see the beast, that he was and is not and will come.'"

"Why do you wonder? I will tell you the mystery of the woman and of the beast that carries her" (dia ti ethaumasas; egō erō soi to mystērion tēs gynaikos kai tou thēriou tou bastazontos autēn). The angel's question implies a gentle rebuke: John should not wonder (thaumazō) at the harlot the way the earth-dwellers wonder at the beast. The remedy for misdirected wonder is interpretation — the angel will tell (erō, future of legō) the mystērion ("mystery, hidden meaning") of both the woman and the beast. The word mystērion appears here for the second time in the chapter (cf. verse 5, the inscription on the forehead). The figure's true identity is a "mystery" — it is not self-evident but requires angelic revelation to decode. The surface appearance (gold, jewels, royal garments) conceals the reality (blood, abomination, blasphemy). The angel's interpretation will strip away the surface and reveal what lies beneath.

The beast is described as tou bastazontos autēn — "the one carrying her." The verb bastazō ("to carry, to bear, to support") indicates that the beast is the vehicle and support for the woman. She rides; the beast carries. The relationship between the two figures — the harlot and the beast — is now made structural: the beast provides the political-military power on which the harlot's system depends. Without the beast, the woman has no platform. Without the woman, the beast has no attractive veneer. Together they form a single system: raw power (the beast) dressed in seductive luxury (the woman).
