"The beast that you saw was, and is not, and is about to come up out of the abyss and go to destruction" (to thērion ho eides ēn kai ouk estin kai mellei anabainein ek tēs abyssou kai eis apōleian hypagei). This is one of the most theologically dense statements in the chapter. The beast is described with a threefold temporal formula: ēn ("was"), ouk estin ("is not"), mellei anabainein ("is about to come up"). This formula is a deliberate parody of the divine self-identification that runs throughout the document.

In 1:4, God is described as "him who is and who was and who is to come" (ho ōn kai ho ēn kai ho erchomenos). In 1:8: "I am the Alpha and the Omega, says the Lord God, who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty." In 4:8, the four living creatures declare "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty, who was and who is and who is to come." In 11:17: "We give you thanks, O Lord God, the Almighty, who are and who were." In 16:5: "Righteous are you, who are and who were, O Holy One."

God's threefold temporal designation expresses his eternal, sovereign existence across all time. He is (present), he was (past), he is coming (future). The beast's formula inverts this. The beast "was" (past existence), "is not" (present non-existence), and "is about to come up" (future reappearance). Where God eternally is, the beast currently is not. Where God's "coming" is sovereign and salvific, the beast's "coming up" is from the abyss (ek tēs abyssou) — the domain of demonic powers and imprisonment (9:1-2, 11; 11:7; 20:1-3) — and terminates in "destruction" (apōleia). The beast's trajectory is from non-existence through a brief reappearance to permanent ruin. God's existence has no beginning and no end; the beast's existence is interrupted, temporary, and doomed.

The phrase ek tēs abyssou ("from the abyss") connects this beast directly to 11:7, where "the beast that comes up out of the abyss" (to thērion to anabainon ek tēs abyssou) killed the two witnesses. The abyss is the prison of destructive forces: in 9:1-2, the shaft of the abyss was opened and smoke and locusts poured out; in 9:11, the king of the locusts was "the angel of the abyss." In 20:1-3, an angel will seize the dragon and throw him into the abyss, sealing it over him. The beast's origin from the abyss identifies it as a creature of the underworld, not of heaven — its power comes from below, not from above. And its destination is apōleia — "destruction, perdition, ruin" — the same word used in 2 Thessalonians 2:3 for "the man of lawlessness, the son of destruction (tēs apōleias)." The beast's arc is from ruin to ruin, with a brief interlude of apparent power.

For the first-century hearer, the "was, is not, and is about to come" may evoke the Nero redivivus expectation discussed in the analysis of 13:3 and 13:18. Nero "was" (he lived and reigned), "is not" (he died in 68 CE), and popular expectation held that he would return — "is about to come up." The author may be using this widely known expectation as the vehicle for his theological point: the beast's power is a parody of God's eternal existence. Even if the beast reappears, its trajectory ends in destruction, not in eternal reign.

"And those who dwell on the earth, whose name has not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world, will wonder when they see the beast, that he was and is not and will come" (kai thaumasthēsontai hoi katoikountes epi tēs gēs, hōn ou gegraptai to onoma epi to biblion tēs zōēs apo katabolēs kosmou, blepontes to thērion hoti ēn kai ouk estin kai parestai). The earth-dwellers' response to the beast is thaumasthēsontai — "they will wonder, they will be amazed." This is the same response noted in 13:3: "the whole earth was amazed (ethaumasthē) and followed after the beast." The wonder of the earth-dwellers is the precursor to worship, as established in 13:3-4: amazement leads to following, and following leads to worship. The earth-dwellers marvel at the beast's apparent conquest of death — the "was, is not, and will come" formula impresses them as evidence of supernatural power. They see a counterfeit of divine eternity and are deceived.

The qualification is the same as in 13:8: the earth-dwellers whose names have not been written in the book of life are the ones who wonder. Those whose names are written do not wonder — they see through the beast's pretension because they know the truly eternal One, "who is and who was and who is to come." The "book of life from the foundation of the world" (to biblion tēs zōēs apo katabolēs kosmou) reasserts that God's registration of his people precedes history. The phrase functions pastorally: the faithful are not newly or tenuously inscribed but have been known to God since the beginning.

The final word in the beast's description shifts from mellei anabainein ("is about to come up") in verse 8a to parestai ("will come" or "will be present") in verse 8b. The verb parestai (future of pareimi, "to be present, to arrive") may allude to the concept of parousia — the "coming" or "presence" of a divine or royal figure. If so, the beast's parestai is a parody of Christ's parousia: the beast has its own "coming," its own moment of appearing, but it terminates in destruction, not in eternal reign.

div.title: Verses 9-11: The Seven Heads Interpreted
div.p: "Here is the mind which has wisdom. The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits, and they are seven kings; five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come; and when he comes, he must remain a little while. The beast which was and is not, is himself also an eighth and is one of the seven, and he goes to destruction."

"Here is the mind which has wisdom" (hōde ho nous ho echōn sophian). This formula parallels 13:18: "Here is wisdom. Let him who has understanding calculate the number of the beast." Both formulae introduce interpretive riddles that require discernment. The word nous ("mind, understanding, intellect") indicates that what follows is not transparent but demands reflection. The sophia ("wisdom") required is not worldly cleverness but the spiritual perception that comes from knowing God's ways — the wisdom that enables the hearer to decode the imagery.

"The seven heads are seven mountains on which the woman sits" (hai hepta kephalai hepta orē eisin, hopou hē gynē kathētai ep' autōn). The first identification: the seven heads are seven mountains (hepta orē). The word oros ("mountain, hill") in Greek does not distinguish between a mountain and a hill. The identification of a city with seven hills/mountains would be immediately recognizable to any first-century hearer in the Greco-Roman world. Rome was universally known as the city built on seven hills (septem montes/colles): the Palatine, Aventine, Caelian, Esquiline, Viminal, Quirinal, and Capitoline. Roman poets and writers routinely referred to Rome by this designation. Virgil (Georgics 2.535) described "Rome who has compassed for herself seven hills with a single wall." Martial (Epigrams 4.64) called Rome "the city of the seven dominating hills" (septem dominos montes). Cicero (Ad Atticum 6.5) referenced the same. Ovid, Propertius, and others use the phrase. Coins from the late Republic and early Empire depicted Roma seated on seven hills. The festival of the Septimontium celebrated the seven hills explicitly. A first-century audience hearing "seven mountains on which the woman sits" would not need the angel's subsequent explanation: they would recognize Rome.

The woman "sits" (kathētai) on the mountains — the same verb used in verse 1 for the harlot "sitting" on many waters. She sits on the mountains and on the waters: on the geographical foundation of the city and on the peoples who sustain her. Her sitting is a posture of enthroned authority — she is seated as on a throne, established and secure. The irony is that her throne is the beast itself, and the beast's trajectory is toward destruction.

"And they are seven kings" (kai basileis hepta eisin). The second identification: the seven heads are also seven kings (basileis). The heads carry a double meaning — they are both geographical (mountains) and political (kings). The word basileus ("king") in the Roman context most naturally refers to the emperor, the supreme ruler. The fact that the heads are simultaneously mountains (the city's geography) and kings (the city's rulers) merges the identity of Rome-the-place with Rome-the-power. The city and its rulers are inseparable.

"Five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come; and when he comes, he must remain a little while" (hoi pente epesan, ho heis estin, ho allos oupō ēlthen, kai hotan elthē oligon auton dei meinai). The seven kings are distributed across three temporal categories: five have fallen (past), one currently exists (present), and one has not yet come (future). The statement "five have fallen" (hoi pente epesan) uses the verb epiptō ("to fall"), which in this document describes the fall of cities and powers — Babylon "fallen, fallen" (14:8; 18:2) uses the same verb (epesen). The five fallen kings are five past rulers whose reigns have ended.

The identification of these kings with specific Roman emperors has been debated extensively even among first-century listeners, and the text itself does not name them. The difficulty lies in determining where to begin the count (with Julius Caesar, with Augustus, or with another figure) and whether to include the three short-lived emperors of 68-69 CE (Galba, Otho, Vitellius). Several arrangements are possible:

If the count begins with Augustus (the first princeps, the formal founder of the imperial system), the sequence would be: (1) Augustus, (2) Tiberius, (3) Caligula, (4) Claudius, (5) Nero — "five have fallen"; (6) the one who "is" would be the sixth in sequence. If the three short-lived emperors of 68-69 are skipped (as many ancient lists did, treating them as interruptions rather than legitimate reigns), the sixth would be Vespasian, and the seventh who "has not yet come" and "must remain a little while" would be Titus, whose reign lasted only about two years (79-81 CE) — which fits "a little while" (oligon) precisely.

If the count begins with Julius Caesar (whom some ancient historians treated as the first ruler of the imperial system, as in Suetonius' Lives of the Twelve Caesars), the sequence shifts forward by one, and the "one who is" would be Nero or a later emperor, depending on inclusions.

The text does not resolve this question definitively, and the author may not intend a strict one-to-one correlation. The number seven, throughout this document, is the number of completeness. Seven kings may represent the complete sequence of imperial rulers — the fullness of the beast's political expression — rather than a precise historical inventory. The statement that "five have fallen, one is, the other has not yet come" may function to locate the audience in time (the document is written during the reign of the sixth) while also indicating that the entire imperial system is nearing its end (only one more to come, and his stay is brief).

"The beast which was and is not, is himself also an eighth and is one of the seven, and he goes to destruction" (kai to thērion ho ēn kai ouk estin, kai autos ogdoos estin kai ek tōn hepta estin, kai eis apōleian hypagei). The beast itself — not merely one of its heads but the beast as a whole — is an eighth (ogdoos) king, yet "one of the seven" (ek tōn hepta). This paradoxical statement indicates that the beast transcends the sequence of individual rulers while being embodied in one of them. The beast is more than any single king; it is the imperial system as such, the principle of blasphemous, coercive, blood-drunk power. And yet it is also "one of the seven" — it manifests in a particular ruler, one who "was and is not" (a ruler who lived, died, and is expected to return).

The Nero redivivus expectation again provides the most natural first-century referent. Nero was one of the seven emperors (one of the "heads"). He died ("was and is not"). Popular belief held he would return ("is about to come up from the abyss"). The author seems to use this expectation to describe the beast's own nature: the beast embodies the worst of imperial power (Nero being the paradigmatic persecutor of the faithful, having executed believers in Rome after the fire of 64 CE, as attested by Tacitus, Annals 15.44), and its future manifestation will recapitulate Nero's character.

The phrase kai eis apōleian hypagei ("and he goes to destruction") repeats the verdict of verse 8. The beast's destination is not eternal reign but apōleia — ruin, perdition. This is the third time destruction has been named as the beast's end-point (17:8a, 17:8b, 17:11). The repetition is emphatic: regardless of the beast's impressive reappearance, its trajectory is fixed and terminal.

div.title: Verses 12-14: The Ten Horns Interpreted — Kings Who Wage War on the Lamb
div.p: "The ten horns which you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom, but they receive authority as kings with the beast for one hour. These have one purpose, and they give their power and authority to the beast. These will wage war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those who are with him are the called and chosen and faithful."

"The ten horns which you saw are ten kings who have not yet received a kingdom" (kai ta deka kerata ha eides deka basileis eisin, hoitines basileian oupō elabon). The ten horns, like the seven heads, are identified as kings (basileis). But unlike the seven head-kings, these ten have "not yet received a kingdom" (basileian oupō elabon). They are kings-in-waiting, rulers who have not yet assumed their power. In Daniel 7:24, the ten horns of the fourth beast are likewise ten kings: "The ten horns are ten kings who will arise from this kingdom." In Daniel's vision, the horns grow from the fourth beast's head and represent rulers who emerge from within the imperial system. The author of Revelation follows Daniel closely: the ten horns are kings who derive their existence and authority from the beast system.

The fact that they have "not yet received a kingdom" places them in the future from the author's stated temporal perspective (the "one who is" of verse 10). These are not current rulers but anticipated ones — figures who will arise within the beast system at a later stage.

"But they receive authority as kings with the beast for one hour" (alla exousian hōs basileis mian hōran lambanousin meta tou thēriou). Their authority (exousia) is exercised "as kings" (hōs basileis) — they function with royal power but perhaps lack the formal, established status of the seven head-kings. And their reign is extraordinarily brief: "one hour" (mian hōran). The "hour" (hōra) in this document is the decisive but brief moment of crisis. In 3:10, the Philadelphian assembly was promised protection from "the hour of testing" (tēs hōras tou peirasmou). In 9:15, the four angels at the Euphrates were prepared for "the hour and day and month and year." In 14:7, "the hour of his judgment has come." In 18:10, 17, 19, the mourners over Babylon will lament that her judgment came "in one hour" (mia hōra). The ten kings' authority lasts for the same "one hour" as Babylon's destruction — their brief reign coincides with the final crisis. Their power is real but fleeting, given and taken in the space of the climactic moment.

The phrase meta tou thēriou ("with the beast") indicates that their authority is exercised in partnership with, or as subordinates of, the beast. They do not reign independently but as the beast's allies.

"These have one purpose, and they give their power and authority to the beast" (houtoi mian gnōmēn echousin, kai tēn dynamin kai exousian autōn tō thēriō didoasin). The ten kings share "one purpose" (mian gnōmēn — literally "one mind, one counsel, one resolve"). The word gnōmē ("opinion, purpose, resolve, judgment") indicates unified will. The ten kings are not merely aligned politically; they are of a single mind. They voluntarily transfer their dynamis ("power, might") and exousia ("authority") to the beast. The transfer inverts the proper order of authority described in this document. In 4:11, "worthy are you, our Lord and our God, to receive glory and honor and power (dynamin)" — power properly flows upward to God. The ten kings direct their power downward to the beast. The beast system operates through willing subordination: the kings choose to serve the beast, surrendering their sovereignty to the beast's purposes.

"These will wage war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them" (houtoi meta tou arniou polemēsousin, kai to arnion nikēsei autous). The ten kings and the beast make war against the Lamb. The verb polemēsousin ("will make war") echoes the dragon's war against the woman's offspring (12:17), the beast's war against the saints (13:7), and the dragon's war in heaven (12:7). The entire document has been building toward this confrontation: the dragon empowered the beast, the beast made war on the saints, and now the beast and its royal allies directly engage the Lamb.

The outcome is stated with absolute brevity: kai to arnion nikēsei autous — "and the Lamb will overcome them." The verb nikēsei (future of nikaō, "to conquer, to overcome") declares the Lamb's victory in a single word. No description of the battle is given here; the full narration will come in 19:11-21, where the rider on the white horse — "The Word of God" — defeats the beast and the kings of the earth with "the sword which came from his mouth" (19:15, 21). Here the victory is simply announced as a certainty.

"Because he is Lord of lords and King of kings" (hoti kyrios kyriōn estin kai basileus basileōn). The basis of the Lamb's victory is stated: he bears the supreme title. "Lord of lords and King of kings" (kyrios kyriōn kai basileus basileōn) is the title of ultimate sovereignty, asserting authority over all other lords and kings. The title appears in the LXX in Deuteronomy 10:17: "For the LORD your God is the God of gods and the Lord of lords (kyrios tōn kyriōn), the great God (ho theos ho megas), mighty and awesome." Daniel 2:47: "Your God is indeed God of gods and Lord of kings (kyrios tōn basileōn) and a revealer of mysteries." In both passages, the title expresses God's supremacy over all competing authorities.

In this document, the same title appears in 19:16 on the rider's robe and thigh: "KING OF KINGS, AND LORD OF LORDS." The Lamb who appears slain (5:6), who was rejected and killed, who is the seeming opposite of a conquering king, bears the title that belongs to the supreme sovereign of all creation. The ten kings gave their power to the beast; the Lamb does not need donated power. He is the source of all authority.

"And those who are with him are the called and chosen and faithful" (kai hoi met' autou klētoi kai eklektoi kai pistoi). The Lamb's army is described with three adjectives, not with military terminology. His companions are not warriors in the conventional sense but klētoi ("called"), eklektoi ("chosen, elect"), and pistoi ("faithful, trustworthy"). Each term carries scriptural weight.

Klētoi ("called") designates those whom God has summoned. In Isaiah 41:9 (LXX), God says to Israel: "I called you (ekalesa se) from the ends of the earth, and from its remote parts I called you (ekalesa se), and said to you, 'You are my servant, I have chosen you and not rejected you.'" The called are those whom God has actively summoned into relationship and service.

Eklektoi ("chosen, elect") in the LXX refers to those whom God has selected for his purposes. In Isaiah 42:1 (LXX): "Behold my servant, whom I uphold; my chosen one (ho eklektos mou) in whom my soul delights." In Isaiah 43:20: "my chosen people" (ton laon mou ton eklekton). In this document's broader scriptural context, election is primarily corporate and vocational — God chooses a people for a purpose (service, witness, being a light to the nations), not merely individuals for personal salvation.

Pistoi ("faithful") is the crowning term. The word describes those who have maintained loyalty — who have endured the beast's pressure, refused the mark, kept the commandments of God and the testimony of Jesus (12:17; 14:12). Faithfulness is the quality that has been demanded throughout the letters to the seven churches: "Be faithful until death, and I will give you the crown of life" (2:10). The Lamb's army consists of those who were called by God, chosen for his purposes, and proved faithful through the ordeal.

The order is significant: called first (God's initiative), chosen second (God's purpose), faithful third (the human response). The sequence moves from divine action to human fidelity. The faithful did not choose themselves; they were called and chosen. But their inclusion among the Lamb's companions is confirmed by their faithfulness — they responded to the call and fulfilled the purpose of their election by enduring. The three terms together describe a community whose identity originates in God's action and is validated by their perseverance.

div.title: Verses 15-18: The Waters, the Horns' Betrayal, and the Woman Identified
div.p: "And he said to me, 'The waters which you saw where the harlot sits, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues. And the ten horns which you saw, and the beast, these will hate the harlot and will make her desolate and naked, and will eat her flesh and will burn her up with fire. For God has put it in their hearts to execute his purpose by having a common purpose, and by giving their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God will be fulfilled. The woman whom you saw is the great city, which reigns over the kings of the earth.'"

"The waters which you saw where the harlot sits, are peoples and multitudes and nations and tongues" (ta hydata ha eides, hou hē pornē kathētai, laoi kai ochloi eisin kai ethnē kai glōssai). The angel now interprets the "many waters" of verse 1. The waters are not literal seas or rivers but peoples (laoi), multitudes (ochloi), nations (ethnē), and tongues (glōssai). This fourfold formula is the author's standard expression for universal humanity, used throughout the document (5:9; 7:9; 10:11; 11:9; 13:7; 14:6). The harlot "sits" on the peoples as she sits on the beast and on the mountains — she is sustained by, enthroned upon, and exercises dominion over the populations of the earth. Her power rests on the masses who support, serve, and enrich her.

The image of waters as nations is drawn from Isaiah 17:12-13 (LXX): "Woe, the multitude of many nations (ethnōn pollōn), like the roaring of the sea (hōs thalassa), they will roar. And many nations (ethnē polla) will roar like the roaring of many waters (hydatōn pollōn)." Psalm 93:3-4 (LXX 92:3-4): "The floods have lifted up, O LORD, the floods have lifted up their voice... The LORD on high is mightier than the sound of many waters (hydatōn pollōn), mightier than the breakers of the sea." In both texts, the turbulent waters represent the surging nations that threaten but are ultimately subject to God's authority.

"And the ten horns which you saw, and the beast, these will hate the harlot and will make her desolate and naked, and will eat her flesh and will burn her up with fire" (kai ta deka kerata ha eides kai to thērion, houtoi misēsousin tēn pornēn kai ērēmōmenēn poiēsousin autēn kai gymnēn, kai tas sarkas autēs phagontai kai autēn katakausousin en pyri). This is the critical turning point in the chapter. The beast and its ten horns — the very power structure that carried the harlot and sustained her position — now turn against her. The alliance that supported Babylon is revealed to be unstable, and the destruction of the harlot comes not from an external attack but from within the beast system itself.
The verbs describe total destruction through four actions:

First, they "will hate" (misēsousin) her — the emotional foundation of the betrayal is visceral hostility. The alliance that seemed solid was held together by self-interest, not by genuine loyalty. When the interests shift, hatred replaces partnership.

Second, they "will make her desolate and naked" (ērēmōmenēn poiēsousin autēn kai gymnēn). The word ērēmōmenēn ("made desolate, laid waste") is the same root as erēmos ("wilderness, desert") — they will reduce her to the desolation of the wilderness. The word gymnēn ("naked") indicates the stripping away of her luxurious garments. The woman who was "clothed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls" (verse 4) is now stripped bare. The exposure of nakedness in the prophetic tradition is a standard image of the judgment on a faithless city.

Ezekiel 16:39 (against Jerusalem as harlot): "They will strip you of your clothing and take your beautiful jewels, and they will leave you naked and bare" (LXX: gymnēn kai aischynēn). Ezekiel 23:26-29 (against Oholibah/Jerusalem): "They will strip you of your garments and take away your fine jewelry... and leave you naked and bare (gymnēn kai aischynēn), and the nakedness (aschēmosynē) of your harlotries will be uncovered."
Hosea 2:3 (LXX 2:5): God threatens the unfaithful wife Israel: "I will strip her naked (ekdysō autēn gymnēn) and make her as in the day she was born, and make her like a wilderness (hōs erēmon)."

The stripping and desolation of the harlot recapitulates the prophetic judgment on unfaithful cities. The luxury that seemed permanent is torn away; the beauty that seduced the nations is exposed as a veneer.

Third, they "will eat her flesh" (tas sarkas autēs phagontai). The language of consuming flesh appears in Psalm 27:2 (LXX 26:2): "When evildoers came upon me to eat my flesh (tou phagein tas sarkas mou), my adversaries and my enemies, they stumbled and fell." Micah 3:3 accuses the leaders of Israel: "who eat the flesh (tas sarkas) of my people." But the most direct precedent is the fate of Jezebel in 2 Kings 9:36 (LXX 4 Kingdoms 9:36): "Dogs shall eat the flesh (tas sarkas) of Jezebel in the plot of Jezreel." Jezebel — the foreign queen who promoted Baal worship in Israel, who killed the prophets of the Lord (1 Kings 18:4, 13), who had Naboth murdered for his vineyard (1 Kings 21) — was consumed by dogs. The reference to Jezebel is not accidental in a document that has already named "Jezebel" as a figure in the church at Thyatira who teaches and misleads God's servants to practice immorality and eat things sacrificed to idols (2:20). The harlot Babylon shares Jezebel's fate: her flesh is consumed. The alliance that sustained her becomes the instrument that devours her.

Fourth, they "will burn her up with fire" (autēn katakausousin en pyri). Burning with fire is the prescribed punishment for certain severe transgressions in the Torah. Leviticus 21:9: "If the daughter of a priest profanes herself by playing the harlot (ekporneusē), she profanes her father; she shall be burned with fire (en pyri katakauthēsetai)." The specific punishment for a priest's daughter who commits harlotry is burning — the same fate visited on the harlot Babylon. If the harlot has dressed in the colors of the tabernacle (verse 4, purple and scarlet) and has assumed a priestly identity, then her punishment as a prostituting priest's daughter is contextually appropriate. In 18:8, the harlot's destruction by fire is confirmed: "she will be burned up with fire (en pyri katakauthēsetai); for the Lord God who judges her is strong."

The burning of the harlot by her own allies is also prefigured in Ezekiel 23:25, 47, where God decrees that the unfaithful women will be subjected to fire: "They will burn their houses with fire" (23:47). The instrument of God's judgment is the very power that once sustained the corrupt city.

"For God has put it in their hearts to execute his purpose by having a common purpose, and by giving their kingdom to the beast, until the words of God will be fulfilled" (ho gar theos edōken eis tas kardias autōn poiēsai tēn gnōmēn autou, kai poiēsai mian gnōmēn kai dounai tēn basileian autōn tō thēriō, achri telesthēsontai hoi logoi tou theou). This verse pulls back the curtain on the theological mechanism behind the harlot's destruction. The ten horns' betrayal of the harlot is not random political chaos; it is God's own action. God "put it in their hearts" (edōken eis tas kardias autōn) — the same divine passive (edōken, "gave") used throughout chapter 13 for every capacity the beast received. God is the hidden agent behind the beast's actions, using the beast system's own internal contradictions to accomplish his sovereign purpose.

The word gnōmēn ("purpose, resolve, plan") appears twice. The ten kings execute God's gnōmē ("his purpose") by acting with a common gnōmē ("one purpose") among themselves. The irony is extraordinary: the kings think they are pursuing their own agenda by turning on the harlot, but they are actually carrying out God's plan. Their self-interested betrayal serves the divine will. The very unity that the kings display in giving their kingdom to the beast (verse 13) is the unity that God uses to destroy the harlot. The beast system destroys itself, and God orchestrates the self-destruction.

This pattern has precedent in Israel's scriptures. In Judges 9:23, "God sent an evil spirit between Abimelech and the men of Shechem; and the men of Shechem dealt treacherously with Abimelech." The alliance between Abimelech and Shechem collapsed through divine agency, and both were destroyed. In 2 Chronicles 20:22-23, God set the Ammonites and Moabites against each other, and they destroyed one another without Israel having to fight. The principle is consistent: God uses the internal fractures of hostile powers to accomplish their defeat.

The phrase achri telesthēsontai hoi logoi tou theou ("until the words of God will be fulfilled") introduces a temporal limit. The word telesthēsontai (from teleō, "to bring to completion, to fulfill") is the same verb used in 15:1 for the completion of God's wrath (etelesthē) and in 10:7 for the "mystery of God" being "finished" (etelesthē) at the seventh trumpet. The kings will continue in their role "until" God's words are accomplished. After that, their function ceases. The beast system is a temporary instrument — it serves God's purpose for a bounded period and then is discarded. The words of God (hoi logoi tou theou) that must be fulfilled include the entire sequence of prophetic announcements in the document: the fall of Babylon (14:8), the completion of the bowls (15:1), and the ultimate vindication of the saints.

"The woman whom you saw is the great city, which reigns over the kings of the earth" (kai hē gynē hēn eides estin hē polis hē megalē hē echousa basileian epi tōn basileōn tēs gēs). The angel's final identification is the most direct statement in the chapter. The woman is not an individual person but a polis — a city. She is "the great city" (hē polis hē megalē), the same designation used in 11:8 ("the great city which mystically is called Sodom and Egypt, where also their Lord was crucified") and in 16:19 ("the great city was split into three parts"). She "reigns over" (echousa basileian epi, literally "having kingship/kingdom over") the kings of the earth.

For a first-century hearer in the Roman province of Asia, the identification is unmistakable. What city, in the late first century, sat on seven hills (verse 9), reigned over the kings of the earth (verse 18), grew wealthy through international commerce (the cargo list of 18:12-13), was drunk with the blood of the saints (verse 6, recalling Nero's persecution and the ongoing pressures of the imperial cult), and was sustained by a vast network of subject peoples and nations (verse 15)? The answer is Rome. The identification with Rome does not require any interpretive gymnastics; it is the straightforward reading that any first-century audience would make.

However, the author has not merely identified a particular first-century city. He has used the name "Babylon" — the code-name that draws on the entire prophetic tradition of imperial oppression. The typological identification works on multiple levels: as Babylon was to sixth-century Judah (the destroyer of the temple, the enslaver of God's people, the arrogant blasphemer of God's name), so Rome is to the first-century assemblies. And as Babylon fell (Isaiah 13-14, 21; Jeremiah 50-51), so Rome will fall. The prophetic pattern is not exhausted by any single historical referent; the harlot-city is every city that sets itself up as the center of the world, that sustains itself on the blood of the faithful, and that seduces the nations into idolatrous allegiance. Rome is the present instance; the principle is comprehensive.

div.title: Summary of the Chapter's Argument
div.p: Revelation 17 answers the question that has been hanging since 14:8: who is Babylon the great, and how does she fall? The chapter is an interpretive vision, guided by one of the bowl-angels, in which the harlot-city is unveiled, described, and explained.
The chapter makes five major arguments:

First, the harlot and the beast are distinct but interdependent. The harlot rides the beast — she depends on the beast's political-military power for her position. The beast carries the harlot — it provides the infrastructure of coercion (military force, legal authority, economic control) on which the harlot's seductive system operates. The relationship is symbiotic: the beast gives power; the harlot gives legitimacy, attractiveness, and the intoxicating wine that keeps the earth-dwellers compliant. Yet the relationship is not permanent. The beast system will eventually turn on the harlot and destroy her (verse 16). The alliance is held together by self-interest, not by genuine loyalty, and when God redirects the kings' purposes (verse 17), the alliance collapses. The harlot is destroyed not by the Lamb's direct intervention but by the self-consuming violence of the beast system itself.

Second, the beast is a parody of God. The threefold formula "was, and is not, and is about to come" (verse 8) counterfeits the divine self-identification "who is and who was and who is to come" (1:4, 8; 4:8). Where God eternally exists, the beast has gaps in its existence. Where God's "coming" brings salvation, the beast's coming up is from the abyss and terminates in destruction. The beast impresses the earth-dwellers with its apparent transcendence of death (the healed mortal wound of 13:3; the "was and is not and will come" of 17:8), but this is a counterfeit resurrection. The beast's trajectory is fixed: from the abyss to destruction. Its entire career is bounded by these two poles.

Third, the harlot is identified as a specific historical entity with universal significance. The seven mountains (verse 9) point to Rome. The reign over the kings of the earth (verse 18) confirms the identification. The blood of the saints and witnesses (verse 6) corresponds to the historical reality of Roman persecution. The luxury goods and commercial dominance will be elaborated in chapter 18. Yet the name "Babylon" signals that the identification is typological, not merely historical. The harlot is Rome as Rome occupies the role that Babylon occupied before it. The prophetic principle transcends any single city: every imperial system that sustains itself on violence, seduces the nations with luxury, and demands allegiance that belongs to God alone stands under this judgment.

Fourth, God is sovereign over the beast system's internal politics. The ten kings' betrayal of the harlot is not random chaos but God's own action (verse 17). God put it in their hearts to execute his purpose. The beast system destroys itself, and the self-destruction is divinely orchestrated. The same kings who voluntarily gave their power to the beast (verse 13) are the ones who turn on the harlot and devour her (verse 16). The irony is that the beast's allies become the instruments of God's judgment on the beast's consort. The alliance that seemed monolithic and invincible in chapter 13 is revealed to be fragile and self-contradictory.

Fifth, the Lamb's victory is certain and his companions are identified. The war of the ten kings and the beast against the Lamb is stated in verse 14, and its outcome is declared in a single clause: "the Lamb will overcome them." The basis of this victory is the Lamb's supreme title: "Lord of lords and King of kings." Those who accompany the Lamb are not described in military terms but in covenantal terms: "called, chosen, and faithful." Their identity originates in God's initiative (called, chosen) and is validated by their perseverance (faithful). The faithful community that has endured the beast's persecution is revealed as the Lamb's army — not despite their suffering but through it.

The chapter's pastoral function for its first-century audience is to strip away the harlot's allure. The empire that seems invincible, wealthy, and permanent is revealed as a blood-drunk prostitute riding a doomed beast. The luxury is built on murder. The splendor conceals abomination. The alliance that sustains the system is unstable and will collapse. The angel's interpretation teaches the assemblies to see through the surface — to recognize that the gold cup holds blood, that the purple robes conceal violence, and that the beast's impressive "was, is not, and will come" is a pathetic imitation of the God who truly is, who truly was, and who is truly coming. The assemblies are called not to wonder at the harlot (as John initially did, verse 6) but to discern her identity, understand her doom, and remain among the Lamb's companions — the called, the chosen, and the faithful.

div.title: Revelation 18 — First-Century Reading
Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (Revelation 17): Chapter 17 presented the identity and fate of "Babylon the great" in visionary detail. One of the seven angels who had the seven bowls invited John: "Come, I will show you the judgment of the great harlot who sits on many waters, with whom the kings of the earth committed acts of immorality, and those who dwell on the earth were made drunk with the wine of her immorality" (17:1-2). John was carried to a wilderness, where he saw a woman seated on a scarlet beast "full of blasphemous names, having seven heads and ten horns" (17:3) — the same beast from chapter 13. The woman was "clothed in purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls, having in her hand a gold cup full of abominations and of the unclean things of her immorality" (17:4). On her forehead was written "a mystery: BABYLON THE GREAT, THE MOTHER OF HARLOTS AND OF THE ABOMINATIONS OF THE EARTH" (17:5). Most critically, "the woman was drunk with the blood of the saints, and with the blood of the witnesses of Jesus" (17:6). The angel then explained the mystery: the seven heads are seven mountains and seven kings (17:9-10), the ten horns are ten kings who give their authority to the beast (17:12-13), and these kings "will wage war against the Lamb, and the Lamb will overcome them, because he is Lord of lords and King of kings, and those who are with him are the called and chosen and faithful" (17:14). The chapter concluded with a decisive turn: the ten horns "will hate the harlot and will make her desolate and naked, and will eat her flesh and will burn her with fire" (17:16). The rationale: "God has put it in their hearts to execute his purpose" (17:17). The final verse identified the woman: "The woman whom you saw is the great city, which reigns over the kings of the earth" (17:18).

Chapter 17 thus accomplished three things. First, it identified Babylon as the great city that exercises imperial sovereignty over the earth's kings — a first-century hearer in the Roman province of Asia would recognize this as Rome. Second, it revealed that Babylon's destruction comes not from an external enemy but from the very kings who served her, acting (whether they know it or not) at God's instigation. Third, it established that Babylon is guilty of the blood of the saints and the witnesses of Jesus — her luxury and power are built on martyrdom. Chapter 17 is the unveiling of Babylon's identity and the decree of her sentence. Chapter 18 is the execution of that sentence, narrated as a sustained prophetic lament.

What the author argues immediately after (Revelation 19): Chapter 19 opens with a great multitude in heaven shouting "Hallelujah!" (19:1) — the first of four Hallelujahs (19:1, 3, 4, 6) that celebrate what has just occurred in chapter 18. The content of the praise is explicit: "Salvation and glory and power belong to our God; because his judgments are true and righteous; for he has judged the great harlot who was corrupting the earth with her immorality, and he has avenged the blood of his bond-servants on her" (19:1-2). The verb "has avenged" (exedikesen) answers the martyrs' cry from 6:10: "How long, O Lord, holy and true, will you refrain from judging and avenging our blood on those who dwell on the earth?" The four living creatures and the twenty-four elders fall down and worship (19:4). A voice from the throne calls: "Give praise to our God, all you his bond-servants, you who fear him, the small and the great" (19:5). Then comes the announcement: "The marriage of the Lamb has come and his bride has made herself ready" (19:7). The angel instructs John: "Write, 'Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb'" (19:9). The chapter then turns to the rider on the white horse, called "Faithful and True" and "the Word of God" (19:11, 13), who leads the armies of heaven against the beast and the kings of the earth (19:19). The beast and the false prophet are captured and thrown into the lake of fire (19:20), and the rest are slain by the sword from the rider's mouth (19:21).

Chapter 19 thus moves from celebration to consummation. The Hallelujah chorus celebrates Babylon's fall — the event narrated in chapter 18 — as the vindication of God's servants and the demonstration of his righteous judgment. The marriage supper of the Lamb replaces the harlot's feast: where Babylon intoxicated the nations with her cup (17:2, 4; 18:3), the Lamb invites the faithful to his wedding banquet. The rider on the white horse then defeats the beast and false prophet, the powers behind Babylon. The sequence is: Babylon falls (18), heaven celebrates and the Lamb's marriage is announced (19:1-10), and the beast is destroyed (19:11-21). The harlot falls before the beast falls, because the system that sustained the beast's economy and seduced the nations is dismantled first.

How chapter 18 connects the surrounding argument: Chapter 18 stands between the revelation of Babylon's identity (17) and the celebration of her destruction (19). The transition from chapter 17 to chapter 18 is seamless: 17:16-17 announced that the ten kings would destroy the harlot, and 18:1 opens with an angel descending with the authority to declare that destruction accomplished. The fall of Babylon was first announced in the compressed preview of 14:8: "Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great, she who has made all the nations drink of the wine of the passion of her immorality." That one-verse announcement in chapter 14 is now expanded into an entire chapter of lament, mourning, and irrevocable destruction. The bowl judgments of chapter 16 prepared the ground: the seventh bowl brought the remembrance of "Babylon the great" before God, "to give her the cup of the wine of his fierce wrath" (16:19). Chapter 17 unmasked her. Chapter 18 destroys her. Chapter 19 celebrates.

The chapter draws on a massive body of prophetic precedent, primarily from three oracular traditions: Isaiah's oracles against Babylon (Isaiah 13-14, 21, 47), Jeremiah's extended oracle against Babylon (Jeremiah 50-51, LXX 27-28), and Ezekiel's lament over Tyre (Ezekiel 26-28). The author fuses these traditions into a single, sustained composition. From Isaiah and Jeremiah he takes the announcement of Babylon's fall and the call for God's people to flee. From Ezekiel he takes the commercial lament — the catalog of goods, the mourning merchants, the weeping seafarers. The fusion is deliberate: Babylon's sin is not merely political tyranny (like historical Babylon) but also commercial exploitation (like Tyre), and the judgment encompasses both dimensions. The chapter is not a report of events but a prophetic performance — a funeral dirge sung over a city that, in God's verdict, is already dead.

div.title: Verses 1-3: The Angelic Announcement of Babylon's Fall
div.p: "After these things I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was illumined with his glory. And he cried out with a mighty voice, saying, 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great! She has become a dwelling place of demons and a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean and hateful bird. For all the nations have drunk of the wine of the passion of her immorality, and the kings of the earth have committed acts of immorality with her, and the merchants of the earth have become rich by the wealth of her sensuality.'"

"After these things I saw another angel coming down from heaven, having great authority, and the earth was illumined with his glory" (meta tauta eidon allon angelon katabainonta ek tou ouranou, echonta exousian megalēn, kai hē gē ephōtisthē ek tēs doxēs autou). The formula meta tauta eidon ("after these things I saw") marks a new visionary unit, distinct from but continuous with what preceded. The angel descends from heaven — the movement is downward, from the seat of authority to the earth where Babylon resides. The phrase "having great authority" (echonta exousian megalēn) distinguishes this angel from ordinary messengers. The word exousia ("authority, power, right") here indicates delegated divine authority: this angel carries God's own commission to pronounce judgment. The scope of the authority is signaled by the effect: "the earth was illumined with his glory" (hē gē ephōtisthē ek tēs doxēs autou). The verb ephōtisthē ("was illuminated, was lit up") and the word doxa ("glory, radiance, splendor") together recall the theophanic tradition in which God's presence fills and illuminates:

Ezekiel 43:2 (LXX): "And behold, the glory (doxa) of the God of Israel came from the way of the east; and his voice was like the sound of many waters; and the earth shone with his glory (hē gē exelampen hōs phengos apo tēs doxēs)." In Ezekiel, it is the glory of God himself that illuminates the earth. The author of Revelation applies this language to the angel, indicating that this messenger carries the reflected radiance of God's own presence. The angel is so invested with divine authority that his descent brings a theophanic illumination to the earth. The entire scene signals that what is about to be announced carries the full weight of God's decreed judgment.

"Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great!" (epesen epesen Babylōn hē megalē). The announcement repeats the words of the second angel in 14:8, which in turn drew on Isaiah 21:9 (LXX): "Fallen, fallen (peptōken peptōken) is Babylon, and all the images of her gods are shattered to the ground." The doubling of "fallen" (the repetitive aorist) expresses certainty, irreversibility, and emphatic finality. In Jeremiah 51:8 (LXX 28:8): "Suddenly Babylon has fallen and been broken (epesen Babylōn kai synetribē)." The prophetic aorist tense speaks of what is determined as though it has already occurred. The city that "reigns over the kings of the earth" (17:18) is spoken of in the past tense: she has fallen. For the first-century hearer living under the present reality of Rome's dominion, this declaration redefines the world: the power that appears invincible is already, in heaven's verdict, destroyed.

The epithet "the great" (hē megalē) continues to echo Daniel 4:30 (LXX), where Nebuchadnezzar surveyed his capital and boasted: "Is not this Babylon the great (Babylōn hē megalē), which I myself have built?" The title is ironic in context: the greatness that was Babylon's boast becomes the label on her grave.

"She has become a dwelling place of demons and a prison of every unclean spirit, and a prison of every unclean and hateful bird" (egeneto katoikētērion daimoniōn kai phylakē pantos pneumatos akathartou kai phylakē pantos orneou akathartou kai memisēmenou). The language describes a city reduced to a desolate ruin haunted by demonic inhabitants. The imagery draws on two major prophetic passages:

Isaiah 13:19-22 (LXX): In the oracle against Babylon, Isaiah declared: "Babylon, the glory of kingdoms, the beauty of the Chaldeans' pride, will be as when God overthrew Sodom and Gomorrah. It will never be inhabited... but desert creatures (thēria) will lie down there, and their houses will be full of howling creatures (ēchous); ostriches will dwell there, and demons (daimonia) will dance there." The desolate Babylon of Isaiah is inhabited only by wild animals, howling spirits, and demons. The author of Revelation takes this imagery and applies it to the eschatological Babylon.

Isaiah 34:11-15 (LXX): In the oracle against Edom, Isaiah described the land after judgment: "Pelicans and hedgehogs and ibises and ravens shall dwell in it... thorns shall come up in her fortified cities, and it shall be a habitation of jackals... and demons (onokentauroi) shall meet with donkey-centaurs (or wild creatures), and they shall cry out one to another. There the night creature (onokentauros) has rested." The desolate land becomes the dwelling of unclean creatures and malign spirits.
Jeremiah 50:39 (LXX 27:39): "Therefore desert creatures will live there along with the jackals; ostriches also will live in it, and it will never again be inhabited."
Jeremiah 51:37 (LXX 28:37): "Babylon will become a heap of ruins, a haunt of jackals, an object of horror and hissing, without inhabitants."

The word katoikētērion ("dwelling place, habitation") is significant. In Ephesians 2:22, the same word describes the community of believers as "a dwelling of God in the Spirit" (katoikētērion tou theou en pneumati). Babylon, which was the dwelling of merchants and kings, becomes instead the dwelling of demons. The transformation is complete: where luxury once resided, desolation now inhabits. The word phylakē ("prison, guard post, place of custody") suggests not merely that demons happen to live there but that the desolated city becomes a holding pen — a cage for every unclean thing. The adjective akathartou ("unclean") is the language of ritual impurity drawn from Leviticus 11-15, where certain creatures and conditions are classified as unclean and separated from the holy community. The word memisēmenou ("hated, detested") intensifies the uncleanness: these birds are not merely impure but actively loathsome. The mention of birds (orneou) connects to the unclean birds of Leviticus 11:13-19 (LXX), where certain birds are designated as "detestable" (bdelygma) and not to be eaten. The fallen Babylon is the habitat of everything that the Torah classified as unclean, separated, and excluded from God's presence.

"For all the nations have drunk of the wine of the passion of her immorality" (hoti ek tou oinou tou thymou tēs porneias autēs pepōkan panta ta ethnē). This clause provides the reason (hoti, "because, for") for Babylon's fall. The language repeats 14:8 almost verbatim. The triple genitive "the wine of the passion/wrath of her immorality" (tou oinou tou thymou tēs porneias) carries the same deliberate ambiguity noted in the analysis of 14:8: thymos can denote either Babylon's own intoxicating passion (the fury of her seductive power) or the divine wrath that her immorality provokes. Both dimensions are operative. The nations drank willingly of Babylon's intoxicating influence; what they consumed was, simultaneously, the cup of God's judgment on those who participate in her system.

The word porneia ("sexual immorality, prostitution") functions in the prophetic register as idolatrous unfaithfulness — the harlotry of the nations with the imperial system, the exchange of allegiance to God for the seductions of Babylon's wealth, power, and splendor. The verb pepōkan (perfect active of pinō, "to drink") indicates a completed, settled state: the nations have drunk and are in the condition of having drunk. The intoxication is not a momentary lapse but an established condition.

"And the kings of the earth have committed acts of immorality with her" (kai hoi basileis tēs gēs met' autēs eporneusan). The kings' relationship with Babylon is expressed in the language of sexual commerce: they "committed immorality" (eporneusan, from porneuō) with her. The prophetic background is Ezekiel 16 and 23, where Jerusalem's alliances with foreign powers are described as harlotry, and Nahum 3:4, where Nineveh is called "the charming one, the mistress of sorceries, who sells nations by her harlotries (porneiais) and families by her sorceries." The kings' "immorality" with Babylon consists in their political and economic entanglement with the imperial system — their willing participation in the structures of power, wealth, and domination that Babylon represents. They are not merely her victims; they are her partners.

"And the merchants of the earth have become rich by the wealth of her sensuality" (kai hoi emporoi tēs gēs ek tēs dynameōs tou strēnous autēs eploutēsan). This clause introduces a figure not present in the prophetic Babylon-oracles but drawn from Ezekiel's Tyre-lament: the merchant (emporos). In Ezekiel 27, Tyre's glory and fall are described entirely in commercial terms — the lists of goods, the trading partners, the seafarers who weep at her destruction. The author of Revelation merges the political tyranny of Babylon with the commercial exploitation of Tyre. The result is a figure that is both imperial oppressor and commercial exploiter — a power whose sin involves not only political domination and idolatrous worship but the economic system that enriches the few through the labor and blood of the many.

The word strēnous (from strēnos, "luxury, wanton excess, voluptuous living") appears only here and in 18:7, 9 in the entire New Testament. The noun denotes extravagant, arrogant indulgence — luxury that flaunts itself. The related verb strēniaō ("to live luxuriously, to revel") appears in 18:7, 9. The word carries a note of insolent self-indulgence — not merely wealth but wealth displayed with contempt for those who lack it. The word dynamis ("power, strength") here denotes the economic power generated by Babylon's luxury trade — the purchasing force, the demand, the engine of commerce that her appetite for excess drives. The merchants grew rich not from their own merit but from the dynamin of Babylon's strēnos — from the economic power generated by her insatiable luxury. Their wealth is parasitic on her excess.

div.title: Verses 4-8: The Voice from Heaven — Come Out of Her, My People
div.p: "I heard another voice from heaven, saying, 'Come out of her, my people, so that you will not participate in her sins and receive of her plagues; for her sins have piled up as high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities. Pay her back even as she has paid, and give back to her double according to her deeds; in the cup which she has mixed, mix twice as much for her. To the degree that she glorified herself and lived sensuously, to the same degree give her torment and mourning; for she says in her heart, "I sit as a queen and I am not a widow, and will never see mourning." For this reason in one day her plagues will come, pestilence and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for the Lord God who judges her is strong.'"

"Come out of her, my people, so that you will not participate in her sins and receive of her plagues" (exelthate ex autēs, ho laos mou, hina mē synkoinōnēsēte tais hamartiais autēs, kai ek tōn plēgōn autēs hina mē labēte). The call to come out is drawn directly from Jeremiah 51:45 (LXX 28:45): "Come out of her midst, my people (exelthate ek mesou autēs, ho laos mou), and save each man his soul (sōsate hekastos tēn psychēn autou) from the fierce anger of the LORD." The same call appears in Jeremiah 50:8 (LXX 27:8): "Wander away from the midst of Babylon and go out from the land of the Chaldeans." And in Jeremiah 51:6 (LXX 28:6): "Flee from the midst of Babylon, and deliver each one his life."
Isaiah 48:20 (LXX): "Go out from Babylon (exelthate ek Babylōnos), flee from the Chaldeans."

Isaiah 52:11 (LXX): "Depart, depart (apostēte apostēte), go out from there (exelthate ekeithen), touch nothing unclean (akathartou mē haptesthe); go out from the midst of her (exelthate ek mesou autēs), purify yourselves, you who carry the vessels of the LORD."

The call is addressed to "my people" (ho laos mou) — the covenant designation. The voice is God's own, claiming Babylon's residents (or participants) who belong to him. The existence of God's people within Babylon is itself significant: the faithful are not in a separate, sealed-off community but are living within the imperial system. The call to "come out" assumes they are currently inside. The verb exelthate (aorist imperative of exerchomai, "to go out, to depart") is a command, not an invitation. The urgency is motivated by two purposes, each introduced by hina ("so that, in order that"): first, "so that you will not participate in her sins" (hina mē synkoinōnēsēte tais hamartiais autēs), and second, "so that you will not receive of her plagues" (ek tōn plēgōn autēs hina mē labēte). Participation in sin leads to reception of plague. The verb synkoinōnēsēte (from synkoinōneō, "to share in, to participate with, to have fellowship with") indicates shared involvement — not merely proximity to Babylon but active participation in her system. The call demands extraction from the system, not merely geographical relocation. The "coming out" is a disengagement from the economic, religious, and political structures that constitute Babylon's web.

The historical resonance is the Exodus. God called his people out of Egypt (Exodus 3:10: "I will send you to Pharaoh, so that you may bring my people, the sons of Israel, out of Egypt"). God called his people out of Babylon (the Jeremiah and Isaiah texts cited above). The new Exodus that runs through this entire document (the song of Moses in 15:3, the plagues echoing Egypt, the sea crossing in 15:2) now includes the call to leave Babylon as Israel once left Egypt and later left historical Babylon. Each exodus is a departure from a system of domination and idolatry into the freedom of God's covenant.

"For her sins have piled up as high as heaven, and God has remembered her iniquities" (hoti ekollēthēsan autēs hai hamartiai achri tou ouranou, kai emnēmoneusen ho theos ta adikēmata autēs). The verb ekollēthēsan (from kollaō, "to join, to glue, to cleave together") depicts sins adhering to one another, accumulating, piling up like bricks in a tower. The image recalls Genesis 11:4 (the Tower of Babel): "Come, let us build for ourselves a city, and a tower whose top will reach into heaven (heōs tou ouranou)." Babylon's original sin in Israel's memory was the tower that sought to reach heaven; now her sins have built their own tower reaching heaven. The parallel is structural: Babel's arrogance reached toward heaven in defiance; Babylon's sins reach heaven as a testament against her.

Jeremiah 51:9 (LXX 28:9): "For her judgment (to krima autēs) has reached to heaven (ēngisen eis ton ouranon) and has been lifted up to the clouds (exēren heōs tōn astrōn)." The Jeremiah parallel is precise: Babylon's guilt has accumulated to the point where it has reached God's dwelling, and God can no longer overlook it.

"God has remembered" (emnēmoneusen ho theos): The verb mimnēskomai ("to remember") in the LXX denotes not a mental recollection (as if God had forgotten) but a decision to act on what has been stored up. Genesis 8:1: "God remembered (emnēsthē) Noah" — and the flood subsided. Exodus 2:24: "God heard their groaning, and God remembered (emnēsthē) his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob" — and the Exodus began. In 16:19, the same language was used: "Babylon the great was remembered before God (emnēsthē enōpion tou theou), to give her the cup of the wine of his fierce wrath." To say God "remembered" Babylon's iniquities is to say that the appointed time for judgment has arrived. The sins have been accumulating; now God acts.

"Pay her back even as she has paid, and give back to her double according to her deeds; in the cup which she has mixed, mix twice as much for her" (apodote autē hōs kai autē apedōken, kai diplōsate ta dipla kata ta erga autēs; en tō potēriō hō ekerasen kerasate autē diploun). The instruction to "pay back" (apodote, aorist imperative of apodidōmi, "to give back, to render, to repay") is addressed either to the agents of God's judgment (the kings and nations who will destroy Babylon, as in 17:16-17) or more broadly to the heavenly court that oversees the execution of justice. The principle is strict reciprocity: as she has done, so it will be done to her.
The "double" (dipla, diploun) repayment draws on multiple prophetic precedents:

Isaiah 40:2 (LXX): "Speak to the heart of Jerusalem, comfort her, because she has received from the LORD's hand double (dipla) for all her sins." In Isaiah, Jerusalem has already received double punishment; here, Babylon is to receive the same measure.
Jeremiah 16:18 (LXX): "I will first doubly repay (antapodōsō... diplas) their iniquity and their sin."
Jeremiah 50:29 (LXX 27:29): "Repay (antapodote) her according to her work (kata ta erga autēs); according to all that she has done, do to her."

The "cup which she has mixed" (en tō potēriō hō ekerasen) recalls the golden cup in the harlot's hand from 17:4: "having in her hand a gold cup full of abominations and of the unclean things of her immorality." It also recalls Jeremiah 51:7 (LXX 28:7): "Babylon was a golden cup in the LORD's hand, making all the earth drunk." The cup Babylon used to intoxicate the nations is now turned against her. The verb kerasate ("mix," aorist imperative of kerannymi) uses the same language of wine preparation that appeared in 14:10, where God's wrath was "mixed in full strength" (kekerasmenou akratou). Babylon mixed the cup for others; now a cup is mixed for her, and the measure is doubled.

"To the degree that she glorified herself and lived sensuously, to the same degree give her torment and mourning" (hosa edoxasen autēn kai estrēniasen, tosouton dote autē basanismon kai penthos). The verb edoxasen (from doxazō, "to glorify") here means not to give God glory but to glorify herself — self-exaltation, self-aggrandizement. The reflexive autēn ("herself") makes the direction explicit: her glory was directed inward, not upward. The verb estrēniasen (from strēniaō, "to live in wanton luxury") reappears from verse 3 (strēnous). Babylon's twin sins are named: self-glorification and wanton luxury. The judgment is calibrated exactly to the sin: "to the same degree" (tosouton... hoson). The measure of her luxury determines the measure of her torment (basanismon, "torment, anguish") and mourning (penthos, "grief, sorrow, lamentation"). The principle is not arbitrary vengeance but proportional justice — the punishment mirrors the crime.

"For she says in her heart, 'I sit as a queen and I am not a widow, and will never see mourning'" (hoti en tē kardia autēs legei hoti Kathēmai basilissa, kai chēra ouk eimi, kai penthos ou mē idō). This self-declaration is drawn directly from Isaiah 47:7-8 (LXX), the oracle against the "virgin daughter of Babylon":
Isaiah 47:7 (LXX): "You said, 'I shall be queen (archōusa) forever' — you did not take these things to heart, you did not remember the end of them."

Isaiah 47:8 (LXX): "Now then, hear this, you sensual one (trypherā), who dwells securely, who says in her heart (hē legousa en tē kardia autēs), 'I am (egō eimi), and there is no one besides me. I will not sit as a widow (chēra ou kathiō), nor will I know (ou gnōsomai) loss of children.'"

The verbal echoes are precise: "says in her heart" (en tē kardia legei / legousa en tē kardia), "I sit" (kathēmai / kathiō), "not a widow" (chēra ouk eimi / chēra ou kathiō), and the denial of mourning or loss. Isaiah's Babylon spoke with absolute self-assurance: she would never be reduced, never be bereaved, never experience the vulnerability of widowhood. The author of Revelation places the same words in the mouth of the eschatological Babylon. Her arrogance is not new; it is the same voice that Isaiah heard, the same imperial presumption that refuses to acknowledge mortality, limitation, or judgment.

The three claims constitute a comprehensive denial of vulnerability: "I sit as a queen" (present sovereignty), "I am not a widow" (absence of loss), and "I will never see mourning" (future invulnerability). Each claim will be directly contradicted by the judgments that follow.

"For this reason in one day her plagues will come, pestilence and mourning and famine, and she will be burned up with fire; for the Lord God who judges her is strong" (dia touto en mia hēmera hēxousin hai plēgai autēs, thanatos kai penthos kai limos, kai en pyri katakauthēsetai; hoti ischyros kyrios ho theos ho krinas autēn). The phrase "in one day" (en mia hēmera) emphasizes the suddenness of the reversal. What Babylon denied would ever happen comes in a single day.

Isaiah 47:9 (LXX): "But these two things will come upon you suddenly (exaiphnēs), in one day (en hēmera mia): loss of children and widowhood. They will come upon you in full measure (en tē teleiotēti sou) — in the multitude of your sorceries, in the great power of your enchantments." The "one day" timeline is directly from Isaiah's Babylon oracle. The suddenness is the divine response to Babylon's self-assurance: she said "never"; the answer is "today."

The four plagues — thanatos ("death, pestilence"), penthos ("mourning"), limos ("famine"), and fire (en pyri katakauthesetai, "she will be burned with fire") — correspond inversely to Babylon's self-declarations. She said she would never see mourning (penthos); mourning comes. She said she sat as a queen; pestilence and famine replace her sovereignty. She will be burned with fire — the same fate described for the harlot in 17:16: "they will burn her with fire."

The clause "the Lord God who judges her is strong" (ischyros kyrios ho theos ho krinas autēn) answers the implied question of how such a powerful city can fall in a single day. The answer is not a military explanation but a theological one: the God who has decreed her judgment is ischyros — "strong, mighty, powerful." Jeremiah 50:34 (LXX 27:34): "Their Redeemer is strong (ischyros); the LORD of hosts is his name. He will vigorously plead their case so that he may bring rest to the earth." The strength of the judge overmatches the strength of the judged. Babylon's power, however "great" (megalē, 17:18), is no match for the God who judges her.

div.title: Verses 9-10: The First Lament — The Kings of the Earth
div.p: "And the kings of the earth, who committed acts of immorality and lived sensuously with her, will weep and lament over her when they see the smoke of her burning, standing at a distance because of the fear of her torment, saying, 'Woe, woe, the great city, Babylon, the strong city! For in one hour your judgment has come.'"

"The kings of the earth, who committed acts of immorality and lived sensuously with her" (hoi basileis tēs gēs hoi met' autēs porneusantes kai strēniasantes). The kings are identified by their relationship to Babylon: they "committed immorality" (porneusantes) and "lived sensuously" (strēniasantes) with her. These are the same kings described in 17:2 ("the kings of the earth committed acts of immorality with her") and 17:12-14 (the ten kings who gave their power to the beast). Their relationship with Babylon was one of mutual exploitation: they participated in her system, shared in her luxury, and validated her authority. Now they stand at a distance and watch her burn.

"Will weep and lament over her when they see the smoke of her burning" (klausousin kai kopsontai ep' autēn, hotan blepōsin ton kapnon tēs pyrōseōs autēs). The verbs klaiō ("to weep") and koptō ("to beat the breast, to mourn, to lament") are the standard vocabulary of mourning in the LXX and first-century usage. The mourning is triggered by a specific visual: "the smoke of her burning" (ton kapnon tēs pyrōseōs autēs). The smoke recalls the destruction of Sodom as witnessed by Abraham: "He looked down toward Sodom and Gomorrah, and toward all the land of the valley, and he saw, and behold, the smoke of the land ascended like the smoke of a furnace" (Genesis 19:28, LXX). The smoke also recalls 14:11 ("the smoke of their torment goes up forever and ever") and anticipates 19:3 ("her smoke rises up forever and ever"). The smoke is the visible evidence of irreversible destruction.

"Standing at a distance because of the fear of her torment" (apo makrothen hestēkotes dia ton phobon tou basanismou autēs). The kings do not approach the burning city. They stand "at a distance" (apo makrothen) — far enough to see but not be caught in the destruction. The phrase reflects Ezekiel 26:16-17 (LXX), where the princes of the sea "will come down from their thrones and remove their robes and strip off their embroidered garments" and "tremble at every moment" over fallen Tyre. The distance is motivated by "fear of her torment" (ton phobon tou basanismou) — they are afraid that proximity will draw them into the same destruction. Their fear reveals the nature of their partnership: it was one of convenience and profit, not loyalty. When the cost of association becomes clear, they retreat.

"Woe, woe, the great city, Babylon, the strong city! For in one hour your judgment has come" (ouai ouai, hē polis hē megalē, Babylōn hē polis hē ischyra, hoti mia hōra ēlthen hē krisis sou). The threefold lament structure — introduced by the kings (18:10), repeated by the merchants (18:16), and repeated again by the seafarers (18:19) — is one of the chapter's most distinctive literary features. Each lament begins with "woe, woe" (ouai ouai) and includes the phrase "the great city" (hē polis hē megalē). The ouai ("woe, alas") is not a curse but a cry of grief — the exclamation of those who witness catastrophe and are overwhelmed by it.

The kings call Babylon both "the great city" (hē polis hē megalē) and "the strong city" (hē polis hē ischyra). The adjective ischyra ("strong, powerful, mighty") was used of God in verse 8 (ischyros kyrios ho theos). The irony is deliberate: the city that was called "strong" has been judged by the God who is truly strong. The word that Babylon applied to herself is revealed as misappropriated; true strength belongs to God alone.

"In one hour" (mia hōra): The timeframe compresses even further from "one day" in verse 8 to "one hour" here. The same phrase will be repeated by the merchants (18:17) and the seafarers (18:19). The hōra ("hour") in this author's usage is the decisive, appointed moment of divine action (cf. John 2:4, 12:23, 17:1; Revelation 3:10, 14:7, 15). The speed of the destruction underscores its completeness: Babylon's centuries of accumulated power and wealth are undone in a single hour.

div.title: Verses 11-17a: The Second Lament — The Merchants of the Earth
div.p: "And the merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her, because no one buys their cargoes any more — cargoes of gold and silver and precious stones and pearls and fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet, and every kind of citron wood and every article of ivory and every article made from very costly wood and bronze and iron and marble, and cinnamon and spice and incense and perfume and frankincense and wine and olive oil and fine flour and wheat and cattle and sheep, and cargoes of horses and chariots and slaves and human lives. The fruit you long for has gone from you, and all things that were luxurious and splendid have passed away from you and men will no longer find them. The merchants of these things, who became rich from her, will stand at a distance because of the fear of her torment, weeping and mourning, saying, 'Woe, woe, the great city, she who was clothed in fine linen and purple and scarlet, and adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls; for in one hour such great wealth has been laid waste!'"

"The merchants of the earth weep and mourn over her, because no one buys their cargoes any more" (hoi emporoi tēs gēs klaiousin kai penthousin ep' autēn, hoti ton gomon autōn oudeis agorazei ouketi). The emporoi ("merchants, traders, wholesalers") are distinct from the kapēloi (retail traders). The emporos is the large-scale trader, the international merchant who deals in the luxury goods that flow through the arteries of imperial commerce. Their grief is not primarily for Babylon herself but for their lost market: "no one buys their cargoes any more" (ton gomon autōn oudeis agorazei ouketi). The word gomos ("cargo, freight, shipload") emphasizes the scale of their commerce. The verb agorazei ("buys") is the same word used in 13:17 for the buying and selling that required the beast's mark, and in 5:9 and 14:3-4 for the Lamb's redemptive "purchase." The merchants' grief exposes the nature of their relationship with Babylon: it was commercial, transactional, driven by profit. They mourn the loss of revenue, not the loss of a soul.

The literary model for this section is Ezekiel 27, the lament over Tyre. Ezekiel 27:12-25 contains a detailed catalog of Tyre's trading partners and goods — silver, iron, tin, bronze, horses, mules, ivory, ebony, purple, embroidered work, fine linen, coral, rubies, wheat, honey, oil, balm, wine, white wool, wrought iron, cassia, calamus, precious cloths, lambs, rams, goats, spices, gold, and more. The author of Revelation draws on this tradition and creates his own cargo list, adapted to reflect the commerce of the first-century Roman Empire.

The Cargo List (verses 12-13): The list of twenty-eight (or twenty-nine) items is organized in a deliberate descending order, moving from the most precious to the most common, and culminating in the most disturbing:

Gold and silver and precious stones and pearls (chrysou kai argyrou kai lithou timiou kai margaritōn): The list begins with the most valuable commodities — the luxury materials used for adornment and display. Gold and silver are the currencies and status symbols of empire. Precious stones and pearls are the personal adornments of the wealthy. These are the materials of Babylon's own clothing as described in 17:4: "adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls."

Fine linen and purple and silk and scarlet (byssinou kai porphyras kai sirikou kai kokkinou): The textile luxury goods. Byssinos ("fine linen") was among the most expensive fabrics of the ancient world, imported from Egypt. Porphyra ("purple") was the dye extracted from murex shellfish at extraordinary cost; a single pound of Tyrian purple dye could cost more than a laborer's annual wages. Serikon ("silk") came from China along the overland trade routes, making it perhaps the most expensive fabric by weight in the Roman world. Kokkinos ("scarlet") was another costly dye, produced from the kermes insect. These are the fabrics of power and privilege. In 17:4, the harlot was "clothed in purple and scarlet" (peribeblēmenē porphyroun kai kokkinon). In 19:8, by contrast, the Lamb's bride is "clothed in fine linen, bright and clean" (byssinon lampron katharon), and the fine linen is identified as "the righteous acts of the saints." Babylon clothes herself in expensive fabrics; the bride is clothed in righteousness.

Every kind of citron wood and every article of ivory and every article made from very costly wood and bronze and iron and marble (pan xylon thyinon kai pan skeuos elephantinon kai pan skeuos ek xylou timiōtatou kai chalkou kai sidērou kai marmarou): The list moves to luxury furnishings and building materials. Thyinos xylon ("citron wood") was a prized North African wood used for expensive furniture, particularly tabletops; Pliny the Elder records prices for citron-wood tables that exceeded the cost of large estates (Natural History 13.29). Ivory was imported from Africa and India. The progression from wood to bronze to iron to marble traces the materials of construction and decoration in the great houses and temples of Rome. The scope is comprehensive: "every kind" (pan) and "every article" (pan skeuos) emphasize the totality of Babylon's material appetite.

Cinnamon and spice and incense and perfume and frankincense (kinnamōmon kai amōmon kai thymiamata kai myron kai libanon): The aromatic spices and incense. Kinnamōmon ("cinnamon") was imported from the East at great expense. Amōmon ("spice," possibly cardamom or a related aromatic plant) was another luxury import. Thymiamata ("incense") and libanon ("frankincense") were used in both religious and domestic contexts. Myron ("perfume, ointment") was a luxury item associated with feasting and self-indulgence. The spice trade was one of the most profitable sectors of the Roman commercial network, with goods flowing from Arabia, India, and the Far East.

Wine and olive oil and fine flour and wheat (oinon kai elaion kai semidalin kai siton): The list moves to foodstuffs, but these are not ordinary provisions. Semidalis ("fine flour") was the premium wheat flour used in baking for the wealthy. These staples, in the context of Babylon's luxury trade, are not the daily bread of common people but the refined provisions of the elite.
Cattle and sheep (ktēnē kai probata): Livestock, both for food and for sacrifice. The list is descending from the most refined to the most basic.

Horses and chariots (hippōn kai rhedōn): Horses were military and luxury animals in the ancient world; rhedai (a Latin loanword, "four-wheeled carriages") were vehicles of the wealthy. The inclusion of a Latin loanword is significant: it signals the specifically Roman character of the commercial system being described.

Slaves and human lives (sōmatōn, kai psychas anthrōpōn): The list reaches its climax and its most devastating entry. The word sōmatōn (genitive plural of sōma, "body") is the standard Greek commercial term for slaves — human beings traded as "bodies." The addition "and human lives" (kai psychas anthrōpōn, literally "and souls of human beings") refuses to let the commercial euphemism stand. The author will not allow slaves to remain mere "bodies" in the ledger. They are psychai anthrōpōn — human souls, living persons. The deliberate shift from the commercial term (sōmata, "bodies") to the personal term (psychai, "souls, lives") strips away the dehumanizing language of the slave trade and insists that what Babylon traffics in is human persons.

The language draws on Ezekiel 27:13 (LXX): "Javan, Tubal, and Meshech — they were your traders; they traded with you in the persons (sōmata) of men and in vessels of bronze." The LXX already described the slave trade using sōmata. But the author of Revelation adds the phrase kai psychas anthrōpōn — a phrase that echoes Ezekiel 27:13 in the Hebrew, where the text reads nephesh adam ("human souls/lives"), which the LXX rendered simply as sōmata. The author of Revelation, whether working from the Hebrew or restoring the original force of the text, insists on both terms: Babylon trades in bodies, and those bodies are human souls.
