The wall (teichos) is described as mega kai hypsēlon ("great and high") — the same pair of adjectives used for the mountain in 21:10. The wall's primary function in an ancient city was protection and demarcation: it defined who was inside and who was outside, what was sacred and what was profane. The new Jerusalem's wall, despite the city's security under God's presence, serves a demarcating function: it defines the boundary of the holy city and gives structure to the entrance points.

The twelve gates (pylōnes) correspond to Ezekiel's vision of the eschatological city. Ezekiel 48:30-34 (LXX) describes the gates of the city: three gates on the north (named for Reuben, Judah, and Levi), three on the east (Joseph, Benjamin, Dan), three on the south (Simeon, Issachar, Zebulun), and three on the west (Gad, Asher, Naphtali). The author of Revelation follows Ezekiel's arrangement: twelve gates, three on each side, named for the twelve tribes. The inscribed names of the twelve tribes of the sons of Israel (ta onomata tōn dōdeka phylōn huiōn Israēl) declare that the entrance to the new Jerusalem is through Israel. The covenant community that God formed through Abraham, organized through Jacob's twelve sons, and sustained through the wilderness, the monarchy, the exile, and the return is the gateway into the eschatological city. There is no entrance to the new Jerusalem that does not pass through Israel's gate.

The twelve angels at the gates (epi tois pylōsin angelous dōdeka) serve as guardians. In Genesis 3:24, cherubim were placed at the east of the garden of Eden to guard the way to the tree of life. In the new Jerusalem, angels guard the gates — but the gates are never shut (21:25). The angels are sentinels, not barriers. They guard the entry but do not prevent it for those who belong.

"There were three gates on the east and three gates on the north and three gates on the south and three gates on the west" (apo anatolēs pylōnes treis, kai apo borra pylōnes treis, kai apo notou pylōnes treis, kai apo dysmōn pylōnes treis). The four-directional arrangement — east, north, south, west — declares universal accessibility. The city is not oriented toward one direction or one people. Entry is possible from every point of the compass, from every part of the world. The four directions correspond to the "every tribe and tongue and people and nation" (5:9) from which the Lamb has purchased his people.

The east is named first (apo anatolēs, "from the rising [of the sun]"), consistent with the traditional orientation of Israel's sacred structures. The tabernacle entrance faced east (Exodus 27:13-14). The temple's entrance faced east (Ezekiel 43:1-4, where the glory of God returns from the east). The angel of the seal in 7:2 ascended "from the rising of the sun" (apo anatolēs hēliou). The east is the direction of God's approach and the beginning of new light.

"And the wall of the city had twelve foundation stones, and on them were the twelve names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb" (kai to teichos tēs poleōs echon themelious dōdeka, kai ep' autōn dōdeka onomata tōn dōdeka apostolōn tou arniou). The wall has twelve themelious ("foundations, foundation stones"). In the LXX, themelios refers to the foundation upon which a structure is built: Isaiah 28:16, "Behold, I am laying in Zion a stone, a tested stone, a costly cornerstone for the foundation (eis ta themelia), firmly placed." The twelve foundation stones bear the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb. The apostles (apostoloi, "sent ones, commissioned messengers") are the foundation upon which the community is built.

The combination of the twelve tribes on the gates and the twelve apostles on the foundations creates a unified architectural statement. The gates — the points of entry — bear Israel's tribal names: the covenant history of God's people from Abraham onward provides the access. The foundations — the structural base — bear the apostles' names: the witness of the Lamb's commissioned messengers provides the support. The city is built on the apostolic witness and entered through Israel's covenant identity. The two groups — Israel and the apostolic community — are not separate structures but integrated parts of a single city. The gates rest on the foundations. Israel's history and the apostles' testimony form a single, coherent whole.

Ephesians 2:20 expresses a similar architectural metaphor: "having been built on the foundation (themelion) of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus himself being the corner stone." The author of Revelation may be drawing on a shared early tradition that described the community in architectural terms with the apostles as its foundation.

div.title: Verses 15-17: The Measurement of the City
div.p: "The one who spoke with me had a gold measuring rod to measure the city, and its gates and its wall. The city is laid out as a square, and its length is as great as the width; and he measured the city with the rod, twelve thousand stadia; its length and width and height are equal. And he measured its wall, seventy-two yards, according to human measurements, which are also angelic measurements."

"The one who spoke with me had a gold measuring rod to measure the city" (kai ho lalōn met' emou eichen metron kalamon chrysoun, hina metresē tēn polin kai tous pylōnas autēs kai to teichos autēs). The measuring of a city by an angelic figure draws on two primary prophetic precedents.

Ezekiel 40:3-5 (LXX): "He brought me there; and behold, there was a man whose appearance was like the appearance of bronze, and in his hand was a builder's linen cord and a measuring reed (kalamos metrou), and he was standing in the gate." The angel-like figure in Ezekiel proceeded to measure the entire temple complex in exhaustive detail (Ezekiel 40-42), producing the most detailed architectural vision in the Hebrew Bible. The measuring demonstrated God's precise plan, his sovereignty over the dimensions of his dwelling, and the reality (not merely the idea) of the eschatological temple. The author of Revelation follows Ezekiel's pattern: an angelic figure, a measuring instrument, a detailed survey.

Zechariah 2:1-5 (LXX 2:5-9): "I lifted up my eyes and looked, and behold, a man with a measuring line (schoinion metrou) in his hand. So I said, 'Where are you going?' And he said to me, 'To measure Jerusalem (dianetresai tēn Ierousalēm), to see how great is its width (to platos) and how great is its length (to mēkos).'" But then an angel intervenes: "Jerusalem will be inhabited as an open country (akarpōs) because of the multitude of men and cattle in her midst. For I, declares the LORD, will be a wall of fire (teichos pyros) around her, and I will be the glory (doxa) in her midst" (Zechariah 2:4-5). In Zechariah, the measuring of Jerusalem reveals that the city cannot be contained by walls because God himself will be its wall and its glory. The author of Revelation draws on this tradition: the new Jerusalem has a wall, but God's glory illuminates it (21:11, 23), and God himself is its temple (21:22).

The measuring rod is chrysous ("golden"), elevating the instrument beyond Ezekiel's reed or Zechariah's cord. Gold is the material of the sacred — the ark, the mercy seat, the altar of incense, the lampstand in the tabernacle were all gold or gold-overlaid (Exodus 25-30). The golden measuring rod signifies that the act of measurement is a sacred, priestly activity — the dimensions are not engineering data but theological statements.

"The city is laid out as a square, and its length is as great as the width; and he measured the city with the rod, twelve thousand stadia; its length and width and height are equal" (kai he polis tetragōnos keitai, kai to mēkos autēs hoson kai to platos. kai emetrēsen tēn polin tō kalamō epi stadiōn dōdeka chiliadōn; to mēkos kai to platos kai to hypsos autēs isa estin). The city is tetragōnos ("four-cornered, square") and its three dimensions are isa ("equal"): length, width, and height are the same. The resulting shape is a perfect cube.

The cube is the shape of exactly one structure in Israel's entire sacred architecture: the Holy of Holies (debir) in Solomon's temple. 1 Kings 6:20 (LXX 3 Kingdoms 6:20): "The inner sanctuary was twenty cubits in length and twenty cubits in width and twenty cubits in height (to mēkos autēs eikosi pēcheis kai to platos eikosi pēcheis kai to hypsos autēs eikosi pēcheis)." The Holy of Holies — the innermost chamber of the temple, where the Ark of the Covenant rested, where the cherubim spread their wings over the mercy seat, where God's presence dwelled in concentrated form, where only the high priest could enter once a year on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16) — was a perfect cube. The new Jerusalem is shaped as the Holy of Holies because the entire city is what the Holy of Holies was: the place of God's immediate, unmediated presence. What was once restricted to one chamber, accessible to one person on one day per year, is now the shape of the entire city in which God dwells with all his people.

The dimension is twelve thousand stadia (dōdeka chiliadōn stadiōn). Twelve thousand stadia is approximately 1,380 miles or 2,220 kilometers — a dimension of staggering scale, far exceeding any historical city and clearly symbolic rather than literal. The number twelve is the structuring number of the entire description: twelve gates, twelve angels, twelve tribes, twelve foundations, twelve apostles. Twelve thousand (12 x 1,000) combines the covenant number (twelve) with the number of fullness/completion (one thousand). The measurement conveys not architectural specification but theological comprehensiveness: the city of God is vast enough to contain the full number of God's people, all twelve tribes, the entire redeemed community from every nation.

"And he measured its wall, one hundred and forty-four cubits" (kai emetrēsen to teichos autēs hekaton tesserakonta tessarōn pēchōn). The wall is 144 cubits — approximately 216 feet or 66 meters. This dimension is strikingly small relative to the city's twelve-thousand-stadia proportions. A 144-cubit wall around a city that is 1,380 miles per side would be negligible. The contrast reinforces the symbolic nature of the measurements. The wall's function is not defensive (the city needs no defense; God's presence is its security) but definitional — it marks the boundary of the holy city.

The number 144 is 12 x 12 — the square of the covenant number. It recalls the 144,000 of 7:4 and 14:1 (12 x 12 x 1,000). The wall's measurement encodes the same symbolic system as the sealed community: twelve squared, the covenant people in their completeness.

"According to human measurements, which are also angelic measurements" (metron anthrōpou, ho estin angelou). This parenthetical note assures the hearer that the measurements given in human terms (cubits, stadia) correspond to the angelic measurements. The angel's measuring rod produces results that are intelligible in human units. The dimensions are not alien or untranslatable but correspond to human categories of measurement even though they describe a divine reality.

div.title: Verses 18-21: The Materials of the City
div.p: "The material of the wall was jasper; and the city was pure gold, like clear glass. The foundation stones of the city wall were adorned with every kind of precious stone. The first foundation stone was jasper; the second, sapphire; the third, chalcedony; the fourth, emerald; the fifth, sardonyx; the sixth, sardius; the seventh, chrysolite; the eighth, beryl; the ninth, topaz; the tenth, chrysoprase; the eleventh, jacinth; the twelfth, amethyst. And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; each one of the gates was a single pearl. And the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass."

"The material of the wall was jasper; and the city was pure gold, like clear glass" (kai he endomēsis tou teichous autēs iaspis, kai he polis chrysion katharon homoion hualō katharō). The wall is built of jasper (iaspis) — the same stone that characterized God's appearance on the throne (4:3) and the city's brilliance (21:11). The jasper wall is a wall made of the substance of God's visible glory. The city itself is chrysion katharon ("pure gold"), but this gold is described as homoion hualō katharō ("like pure/clear glass") — transparent. Gold that is transparent is not ordinary gold; it is gold that has been transfigured, purified beyond any earthly counterpart. The transparency of the city's gold means that the divine glory within is not obscured by the structure that contains it. The city is luminous because its very material transmits light rather than blocking it.

"The foundation stones of the city wall were adorned with every kind of precious stone" (hoi themeleioi tou teichous tēs poleōs panti lithō timiō kekosmēmenoi). The verb kekosmēmenoi ("adorned, decorated") is the same word used for the bride's adornment in 21:2. The foundations are adorned as the bride is adorned — reinforcing the identity of city and bride. The foundations are kekosmēmenoi panti lithō timiō ("adorned with every precious stone"), echoing Ezekiel 28:13 (LXX), where the king of Tyre is described as having been "in Eden, the garden of God; every precious stone (panti lithō timiō) was your covering" — followed by a list of stones. The author draws on the paradise tradition: the materials of the new Jerusalem recall the adornment of Eden. The precious stones that decorated the primordial garden now build the eschatological city.
The twelve foundation stones: The list of twelve precious stones has two primary backgrounds in Israel's scriptures.
First, the high priest's breastpiece (choshen) in Exodus 28:17-20 (LXX) contained twelve stones arranged in four rows of three, each inscribed with the name of one of the twelve tribes:
Row 1: sardion (sardius/carnelian), topazion (topaz), smaragdos (emerald)
Row 2: anthrax (carbuncle), sappheiros (sapphire), iaspis (jasper)
Row 3: ligurios (ligure/jacinth), achatēs (agate), amethystos (amethyst)
Row 4: chrysolithos (chrysolite), beryllion (beryl), onychion (onyx)

The correspondence between Exodus 28 and Revelation 21 is not exact in order, but the overlap in stones is extensive. The new Jerusalem's foundations are made of the same materials as the high priest's breastpiece. The high priest bore the names of the twelve tribes on his chest as he entered God's presence; the new Jerusalem bears the names of the twelve tribes on its gates and is built from the materials of the priestly garment. The entire city is what the high priest was: the mediating structure that brings God's people into God's presence.

Second, Isaiah 54:11-12 (LXX) describes the restored Jerusalem: "Behold, I am about to set your stones with antimony, and your foundations (tous themelious sou) with sapphires (sappheirois). I will make your battlements of rubies (iaspin), your gates of crystal stones (lithous krystallou), and your entire wall of choice stones (lithous eklektous)." Isaiah's vision of a jeweled Jerusalem is the immediate prophetic source for Revelation's description. The author expands Isaiah's brief list into the full twelve-stone inventory, integrating the Exodus breastpiece tradition.

The twelve stones, listed in order — jasper, sapphire, chalcedony, emerald, sardonyx, sardius, chrysolite, beryl, topaz, chrysoprase, jacinth, amethyst — represent the full spectrum of precious stones known in the ancient world. Each foundation stone is different, yet all are precious. The variety communicates the comprehensive beauty and richness of the new Jerusalem, while the number twelve maintains the covenant structure.

"And the twelve gates were twelve pearls; each one of the gates was a single pearl" (kai hoi dōdeka pylōnes dōdeka margaritai; ana heis hekastos tōn pylōnōn ēn ex henos margaritou). Each gate is a single pearl (margaritēs) of extraordinary size. The pearl was among the most valued luxury items in the ancient world. In Matthew 13:45-46, the kingdom of heaven is compared to "a merchant seeking fine pearls, who, upon finding one pearl of great value (hena polytimon margaritēn), went and sold all that he had and bought it." The gates made of single pearls declare that the entrance to God's city is of incalculable value.

The pearl also creates a pointed contrast with the harlot's adornment. In 17:4, the harlot was "adorned with gold and precious stones and pearls" (margaritais). In 18:12, pearls were among her traded luxury goods. In 18:16, the mourners lamented the loss of her pearls. The pearls that were the harlot's display of exploitative wealth now form the gates of the new Jerusalem. What Babylon consumed for vanity, the new city integrates into its sacred structure. The same materials appear in both contexts, but their function is transformed: from adornment of the exploiter to gateway for the redeemed.

"And the street of the city was pure gold, like transparent glass" (kai he plateia tēs poleōs chrysion katharon hōs hyalos diaugēs). The plateia ("broad street, main thoroughfare") is the public space of the city — the place where citizens walk, gather, and conduct their common life. The street is the same transparent gold as the city itself (21:18). The public life of the new Jerusalem takes place on ground that transmits the divine glory. The word diaugēs ("transparent, translucent") emphasizes the clarity: the gold does not merely gleam but allows light to pass through. The street of the city will reappear in 22:2, where the river of the water of life flows "in the middle of its street" and the tree of life stands on either side. The transparent golden street, the crystal river, and the healing tree together constitute the public landscape of the new creation.

div.title: Verses 22-23: No Temple, No Sun — God and the Lamb as Temple and Light
div.p: "I saw no temple in it, for the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple. And the city has no need of the sun or of the moon to shine on it, for the glory of God has illumined it, and its lamp is the Lamb."

"I saw no temple in it" (kai naon ouk eidon en autē). This is the most radical departure from Ezekiel's eschatological vision. Ezekiel 40-48 devoted nine chapters to the detailed description, measurement, and regulation of the eschatological temple. The temple was the center of Ezekiel's restored city — the place where God's glory returned (Ezekiel 43:1-7), where sacrifice resumed (Ezekiel 43:18-27), and where the river of life originated (Ezekiel 47:1-12). The absence of a temple in the new Jerusalem is therefore not an oversight but a deliberate, theologically charged revision of Ezekiel's vision.

The naos is the inner sanctuary — the most sacred part of the temple, the chamber that housed God's presence. Throughout this document, the naos has appeared as the heavenly temple from which judgments proceed (11:19, 14:15, 14:17, 15:5-8, 16:1, 16:17). The heavenly temple was the source of the seals, trumpets, and bowls. In 11:19, when the seventh trumpet sounded, "the temple of God which is in heaven was opened; and the ark of his covenant appeared in his temple." The ark, hidden since the destruction of Solomon's temple in 586 BCE, was revealed in the heavenly naos.

But now the naos is absent. The reason is stated: "the Lord God the Almighty and the Lamb are its temple" (ho gar kyrios ho theos ho pantokratōr naos autēs estin, kai to arnion). God and the Lamb are the naos. The function of the temple — to provide the locus of God's presence, the place where God can be encountered — is fulfilled by God and the Lamb themselves. There is no need for a mediating structure because the reality that the structure mediated is now directly present. The temple was always a concession to the gap between God and humanity; when the gap is closed by God's direct dwelling with his people (21:3), the concession becomes unnecessary.

The title ho pantokratōr ("the Almighty") is drawn from the LXX's standard rendering of the Hebrew Yahweh Tsebaoth ("LORD of hosts"). It appears nine times in this document (1:8; 4:8; 11:17; 15:3; 16:7, 14; 19:6, 15; 21:22), more than in any other New Testament book. The Almighty who sits on the throne and the Lamb who was slain together constitute what the temple was. The yoking of God and the Lamb as joint temple corresponds to their joint occupancy of the throne (22:1, 3) and their joint reception of worship (5:13).

"And the city has no need of the sun or of the moon to shine on it, for the glory of God has illumined it, and its lamp is the Lamb" (kai hē polis ou chreian echei tou hēliou oude tēs selēnēs, hina phainōsin autē; hē gar doxa tou theou ephōtisen autēn, kai ho lychnos autēs to arnion). The source is Isaiah 60:19-20 (LXX): "The sun shall no longer be your light by day (eis phōs hēmeras), nor shall the brightness of the moon give you light (eis phōs nyktos); but the LORD will be to you an everlasting light (phōs aiōnion), and God will be your glory (doxan). Your sun shall no longer go down, and your moon shall not be withdrawn; for the LORD will be your everlasting light (phōs aiōnion), and the days of your mourning will be completed." Isaiah's vision of Jerusalem illuminated by God's own light is adopted and applied to the new Jerusalem. The verbal parallels are precise: no sun, no moon, God's glory (doxa) as the illumination.

The author adds a characteristic detail: "its lamp is the Lamb" (ho lychnos autēs to arnion). The lychnos ("lamp") has appeared throughout the document. In 1:12-13, the seven golden lampstands (lychniai) represented the seven assemblies, and the risen Christ walked among them. In 2:5, the threat to Ephesus was removal of her lampstand. In 18:23, one of the silenced features of fallen Babylon was "the light of a lamp (phōs lychnou) will not shine in you any longer." In the new Jerusalem, the lamp is the Lamb himself. Where Babylon's lamp went out, the Lamb provides eternal light. The Lamb who was slain (5:6, 12) and is now the living one (1:18) illuminates the city not with reflected glory but as the source of light. The doxa tou theou ("glory of God") is the comprehensive illumination; the Lamb is the specific lamp through which that glory shines upon the city's inhabitants.

The absence of sun and moon does not mean that these created bodies are destroyed but that their function — providing light — is superseded. In the old creation, God made the sun and moon as luminaries to govern day and night (Genesis 1:14-18). In the new creation, God himself provides what the luminaries provided. The created mediators of light are replaced by the Creator himself as the direct source of illumination. This parallels the absence of the temple: just as the mediating structure of the temple is replaced by God's direct presence, so the mediating luminaries are replaced by God's direct light. Every intermediary between God and his people is removed.

div.title: Verses 24-27: The Nations, the Open Gates, and the Exclusion of the Unclean
div.p: "The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it. In the daytime (for there will be no night there) its gates will never be shut; and they will bring the glory and the honor of the nations into it; and nothing unclean, and no one who practices abomination and lying, shall ever come into it, but only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life."

"The nations will walk by its light, and the kings of the earth will bring their glory into it" (kai peripatēsousin ta ethnē dia tou phōtos autēs, kai hoi basileis tēs gēs pherousin tēn doxan autōn eis autēn). The source is Isaiah 60:3 (LXX): "Nations (ethnē) shall walk (poreuontai) by your light (tō phōti sou), and kings (basileis) by the brightness of your rising (tē lamprotēti sou)." Isaiah 60 is the great oracle of Zion's glory: the nations stream to Jerusalem's light, kings bring tribute, the wealth of the nations pours in, and God's glory illuminates the city. The author of Revelation applies Isaiah 60's vision directly to the new Jerusalem. The nations that walk by the city's light and the kings who bring their glory are the fulfillment of Isaiah's prophetic expectation.

The phrase "the kings of the earth" (hoi basileis tēs gēs) has appeared throughout this document in a predominantly negative role: they committed immorality with the harlot (17:2, 18:3, 9), they waged war against the rider (19:19), they were slain by the sword from his mouth (19:21). The appearance of "kings of the earth" bringing their glory into the new Jerusalem creates a tension that the author does not resolve through explanation but through the transformative logic of the new creation. The kings of the earth — the category of those who wielded political power — are now depicted not as rebels or harlot-partners but as pilgrims bringing tribute to the holy city. The prophetic vision of Isaiah 60 envisions the conversion and willing submission of the nations' rulers. In the new creation, political power is not abolished but redirected: it flows toward God's city rather than toward Babylon.

Isaiah 60:5 (LXX): "The wealth (ploutos) of the sea shall be turned to you, and the wealth of nations (ploutos ethnōn) shall come to you." Isaiah 60:11 (LXX): "Your gates shall be open continually; they shall not be shut day or night, to bring to you the wealth of nations (dynamin ethnōn) and their kings led in procession (basileis agomenous)." The author of Revelation follows Isaiah's vision point by point: the nations' wealth flows in, the gates stand open, kings approach in willing tribute.

"In the daytime (for there will be no night there) its gates will never be shut" (kai hoi pylōnes autēs ou mē kleisthōsin hēmeras, nyx gar ouk estai ekei). Gates in an ancient city were shut at night for security — to prevent enemy attack under cover of darkness. The statement that the gates "will never be shut" (ou mē kleisthōsin, the strongest form of Greek negation with the aorist subjunctive) declares permanent accessibility. No enemy threatens. No darkness provides cover for assault. There is no night (nyx gar ouk estai) in the new Jerusalem because God's glory provides constant illumination (21:23). The perpetual openness of the gates communicates both security (no threat requires closure) and welcome (access is always available).

The source again is Isaiah 60:11 (LXX): "Your gates shall be open (anoichthēsontai) continually (dia pantos); day and night (hēmeras kai nyktos) they shall not be shut (ou kleisthēsontai)." Isaiah says the gates stay open day and night; the author of Revelation says the gates stay open because there is no night at all. The author intensifies Isaiah's promise: Isaiah's city still has night, but the gates remain open despite it; the new Jerusalem eliminates night altogether.

"And they will bring the glory and the honor of the nations into it" (kai oisousin tēn doxan kai tēn timēn tōn ethnōn eis autēn). The nations' doxa ("glory") and timē ("honor, value") are brought into the city. Isaiah 60:5-7 describes this tribute in material terms: camels, gold, frankincense, flocks of Kedar, rams of Nebaioth. Isaiah 60:13: "The glory of Lebanon (hē doxa tou Libanou) will come to you, the juniper, the box tree and the cypress together, to beautify the place of my sanctuary." The "glory and honor" of the nations is what is best, most valuable, and most worthy in the nations' produce and culture. In the new creation, these are not destroyed or rejected but gathered into the holy city. What was exploited and corrupted by Babylon — the wealth and produce of the nations (18:11-13) — is now offered to God in the new Jerusalem.

"And nothing unclean, and no one who practices abomination and lying, shall ever come into it" (kai ou mē eiselthē eis autēn pan koinon kai ho poiōn bdelygma kai pseudos). The double negation ou mē ("by no means, never") is again the strongest available negation. Three categories are excluded: the koinon ("common, profane, unclean"), the one who practices bdelygma ("abomination," the LXX term for idolatrous practices), and the one who practices pseudos ("falsehood, lying," connected to the dragon's deceptive program, 12:9).

The word koinon ("common, profane") in its technical sense means "ritually unclean, not consecrated." In the LXX and first-century Jewish usage, koinon designates what has not been set apart for God's purposes — the opposite of hagion ("holy"). The holy city excludes everything profane. The word bdelygma ("abomination") appeared in 17:4-5, where the harlot's cup was "full of abominations" and her title included "the mother of the abominations of the earth." Abomination characterizes the harlot's system; it has no place in the bride's city. The word pseudos ("lie, falsehood") connects to the 144,000, in whose mouths "no lie (pseudos) was found" (14:5), and contrasts with the dragon, the father of deception, and with "all liars" who face the second death (21:8).

The exclusion statement does not describe an ongoing policing action but defines the character of the new Jerusalem. The city is constitutionally holy; its nature precludes the presence of the unclean, the abominable, and the false. This is not a border patrol but an ontological reality: what is unholy cannot exist in the space defined by God's unmediated presence.

"But only those who are written in the Lamb's book of life" (ei mē hoi gegrammenoi en tō bibliō tēs zōēs tou arniou). The book of life (to biblion tēs zōēs) has appeared at critical moments throughout the document. In 3:5, the overcomer at Sardis is promised: "I will not erase his name from the book of life." In 13:8: "All who dwell on the earth will worship [the beast], everyone whose name has not been written from the foundation of the world in the book of life of the Lamb who has been slain." In 17:8: those who marvel at the beast are those "whose name has not been written in the book of life from the foundation of the world." In 20:12, 15: the book of life was opened at the great white throne judgment, and "if anyone's name was not found written in the book of life, he was thrown into the lake of fire."

The book of life determines entry to the new Jerusalem. The criterion for belonging in the holy city is not tribal identity, moral achievement, or ritual purity in isolation, but inscription in the Lamb's book. The book belongs to the Lamb (tou arniou) — it is his possession, his record, his determination of who belongs to his community. The genitive tou arniou identifies the Lamb as the one whose death and resurrection (5:6, 9) constituted the purchase of the people whose names are recorded. The entire document has moved toward this conclusion: the Lamb's redemptive act creates a people, and that people constitutes the new Jerusalem.

div.title: Summary of the Chapter's Argument
div.p: Revelation 21 presents the culmination of the entire document's narrative and theological movement. Everything that has preceded — the messages to the seven assemblies, the seal and trumpet and bowl judgments, the war between the dragon and the Lamb, the fall of Babylon, the destruction of the beast and false prophet, the binding and final defeat of the dragon, the great white throne judgment, the destruction of death itself — leads to this: a new heaven and a new earth, the holy city descending from God, and God dwelling directly with his people.
The chapter's internal structure moves through four major sections:

First (21:1-2), the seer witnesses the appearance of the new creation. The first heaven and first earth have passed away. The sea — source of chaos, origin of the beast, barrier between God and creation — is no more. The holy city, new Jerusalem, descends from heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband. The direction is downward: God's city comes to humanity, not the reverse.

Second (21:3-8), a voice from the throne declares the theological center of the new creation: God's tabernacle is with humanity, and he will dwell with them. The covenant formula — "they shall be his people, and God himself will be among them" — is fulfilled in its ultimate form. The consequences are comprehensive: tears wiped away, death abolished, mourning and crying and pain eliminated. God declares "I am making all things new" and authenticates the declaration as "faithful and true." The Alpha and Omega offers the water of life freely. The overcomer inherits all things and becomes God's son. Those who capitulated to the beast's system — the cowardly, faithless, abominable, and their companions — face the second death. The two destinies presented throughout the document reach their final expression.

Third (21:9-21), one of the seven bowl-angels — in deliberate mirror of the harlot-showing of 17:1 — invites John to see the bride, the wife of the Lamb. John is carried in the Spirit to a great and high mountain (contrasting the wilderness of 17:3) and shown the holy city in detail. The city has God's glory, radiant like crystal-clear jasper. Its wall has twelve gates inscribed with the twelve tribes' names (the covenant people) and twelve foundations inscribed with the twelve apostles' names (the apostolic witness). The city is measured as a perfect cube — the shape of the Holy of Holies — twelve thousand stadia per side. Its wall measures 144 cubits (12 x 12). Every dimension encodes the covenant number twelve and its multiples. The materials — jasper, gold transparent as glass, the twelve precious stones of the foundations, the pearl gates — draw simultaneously on the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28), Isaiah's jeweled Jerusalem (Isaiah 54:11-12), and Ezekiel's garden of Eden (Ezekiel 28:13). The city is at once temple, garden, and bride.

Fourth (21:22-27), two absences define the new Jerusalem's character: no temple and no sun or moon. God and the Lamb are the temple — the mediating structure is replaced by the unmediated presence. God's glory is the light, and the Lamb is the lamp — the mediating luminaries are replaced by the direct source. The nations walk by this light, and the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city — Isaiah 60's vision of the nations streaming to Zion's light is fulfilled. The gates are never shut because there is no night, no threat, no enemy. The glory and honor of the nations flow into the city. Nothing unclean, no practitioner of abomination or falsehood, enters — only those written in the Lamb's book of life.

The chapter's function within the document is to present the positive counterpart to everything that has been judged and destroyed. The new Jerusalem is the anti-Babylon: where Babylon was adorned with stolen luxury, the new Jerusalem is built of materials that express God's glory; where Babylon was filled with the blood of the saints, the new Jerusalem is filled with God's presence; where Babylon's merchants traded in human souls, the new Jerusalem offers the water of life freely; where Babylon's sorcery deceived the nations, the new Jerusalem draws the nations to walk in God's light; where Babylon sat as a harlot on the beast, the new Jerusalem descends as a bride from God. Every feature of the new Jerusalem corresponds inversely to a feature of fallen Babylon.

The chapter also represents the resolution of the entire biblical narrative as the author and his first-century audience would have understood it. The new creation reverses Genesis 3: death, pain, the curse, and the exile from God's presence are undone. The tabernacle and temple traditions of Exodus and 1 Kings find their fulfillment: God's dwelling with humanity, which required elaborate structures and restricted access, is now direct and universal. The prophetic visions of Isaiah, Ezekiel, and Zechariah — the new heavens and earth, the jeweled city, the measured temple, the nations streaming to Zion — converge and are realized. The covenant formula of Leviticus, Jeremiah, and Ezekiel — "I will be their God and they will be my people" — reaches its definitive expression.

For the first-century hearers in the assemblies of Asia, living under the beast's pressure, tempted by the harlot's luxury, facing the choice between the beast's mark and the Lamb's seal, this chapter declares the outcome for those who overcome. The city they are being asked to hold out for is not a vague hope but a detailed reality — measured, adorned, illuminated, inhabited by God himself. The choice is between Babylon, which is already fallen (14:8, 18:2), and the new Jerusalem, which is already descending. The present suffering of the assemblies is framed by the permanent reality of God's dwelling with his people. The document's final vision answers the document's opening demand: be faithful, overcome, and this is what you inherit.

div.title: Revelation 22 — First-Century Reading
Context and Placement
div.p: What the author was arguing immediately before (Revelation 21): Chapter 21 narrated the appearance of the new creation and the descent of the new Jerusalem. The first heaven and first earth had passed away, the sea was no more, and the holy city came down out of heaven from God, prepared as a bride adorned for her husband (21:1-2). A voice from the throne declared the theological center of the entire new order: "Behold, the tabernacle of God is among men, and he will dwell among them, and they shall be his people, and God himself will be among them" (21:3). Death, mourning, crying, and pain were abolished (21:4). God declared "I am making all things new" and authenticated the words as "faithful and true" (21:5). He identified himself as the Alpha and the Omega, the beginning and the end, and offered the water of life freely to the one who thirsts (21:6). The overcomer was promised inheritance and divine sonship; the cowardly, faithless, abominable, and their companions were assigned to the second death (21:7-8).

One of the seven bowl-angels — in deliberate structural mirror to 17:1, where the same category of angel showed the harlot — invited John to see the bride, the wife of the Lamb (21:9). John was carried in the Spirit to a great and high mountain (contrasting the wilderness of 17:3) and shown the holy city in elaborate detail. The city had God's glory, radiant like crystal-clear jasper (21:11). Its wall had twelve gates inscribed with the names of the twelve tribes of Israel and twelve foundation stones inscribed with the names of the twelve apostles of the Lamb (21:12-14). The city was measured as a perfect cube — twelve thousand stadia per side — the shape of the Holy of Holies in Solomon's temple (1 Kings 6:20), declaring that the entire city is what that innermost sanctum was: the place of God's immediate, unmediated presence (21:15-17). Its materials — jasper, transparent gold, twelve precious foundation stones, pearl gates — drew on the high priest's breastpiece (Exodus 28:17-20), Isaiah's jeweled Jerusalem (Isaiah 54:11-12), and the Eden tradition (Ezekiel 28:13). The entire city is simultaneously temple, garden, and bride (21:18-21).

Two defining absences characterized the new Jerusalem: no temple and no sun or moon. God and the Lamb are the temple; God's glory and the Lamb as its lamp provide all light (21:22-23). The nations walk by this light, the kings of the earth bring their glory into the city, the gates are never shut, nothing unclean enters, and only those written in the Lamb's book of life belong there (21:24-27).

Chapter 21 ended with the vision of the new Jerusalem described architecturally but not yet explored internally. The city has been seen from outside — its shape, dimensions, materials, gates, foundations, and illumination. What remains is the interior: the street, the river, the tree, the throne. Chapter 22 provides this.

How chapter 22 continues the argument: Chapter 22 divides into two distinct sections. The first (22:1-5) completes the new Jerusalem vision that began in 21:9, taking the reader inside the city to show the river of the water of life, the tree of life, the abolition of the curse, and the eternal reign of God's servants. The second (22:6-21) constitutes the closing frame of the entire document — the epilogue that authenticates the prophecy, issues final warnings and invitations, and brings the document to its conclusion with the cry "Come, Lord Jesus" and a grace benediction.

The connection to chapter 21 in the first section is seamless. There is no new visionary marker, no kai eidon ("and I saw"), no meta tauta ("after these things"). The angel who showed the city in 21:9 continues showing in 22:1 (kai edeixen moi, "and he showed me"). The street (plateia) mentioned in 21:21 reappears in 22:2. The throne of God and of the Lamb, present in the city (21:22-23 by implication), is now explicitly located (22:1, 3). The vision flows from the external architecture of chapter 21 to the internal landscape of 22:1-5 without interruption.

The second section (22:6-21) shifts from vision to direct speech, from the new Jerusalem to the present situation of the assemblies receiving the document. This shift corresponds to the document's triple genre identified in chapter 1: it is simultaneously apocalypse (the visions), prophecy (the call to respond), and letter (addressed to specific communities). Chapters 4-22:5 have been predominantly apocalyptic vision. The epilogue returns to the prophetic and epistolary registers, re-engaging the assemblies directly, reinforcing the document's authority, and issuing the final call to faithfulness.

div.title: Verses 1-2: The River and the Tree of Life
div.p: "Then he showed me a river of the water of life, clear as crystal, coming from the throne of God and of the Lamb, in the middle of its street. On either side of the river was the tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit every month; and the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations."

"Then he showed me a river of the water of life, clear as crystal" (kai edeixen moi potamon hydatos zoes lampron hos krystallon). The verb edeixen ("he showed") identifies the angel of 21:9-10 as the continuing guide. The river is described with three elements: it contains the "water of life" (hydor zoes), it is "clear as crystal" (lampron hos krystallon), and it flows from the throne.

The "water of life" (hydor zoes) has been anticipated throughout the document. In 7:17, the Lamb "will guide them to springs of the water of life" (epi zoes pegas hydaton). In 21:6, the one on the throne promised: "I will give to the one who thirsts from the spring of the water of life without cost" (ek tes peges tou hydatos tes zoes dorean). The river of 22:1 is the fulfillment of both promises: the springs to which the Lamb guides and the gift the one on the throne offers are now a river flowing through the city. What was promised to the great multitude in the interlude of chapter 7 and to the thirsty one in chapter 21 is now part of the permanent landscape of the new creation.

The adjective lampron ("bright, radiant, clear") was used for the bride's fine linen in 19:8 (byssinon lampron katharon, "fine linen, bright and clean") and will be used for Christ's self-identification in 22:16 (ho aster ho lampros ho proinos, "the bright morning star"). The river is not merely transparent but radiant — it shines with the quality of the divine presence that permeates the city. The comparison hos krystallon ("like crystal") recalls the "sea of glass like crystal" (thalassa hyaline homoia krystallo) before the throne in 4:6. In chapter 4, the crystalline sea was a barrier between the throne and those before it. In the new Jerusalem, the crystalline substance is not a barrier but a flowing river — the same quality of glassy brilliance, but now in motion, accessible, life-giving. What separated in chapter 4 now nourishes in chapter 22.
The prophetic sources converge from multiple directions.

Ezekiel 47:1-12 is the primary source. In Ezekiel's vision, the prophet was brought to the door of the temple, and "behold, water was flowing from under the threshold of the temple toward the east" (Ezekiel 47:1). The water flowed from the right side of the temple, past the altar, and out the south side of the gate. An angelic guide led Ezekiel through the water as it deepened: ankle-deep, knee-deep, waist-deep, and finally "a river that I could not ford, for the water had risen, enough water to swim in, a river that could not be forded" (47:5). On both banks of the river grew "very many trees" (47:7), and the guide explained: "These waters go out toward the eastern region... and the water becomes fresh... every living creature which swarms in every place where the river goes, will live" (47:8-9). "By the river on its bank, on one side and on the other, will grow all kinds of trees for food. Their leaves will not wither and their fruit will not fail. They will bear every month because their water flows from the sanctuary, and their fruit will be for food and their leaves for healing" (47:12). The verbal and conceptual parallels with Revelation 22:1-2 are extensive: the water flowing from the sanctuary/throne, the trees on both sides of the river, the monthly fruit, the healing leaves.

But the author of Revelation makes critical modifications to Ezekiel's vision. In Ezekiel, the water flows from the temple; in Revelation, there is no temple (21:22), so the water flows from the throne of God and of the Lamb. The author has already established that God and the Lamb have replaced the temple (21:22). The river's source follows this replacement: the function the temple served — as the origin of life-giving water — is now served directly by the throne. In Ezekiel, the river flowed outward from the city toward the Dead Sea; in Revelation, the river flows through the city, in the middle of its street. The life-giving water is not exported to the periphery but fills the center of communal life. In Ezekiel, the trees were "all kinds of trees for food"; in Revelation, the trees become "the tree of life" (to xylon tes zoes) — a specific identification that connects the vision not only to Ezekiel but to Genesis.

Zechariah 14:8 provides a parallel source: "In that day living waters (hydata zonta) will flow out of Jerusalem, half of them toward the eastern sea and the other half toward the western sea; it will be in summer as well as in winter." The "living waters" of Zechariah are perpetual — flowing in all seasons. The river in Revelation 22 is likewise perpetual: the tree yields fruit "every month" (kata mena hekaston), indicating unbroken, continuous supply.

Joel 3:18 (LXX 4:18): "A spring will go out from the house of the LORD and will water the valley of Shittim." Psalm 46:4 (LXX 45:5): "There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy dwelling places of the Most High." The psalm's "river whose streams make glad the city of God" is realized in Revelation 22:1 — the river flows through the city, proceeding from the divine presence.

Genesis 2:10: "Now a river flowed out of Eden to water the garden; and from there it divided and became four rivers." The river in Eden that watered the garden and then divided into the Tigris, Euphrates, Pishon, and Gihon is the prototype. In the new creation, the river again flows from the place of God's presence, but it does not divide — it remains one river, flowing through one city, from one throne. The unity reflects the completeness and wholeness of the new creation: there is no scattering, no division, no branching into remote regions.

"Coming from the throne of God and of the Lamb" (ekporeuomenon ek tou thronou tou theou kai tou arniou). The river's source is the throne, and the throne belongs jointly to God and to the Lamb. The phrase tou theou kai tou arniou ("of God and of the Lamb") presents God and the Lamb as sharing a single throne — not two thrones but one. This shared throne has been anticipated: in 3:21, the overcomer was promised a seat on Christ's throne "as I also overcame and sat down with my Father on his throne"; in 5:6, the Lamb was "in the center of the throne"; in 7:17, "the Lamb in the center of the throne will be their shepherd." The joint occupancy of the throne — God and the Lamb sharing a single seat of sovereignty — is one of the document's most distinctive declarations. The water of life flows from this shared authority: the river proceeds from the unified rule of God and the slain-yet-standing Lamb.

"In the middle of its street" (en meso tes plateias autes). The plateia ("broad street, main thoroughfare") was introduced in 21:21, where it was described as "pure gold, like transparent glass." The river flows down the center of this golden, transparent street. The public, communal space of the city is the location of life-giving water. Access is not restricted, not hidden in an inner chamber, not controlled by priests. The river is in the middle of the street — the most accessible, visible, central location possible.

"On either side of the river was the tree of life" (enteuthen kai ekeithen tou potamou xylon zoes). The phrase enteuthen kai ekeithen ("on this side and on that side," i.e., "on either side") is drawn directly from Ezekiel 47:12 (LXX): "on the river, on its bank, on this side and on that side" (epi tou potamou... enteuthen kai enteuthen). In Ezekiel, the trees on both banks were a plurality — "all kinds of trees." In Revelation, the plural becomes singular with collective force: "the tree of life" (xylon zoes). The singular xylon ("tree, wood") with the genitive zoes ("of life") is the same phrase from Genesis 2:9 (LXX): to xylon tes zoes ("the tree of life"). The shift from Ezekiel's many trees to Genesis's tree of life is the author's most significant interpretive move in these verses. The many trees become the one tree — the specific tree from which humanity was barred after the expulsion from Eden.

The tree of life was promised to the overcomer at Ephesus: "To the one who conquers I will grant to eat of the tree of life, which is in the paradise of God" (2:7). The promise made to the first assembly in the first message is now fulfilled in the last chapter. The tree is accessible, bearing fruit, on both sides of the river — not guarded by cherubim with a flaming sword (Genesis 3:24) but standing openly in the city of God.

"Bearing twelve kinds of fruit, yielding its fruit every month" (poioun karpous dodeka, kata mena hekaston apodidoun ton karpon autou). The twelve kinds of fruit (karpous dodeka) continue the document's structuring number. Twelve gates, twelve angels, twelve tribes, twelve foundations, twelve apostles, twelve thousand stadia, twelve pearls, and now twelve kinds of fruit. The number twelve encodes covenant completeness — the fullness of God's people and God's provision. The tree bears fruit kata mena hekaston ("each month, every month"), indicating perpetual, uninterrupted supply. There is no season of barrenness, no winter, no dormancy. The fruit is always available. Ezekiel 47:12 provides the source: "They will bear every month (kata mena kainon, 'month by month new') because their water flows from the sanctuary."

"And the leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations" (kai ta phylla tou xylou eis therapeian ton ethnon). The word therapeia ("healing, service, care") denotes the restoration of health, the mending of what is damaged. The source is again Ezekiel 47:12 (LXX): "their leaves for healing" (ta phylla autou eis hygiеian, "their leaves for health/healing"). In Ezekiel, the healing leaves suggested the curative properties of the trees watered by the temple stream. In Revelation, the healing is specifically for "the nations" (ton ethnon).

The mention of nations requiring healing in the new creation raises a question: if death, mourning, crying, and pain have been abolished (21:4), what healing remains? The word therapeia does not necessarily denote the curing of disease in a narrow clinical sense. In the LXX, the semantic range includes restoration, service, and care. The leaves serve the nations' therapeia — their ongoing restoration, their continuous renewal. The prophets anticipated the healing of the nations as part of the eschatological vision: Malachi 4:2 (LXX 3:20): "The sun of righteousness will rise with healing in its wings" (iasis en tais pterxyin autou). Isaiah 19:22: "The LORD will strike Egypt, striking and healing" (pataxei kyrios tous Aigyptious plege megale, kai iasetai autous iasei). The nations that walked in darkness (Isaiah 60:3), that were deceived by Babylon's sorcery (18:23), that were made drunk with the harlot's wine (17:2), now receive therapeia — the ongoing healing and restoration that comes from the tree watered by the river from the throne.

The tree of life with its healing leaves for the nations also serves as the final answer to the curse of Genesis 3. The tree that was forbidden is now accessible. The nations that were scattered at Babel (Genesis 11) and deceived by the dragon (12:9) are now healed. The river that watered Eden now flows from the throne. The entire Genesis narrative of creation, fall, curse, and exile is reversed.

div.title: Verses 3-5: No More Curse — The Servants' Eternal Reign
div.p: "There will no longer be any curse. The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it, and his bond-servants will serve him; they will see his face, and his name will be on their foreheads. And there will no longer be any night; and they will not have need of the light of a lamp nor the light of the sun, because the Lord God will illumine them; and they will reign forever and ever."

"There will no longer be any curse" (kai pan katathema ouk estai eti). The word katathema ("curse, accursed thing") is related to anathema, the LXX term for what is devoted to destruction — the ban (Hebrew cherem) that required the total destruction of cursed objects or persons. The declaration that "there will no longer be any curse" reverses the foundational curse of Genesis 3:14-19. In Genesis 3:14, God cursed the serpent. In 3:17, God cursed the ground "because of you" (dia se). In 3:19, the consequence is death: "you are dust, and to dust you shall return." The curse brought enmity, pain in childbirth, thorns and thistles, toilsome labor, and death. The entire created order was subjected to the effects of the curse.

Zechariah 14:11 (LXX) provides the direct prophetic source: "There will no longer be any curse (anathema)" (kai ouk estai anathema eti), using the same construction. Zechariah's oracle envisions the eschatological Jerusalem as a place where the curse — the ban of destruction — is permanently lifted. The author of Revelation follows Zechariah's language precisely.

The abolition of the curse in 22:3 completes a chain of reversals that runs through 21:1-22:5. The sea is no more (21:1) — the source of chaos eliminated. Death, mourning, crying, and pain are no more (21:4) — the consequences of the curse eliminated. There is no temple (21:22) — the mediating structure eliminated. There is no sun or moon needed (21:23) — the mediating luminaries eliminated. There is no night (22:5) — the domain of darkness eliminated. And now there is no curse (22:3) — the root cause of all the others eliminated. The series of negations (ouk... eti, "no longer") traces the dismantling of the fallen order back to its origin: the curse itself is removed, and with it, every consequence that flowed from it.

"The throne of God and of the Lamb will be in it" (kai ho thronos tou theou kai tou arniou en aute estai). The throne — the seat of divine sovereignty — is within the city. The shared throne of God and the Lamb (tou theou kai tou arniou) was established in 22:1 as the source of the river. Now its location is confirmed: it is in the city, among the inhabitants. The throne that appeared in heaven in 4:2, surrounded by living creatures and elders, is now in the new Jerusalem on earth. The descent of the city from heaven (21:2, 10) has brought the throne from heaven to earth. What was above is now among. The vision of chapters 4-5 — God on the throne, the Lamb in the center of the throne — is now the permanent, accessible reality of the new creation.

"And his bond-servants will serve him" (kai hoi douloi autou latreusousin auto). The verb latreuō ("to serve, to worship, to render sacred service") in the LXX is the technical term for priestly, liturgical service. Exodus 3:12: "You shall serve (latreusete) God on this mountain." Deuteronomy 6:13: "You shall fear the LORD your God and serve (latreuseis) him." Deuteronomy 10:12: "What does the LORD your God require of you, but to fear the LORD your God, to walk in all his ways, to love him, and to serve (latreuein) the LORD your God with all your heart and with all your soul." The word combines worship and service; it is the activity of the priest before God and the faithful Israelite in daily devotion. The bond-servants (douloi) are those who have been identified throughout the document as God's faithful people: 1:1 ("to show to his bond-servants"), 7:3 ("the bond-servants of our God"), 19:2 ("the blood of his bond-servants"), 19:5 ("his bond-servants, you who fear him"). Their latreuo — their sacred service-worship — is now performed in the direct presence of God and the Lamb, without temple, without mediating priest, without barrier.

"They will see his face" (kai opsontai to prosopon autou). This is one of the most extraordinary declarations in the entire document. Throughout Israel's scriptures, seeing God's face was understood as impossible for mortal humanity. Exodus 33:20: "You cannot see my face (to prosopon mou), for no man can see me and live (ou dynatai anthropos idein to prosopon mou kai zesai)." When Moses asked to see God's glory, God placed him in the cleft of a rock and covered him with his hand, allowing Moses to see only God's back: "You shall see my back (ta opiso mou), but my face (to prosopon mou) shall not be seen" (Exodus 33:23). Even Moses — the greatest prophet, who spoke with God "face to face" (Exodus 33:11; Deuteronomy 34:10) — was denied the full vision of God's face. The phrase "face to face" (prosopon pros prosopon) in Exodus 33:11 described the intimacy of the encounter, not the literal sight of God's face, as the same chapter makes explicit in 33:20.

The promise that God's servants "will see his face" reverses this prohibition entirely. What was lethal is now life-giving. What was hidden is now revealed. What was granted partially to one prophet is now given fully to all the bond-servants. The change is possible because the conditions have changed: in the old order, sinful humanity could not survive direct contact with the holy God. In the new creation, the curse is abolished (22:3), nothing unclean enters (21:27), and the bond-servants have been purified through the Lamb's blood (7:14) and clothed in righteous deeds (19:8). The barrier between God's holiness and human frailty has been removed.

The priestly blessing of Numbers 6:25-26 (LXX) anticipated this: "The LORD make his face (to prosopon autou) shine upon you (epiphanai... epi se) and be gracious to you; the LORD lift up his countenance (to prosopon autou) upon you and give you peace." The priestly blessing pronounced God's face-turned-toward-his-people as the source of grace and peace. In the new Jerusalem, the priestly blessing is no longer a spoken prayer but a lived reality: the servants see the face that was invoked but never seen.

Psalm 17:15 (LXX 16:15): "As for me, I shall behold your face (opsomai to prosopon sou) in righteousness; I will be satisfied when I awake with your likeness." Psalm 11:7 (LXX 10:7): "The upright will behold his face (opsontai to prosopon autou)." These psalmic hopes — the longing to see God's face, expressed as the highest possible aspiration of the righteous — are now declared fulfilled. The psalmist hoped; the bond-servants see.

"And his name will be on their foreheads" (kai to onoma autou epi ton metopon auton). The name on the forehead has been a defining image throughout the document. In 7:3, the bond-servants of God were sealed "on their foreheads" (epi ton metopon) before the trumpet judgments. In 9:4, the locust-plague was restricted from harming those "who have the seal of God on their foreheads." In 14:1, the 144,000 on Mount Zion had "his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads" (to onoma autou kai to onoma tou patros autou gegrammenon epi ton metopon auton). The mark of the beast was placed on the right hand or the forehead (13:16); the seal of God was placed on the forehead alone. The contrast has been sustained throughout: two marks, two allegiances, two identities.

In 22:4, the name on the foreheads is definitive and permanent. The seal that protected in chapter 7, the name that identified in chapter 14, is now inscribed as the permanent mark of belonging in the new creation. The forehead is the most visible part of the person — the name cannot be hidden. The bond-servants belong to God openly, completely, and permanently.

The background in Israel's priestly tradition is Exodus 28:36-38. The high priest wore a golden plate on his forehead inscribed "Holy to the LORD" (hagion to kyrio, LXX). The plate was the outward sign that the priest was consecrated, set apart for divine service. In the new Jerusalem, every bond-servant bears what only the high priest once bore. The entire community is priestly — which is precisely what the document has declared from the beginning: the Lamb "has made us to be a kingdom, priests to his God and Father" (1:6); "you have made them to be a kingdom and priests to our God; and they will reign upon the earth" (5:10). The name on the foreheads is the visible enactment of this universal priesthood.

"And there will no longer be any night" (kai nyx ouk estai eti). The absence of night was stated in 21:25 as the reason the gates need never be shut. Here in 22:5 it is restated as a feature of life in the city. The elimination of night removes the domain of darkness, the time of danger, the period of diminished sight. In the document's symbolic geography, darkness has been associated with the beast's kingdom: the fifth bowl was poured out on the beast's throne, and "his kingdom became darkened" (eskotomene, 16:10). The absence of night in the new Jerusalem corresponds to the absence of everything the darkness represented — the domain of evil, the cover for deception, the time of fear.

"And they will not have need of the light of a lamp nor the light of the sun" (kai ouk echousin chreian photos lychnou kai photos heliou). This restates 21:23 with a slight expansion. The two sources of light in the old order — artificial (lychnou, "lamp") and natural (heliou, "sun") — are both superseded. The contrast with Babylon is pointed: in 18:23, one of the marks of Babylon's destruction was that "the light of a lamp (phos lychnou) will not shine in you any longer." In Babylon, the lamp went out as a sign of judgment. In the new Jerusalem, the lamp is not needed because a greater light has come. What Babylon lost through judgment, the new Jerusalem transcends through glory.

"Because the Lord God will illumine them" (hoti kyrios ho theos photisei ep' autous). The source is Isaiah 60:19 (LXX): "The LORD will be to you an everlasting light (phos aionion), and God will be your glory (doxan)." Also Psalm 36:9 (LXX 35:10): "In your light we see light" (en to photi sou opsometha phos). God himself is the source of illumination. The verb photizō ("to illumine, to give light to, to enlighten") describes a direct, unmediated act: God shines upon (ep' autous, "upon them") his servants. The created intermediaries — sun, moon, lamp — are replaced by the Creator himself as the direct source of light, just as the temple was replaced by God and the Lamb as the direct location of his presence.

"And they will reign forever and ever" (kai basileusousin eis tous aionas ton aionon). The verb basileuo ("to reign, to exercise royal authority") reaches its final expression here. The promise of reign has run through the entire document:
1:6 — "he has made us to be a kingdom, priests to his God and Father" (epoiesen hemas basileian, hiereis to theo kai patri autou)
5:10 — "you have made them to be a kingdom and priests to our God; and they will reign upon the earth" (basileusousin epi tes ges)
20:4 — the faithful "came to life and reigned with Christ for a thousand years" (ebasileusan meta tou Christou chilia ete)
20:6 — "they will be priests of God and of Christ and will reign with him for a thousand years" (basileusousin met' autou ta chilia ete)

The progression is significant. In 1:6 and 5:10, the faithful are declared to be a kingdom and priests who will reign. In 20:4, 6, they reign with Christ for a bounded period — a thousand years. In 22:5, the reign becomes eis tous aionas ton aionon — "unto the ages of the ages," the strongest expression of unending duration available in Greek. This is the same phrase used for God's own eternal existence (4:9-10; 10:6; 15:7) and for the torment of God's enemies (14:11; 19:3; 20:10). The reign of the bond-servants is elevated from the temporal to the eternal, from the millennium to the perpetual, from "with Christ for a thousand years" to "forever and ever." The document's promise to the assemblies reaches its ultimate fulfillment: those who conquer will not merely rule for a bounded period but will reign eternally.

div.title: Verses 6-7: Authentication and the Sixth Beatitude
div.p: "And he said to me, 'These words are faithful and true'; and the Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, sent his angel to show to his bond-servants the things which must soon take place. 'And behold, I am coming quickly. Blessed is he who heeds the words of the prophecy of this book.'"

"These words are faithful and true" (houtoi hoi logoi pistoi kai alethinoi). The authentication formula repeats 21:5, where God himself spoke from the throne: "Write, for these words are faithful and true." The same formula appeared in 19:9: "These are true words of God." The repetition at this juncture marks the transition from the visionary content to the epilogue. The angel authenticates the entire vision — not merely the immediately preceding verses but the document's full content. The adjectives pistoi ("faithful, trustworthy, reliable") and alethinoi ("true, genuine, real") have been applied to Christ himself (3:14, "the faithful and true witness"; 19:11, "Faithful and True") and to God's judgments (16:7; 19:2). The words partake of the character of the one who speaks them.

"The Lord, the God of the spirits of the prophets, sent his angel to show to his bond-servants the things which must soon take place" (ho kyrios, ho theos ton pneumaton ton propheton, apesteilen ton angelon autou deixai tois doulois autou ha dei genesthai en tachei). This sentence deliberately echoes the document's opening verse: "The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him to show to his bond-servants the things which must soon take place" (1:1). The verbal parallels are precise: deixai tois doulois autou ("to show to his bond-servants") and ha dei genesthai en tachei ("the things which must soon take place") appear in both verses. The epilogue returns to the prologue, forming an inclusio — a literary frame that brackets the entire document. What was announced in 1:1 is now confirmed in 22:6: the same chain of revelation (God — angel — servants) remains operative, and the same urgency (en tachei, "soon, quickly") governs the message.

The title "the God of the spirits of the prophets" (ho theos ton pneumaton ton propheton) identifies God as the one who inspires and governs prophetic speech. The "spirits of the prophets" (ta pneumata ton propheton) refers to the prophetic impulse or gift. In 1 Corinthians 14:32, Paul uses the same phrase: "the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets" (pneumata propheton prophetais hypotassetai). The spirits that animate prophetic speech belong to God — he is their source and their sovereign. The author of Revelation thus claims for his document the same authority as the prophetic tradition of Israel: the God who spoke through Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel has spoken through this vision.

"And behold, I am coming quickly" (kai idou erchomai tachy). The speaker shifts abruptly from the angel to Jesus. The words erchomai tachy ("I am coming quickly") are spoken three times in this chapter (22:7, 12, 20), forming a triple declaration that dominates the epilogue. The same verb erchomenos ("the coming one") was used for God's own self-identification in 1:4, 8 ("who is and who was and who is to come"). The word tachy ("quickly, soon, without delay") reinforces the temporal urgency established in 1:1 (en tachei) and 1:3 ("the time is near"). The first-century assemblies are being told that the interval between their present suffering and the consummation they have been shown is short. The imminent return is not a separate topic from the vision; it is the application of the vision to the hearers' present situation.

"Blessed is he who heeds the words of the prophecy of this book" (makarios ho teron tous logous tes propheteias tou bibliou toutou). This is the sixth of seven beatitudes in the document, and it directly echoes the first: "Blessed is the one who reads aloud the words of this prophecy, and blessed are those who hear and keep what is written in it" (1:3). The verb tereo ("to keep, to guard, to heed, to observe") is the same in both verses. The inclusio extends from the blessing to the vocabulary: the document's first and sixth beatitudes use the same words for the same action — keeping the prophecy. The frame declares that the appropriate response to the document is not merely hearing or understanding but keeping — active, sustained obedience to what has been communicated.

The word propheteia ("prophecy") classifies the entire document as prophetic literature, not merely predictive writing. As noted in the analysis of 1:3, prophecy in the biblical tradition demands response and obedience; the document is not information to be filed but instruction to be acted upon.

div.title: Verses 8-9: The Second Worship-Rebuke
div.p: "I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things. And when I heard and saw, I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel who showed me these things. But he said to me, 'Do not do that. I am a fellow servant of yours and of your brethren the prophets and of those who heed the words of this book. Worship God.'"

"I, John, am the one who heard and saw these things" (Kago Ioannes ho akouon kai blepon tauta). John reasserts his identity as the witness, using the first person singular with his proper name, just as he did in 1:9 ("I, John, your brother and fellow partaker in the tribulation and kingdom and perseverance which are in Jesus"). The repetition of the self-identification near the end of the document confirms the named author and closes the literary frame: the same John who introduced himself in chapter 1 now speaks again in chapter 22. The verbs akouon ("hearing") and blepon ("seeing") in the present participle describe his ongoing experience: he is the one who hears and sees. The sensory language reinforces the nature of the document as eyewitness testimony — John reports what he has directly perceived through divinely enabled senses.

"I fell down to worship at the feet of the angel" (epesa proskynесai emprosthen ton podon tou angelou tou deiknuontos moi tauta). This is the second occurrence of John prostrating before an angel. The first was in 19:10, where John "fell at his feet to worship him" (epesa emprosthen ton podon autou proskynесai auto) and was rebuked. The verbal structure is nearly identical. The repetition is not an editorial mistake or an accidental doublet. It is a deliberate narrative device that reinforces the document's central concern: worship.

The fact that John falls a second time after having been corrected once communicates the persistence and subtlety of the temptation to misdirect worship. If even the seer — the one who has received the entire revelation, who has seen the beast and the harlot judged, who has heard the Hallelujah chorus — can again fall into the error of worshiping a creature, the danger is real and ongoing for every hearer. The assemblies in Asia, surrounded by imperial cult worship, by the beast's demand for proskynesis (13:4, 8, 12, 15), by the pervasive religious culture of Greco-Roman polytheism, needed to hear this correction twice.

"I am a fellow servant of yours and of your brethren the prophets and of those who heed the words of this book" (syndoulos sou eimi kai ton adelphon sou ton propheton kai ton terounton tous logous tou bibliou toutou). The angel's self-identification as a syndoulos ("fellow servant") repeats 19:10 but expands the fellowship. In 19:10, the angel said he was a fellow servant of John and "your brethren who hold the testimony of Jesus" (ton adelphon sou ton echonton ten martyrian Iesou). Here in 22:9, the fellowship includes "your brethren the prophets" (ton adelphon sou ton propheton) and "those who heed the words of this book" (ton terounton tous logous tou bibliou toutou). The expansion is significant. The first rebuke identified the community by their content (the testimony of Jesus). The second rebuke identifies the community by their function (the prophets) and their practice (those who keep the words). The angel, the seer, the prophets, and the obedient hearers all share the same status: syndouloi — fellow servants of the same master. None is worthy of worship. Only God is.

"Worship God" (to theo proskyneson). The imperative is identical to 19:10. The repetition drives home the point: the proper response to the glory of the vision is not to worship the messenger but to worship God. The command encapsulates the document's entire theological program. From 14:7 ("worship him who made the heaven and the earth") through the contrast between beast-worship and God-worship that structures the entire middle section of the document (chapters 13-14), to the Hallelujah chorus that celebrates God's sole worthiness to reign (19:1-6), the document has been arguing for the exclusive worship of God. The final worship-rebuke seals this argument.

div.title: Verses 10-11: Do Not Seal the Book
div.p: "And he said to me, 'Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book, for the time is near. Let the one who does wrong, still do wrong; and the one who is filthy, still be filthy; and let the one who is righteous, still practice righteousness; and the one who is holy, still keep himself holy.'"

"Do not seal up the words of the prophecy of this book" (Me sphragises tous logous tes propheteias tou bibliou toutou). The instruction is a deliberate contrast with Daniel 12:4, 9. In Daniel 12:4 (LXX), the angel told Daniel: "Shut up the words and seal the book (sphragison to biblion), until the time of the end." In Daniel 12:9: "Go, Daniel, for the words are concealed and sealed (esphragismena) until the time of the end." Daniel's vision was for a distant future; it was to be sealed because the time of fulfillment was not yet. The instruction to John is the opposite: do not seal (me sphragises), because "the time is near" (ho kairos engys estin). The reversal signals that what Daniel anticipated as remote has now arrived. The time of the end that required sealing has given way to the time of fulfillment that demands openness. The prophecy must be heard, not stored away.

The word kairos ("season, appointed time, decisive moment"), as in 1:3, designates not mere chronological passage (chronos) but an epoch of significance. The kairos is engys ("near, at hand") — the decisive moment is pressing upon the present. The assemblies are living in the time to which the prophecy speaks; the words must therefore be accessible and active, not sealed and dormant.

"Let the one who does wrong, still do wrong; and the one who is filthy, still be filthy; and let the one who is righteous, still practice righteousness; and the one who is holy, still keep himself holy" (ho adikon adikesato eti, kai ho rhyparos rhypantheto eti, kai ho dikaios dikaiosynen poiesato eti, kai ho hagios hagiastheto eti). These four statements form a chiastic structure: two negative categories (the one who does wrong, the one who is filthy) and two positive categories (the righteous, the holy). The aorist imperatives (adikesato, "let him do wrong"; rhypantheto, "let him be filthy"; poiesato, "let him practice"; hagiastheto, "let him be holy") are startling in the first two cases. They do not express divine approval of wrongdoing but declare the finality of the present moment's decisions. Because the time is near, because the kairos is engys, the postures people have adopted will define their destiny. There is no neutral ground. The wrongdoer and the filthy person will remain in their condition; the righteous and the holy person will remain in theirs.

The prophetic background is Daniel 12:10 (LXX): "Many will be purged, purified, and refined, but the wicked will act wickedly; and none of the wicked will understand, but those who have insight will understand." Daniel described a time when the trajectories of the wicked and the wise would diverge permanently. The author of Revelation applies the same principle to the present moment of the assemblies: the time for decision is now, and the consequences of that decision are being fixed.

The statements also echo Isaiah 6:9-10, where the prophet's commission included the paradoxical instruction to make the people's hearts dull, their ears heavy, and their eyes dim, "lest they see with their eyes, and hear with their ears, and understand with their hearts, and return and be healed." The hardening dynamic — where continued rejection results in confirmed rejection — is part of the prophetic tradition's understanding of how divine revelation functions. For those who receive it, it illuminates and transforms; for those who reject it, it confirms the rejection. The four statements of 22:11 express this principle as a declaration over the present moment: the revelation has been given, and the response defines the responder.

div.title: Verses 12-13: Coming Soon with Reward — The Alpha and Omega
div.p: "'Behold, I am coming quickly, and my reward is with me, to render to every man according to what he has done. I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end.'"

"Behold, I am coming quickly, and my reward is with me" (idou erchomai tachy, kai ho misthos mou met' emou). The second declaration of "I am coming quickly" (repeated from 22:7). The speaker is the risen Christ. The new element is the phrase "my reward is with me" (ho misthos mou met' emou). The word misthos ("reward, wages, recompense") appears in Isaiah 40:10 (LXX): "Behold, the Lord comes with might (meta ischyos), and his arm with authority; behold, his reward is with him (idou ho misthos autou met' autou), and his work (to ergon) before him." Also Isaiah 62:11 (LXX): "Say to the daughter of Zion, 'Behold, your Savior comes; behold, his reward is with him (idou ho misthos autou met' autou), and his work (to ergon autou) before him.'" Both Isaiah passages describe God coming with his reward already in hand — the recompense is not something he will discover upon arrival but something he brings. The author of Revelation applies these divine-coming passages to the risen Christ, consistent with the document's sustained identification of Christ's coming with YHWH's eschatological arrival.
